The State Boe.rd of Agriculture having extended an invitation to this Grand Body

corner-stone of the superstructure according to ancient form and custom. Although
the weather was excessively we.rm and 11 disagreeable north wind prevailed, a large
concourse of people were present, Including the officers of State in a body. At the
conclusion of the ceremonies we were much rejoiced to receive the congratulations
of distinguished guests, on having well and truly laid the corner-stone of an edifice
destined to mark a new era in the progress of our Golden State.
Our enterprising brethren at Stockton, with a spirit of commendable pride and
true Masonic ambition, determined to erect a new Masonic Temple in that city, and
having ine.ogorated the goodly enterprise, extended a oordle.l lnvit"tlon to the Grand
Lodge to perform the ceremony of laying the corner-stone, and having accepted, the
Grand Lodge convened at Me.sonic Hall for the occasion on the ninth day of June.
The vacant stations and places were filled by appointment from among the brethren
of the various Lodges represented and visiting brethren, and the Grand Body opened
In Ample Form, and on being called to refreshment was formed in proceaslon and
marched to the location of the proposed new Temple under escort of Stockton Com·
mandery of Knights Templar. On arriving at the appointed spot we found that our
zealous brethren had made complete arrangements and taken every precaution to
secure our comfort and facilitate the performance of our mystic rites and ceremonies.
A large and roomy platform had been erected, see.ts were provided, while overhead
were stretched large awnings of canvas which protected the assembly from the scorching rays of the son, thus rendering the performance of the work plee.se.nt and agreeable, notwithstanding lhe excessively heated term which prevailed at that period.
The corner-stone, 11 massive blook of granite, was suspended by 11 strong derrick,
and, at the giving of the Grand Honore, we.a lowered to if.8 final resting place at three
separate intervals, with a regularity and preclsio~ that would have done credit to the
ancient builders who wrought at the building of the original Temple. Having been
duly squared, plumbed and leveled, and cons6cr11ted with the corn of nourishment,
the wine of refreshment, and the oil of joy, it is confidently predicted that npon It
will rest"' beautiful temple which will stand 118 a beaoon·light to the weary and wayworn traveler, a haven to the homeless, the hope of the widow and orpha-n, and an
enduring monument to the untiring and unending indoetr7 and universe.I benevolence
of the craftsmen of tbatjorladiction in particular and of .MllBonry In general. An eloquent and highly Interesting and instructive oration was delivered by Bro. E. H.

Many questions have been a.sired upon Me.sonic faw ang usage, and decisions
invoked upon facts given, which involved either the pointing out or construction
of some rule, regulation, edict or resolution. From among the number the following
are submitted as being probably of sufficient interest to merit your review :1. Is 11 Lodge in duty bound to provide relief for the widow of 11 deceased member, e.fter she has removed from its territorial jurisdiction?
The faot of her removal in no manner relieves the Lodge from its duty and respon·
~ibility to see that she is properly provided for.
2. Application was made for 11 dispensation to re-ballot upon the petition of 11
candidate who had been reje~ted by, and was residing within, the jurisdiction of 11
neighboring subordine.te Lodge. The dispensation was refused.
3. Has 11 Lodge the right to establish a contingent fund from receipts for rent
of its ball!
If the object is to use such fund for other purposes than those of charity and
society, I e.nsw er no.
•
4. Is 11 cube 11 legal substitute for the black ball, and in balloting for candidates
can anything be substitu~d therefor?
There are no me.nde.tory provisions in our laws, the.t I am aware of, respe<itl'ng
the form of the ballot; that Is to say, whether it shall be 11 ball or 11 cnbe. Wherever the matter is referred to In our Constitution and laws, the word '•ball" is used,
from which 11 very proper inference may be drawn that the ballot Is to be in the form
of a be.ll. That the use of white and black balls is proper there can be no question.
That it has long been the custom in this jurisdiction to use cubes is also true, and
there can be no serious objection thereto.
5. Can an appllce.t!on for e.ffiliation be withd.rawn after its reference to a
committee?
No ; unless the committee report e.dversely on account of want of residence
within the jurisdiction of the Lodge. It should be treated in all respects as 11 petition
for the degrees.
6. Mention made of 11 case where the Me.ster of the Lodge decle.red a candidate
rejected upon the first ballot, although but one black ball appeared, without ordering
e. second ballot.
The Lodge was directed to notify 111\ members whc> were present, and also n\l
other members, and at the next stated meeting to again ballot upon the application.
7. A case was reported where A. ballot having been taken and 11 black ball
appearing, the ballot was passed the second time with 11 like result, whereupon the
Master, without declaring the result, 01·dercd a recess; 'after some ten minut~s the
Lodge was again called to order, and another ballot taken, upon the ground that the
Master he.d failed to announce the effect of voting balls e.ud cubes; during the recess,
some of the members who were present at the passing of the ballot the first time,
departed and were not present after recess. Upon the last n.nd third ballot, the
candidate was declared elected. I was asked if such election was legal.
I answered that the passing of the ballot for the third time was irregular and
without authority, and, in my judgment, the election void.
8. Does an appeal stay the execution of 11 sentence of reprimand f

le

Upon this point tho authorities are conflicting. I felt constrained, however, to
hold that an appeal stays the judgment. The matter is important, and should be
carefully considered.
9. Is an applicant who is ruptured eligible for the degrees of Masonry?
One who is ruptnred is not hale and sound in his physical conformation, and
therefore not eligible.
10. Is a member of a Lodge eligible for election as a trial commissioner, if he is
not present at the time and place of election?
Yes; if otherwise qualified.
11. A Lodge cannot rid itself of a member . by granting him a dimit wHhout his
knowledge. No dimit should be granted nnless application therefor is made by the
member or some one authorized by him so to do.
12. A petition for affiliation having been once acted upon, the applicant desiring
to again apply should be required to present e. new and distinct petition.
.
13. At an election of officers, the Master annonnced that no member who was m
. arree.rs for dues should be permitted to vote, or be eligible to any office, notwith·
sie.nding which several brethren who were in arrears· voted, and one of them was
elected Master. I was asked if he could be lege.!!y inbtalled.
I answered that under Section three, of Article one , Part four, of our Constitution,
brethren who are in arrears for dues, are not entitled to vote, nor eligible to office;
tbe.t the election of one who is not eligible is e. void and vain thing. Tbe.t if objection
was made, and the alleged facts established, the Me.ster elect should not be installed.
14. The committeb of a subordinate Lodge propounded the following interrogatoriiS : 1. Is it left discretionary with tho Master of a Lodge to bury or refuse to
bury a Mason whose life has been notoriously licentions t 2. Is a member of a
Lodge compelled to attend the funeral of a Mason of the.t kind, or can h~ use his
discretion?
To the first query I answered no. The right to e. Masonic burial is one that
belongs to every Master Mason who dies while in good standing.
To the second I answered that" I know of no authority which can compel a Mason
to attend the fnneral of a deceased brother; that is to say, we have no law, rule or
regalation '9"hich in terms requires him to do so."
The queries were preceded by a preamble e.nd resolution, which had been offered
for e.doption in the Lodge, and in which preamble it was declared the.t "e. Masonic
burial is the last and highest tribnte of respect we can pay a decee.sed brother, e.nd
to perform our solemn services over the remains of one wboa11 life has been noto·
riously licentious, would be hypooritlcal and e. mere mockery, calculated to bring
Masonry into contempt."
In giving my decision I felt constre.ined to say that if e. Mason Is not considered
too licentious to maintain h is good ste.nding in the Lodge ; not too licentious to be
received and acknowledged as a brother while in life and health , he ought not to be
considered (all at once) as too licentious for Masonic burial whdn dead. Unmasonic
conduct should and will subject him to suspension or expulsion, and if bis brethren
and Lodge countenance i)im while living, and refuse or negleot to suspend or expel
bim, or p erhaps even attempt to do so, they should not, in effect, do so after his
deat.h by refusing bis hody burial with Masonic honors. 'Tis no more a mockery to
bury the dead who have been licentious, than to maintain and uphold the Jiving who
are so. Let the war a.go.inst licentiousness and vice of every nature be made against
the living and not e.gainst the dead.
Upon this decision e. re·heulng was asked and the opinions expressed were re·
afllrmed. I hope it may receive your careful attention.

Accompanied by the Grand Lecturer, on the evening of June sixth I made an
otllcial visit to Banta Rosa Lodge, No. 57, at Santa Rosa. For some time prior to
the visit the peace and harmony of the Lodge had been much disturbed , owing to
the action of one of' the Craftsmen in rejecting material for the temple which all
others deemed the very best and 111ost desirable. The rejection itself was a matter
of exceeding regret to all save one, bnt a more aggravating circumstance was found
In the faot, as alleged, that its author, after admitting the fact, declared that he
would not do so again, and that he hoped an opportanity would be given him to
osbblish the truth of his declarll.lion and sincerity of purpose by the procuring of a
di~peneation; that relying upon such declarations, a dispensation to re-ballot was
procured, and much to the chagrin and mortification of the Lodge, the same result
obtained as before, and was again exposed by ita author, which fact seemed to cause
the Lodge to tremble from its very center, and fraternal forbearance alone restrained
Incautious action. A. very full attendance of the brethren was present, and a de_ep
Interest manifested.
Without reverting directly to the particular cause then agitating the Lodge, the
prinsiples applicable to and which should govern the situu.tion were very thoroughly
and carefully brought to the view of the Lodge, in order that I!. full knowledge and
understanding of them might, if possible, extricate it from the unpleasant situation,
and it is hoped not without benefit. After the Lodge was closed all repaired to a
large dining hall, where a snmptuons repast was spread, which was partaken of with
Joy and gladness. Impromptu speeches followed, good cheer prevailed and much
fraternal feeling and good will was inculcated.
During the year visitations were also made to Reading Lodge, No. 25,, and
Western Star, No. 2.
The manifold dntles incident to a legislative official position, and the practice of a
profession-made unavoidably necessary in the fulfillment of the divine edict, "by
the sweat of thy brow thou shalt eat bread,"-have rendered it ntterly impossible
for me to make other official visitations which would have been exoeedingly pleasant
and agreeu.ble.
Reports have been received from Inspectors of twenty-eight of the thirty-four
Masonic districts within the juriadict!on, and , while all are creditable, many
of them are very full and complete, and show a degree of attention to the duties of
the office which is truly commendable. A careful scrutiny of them discloses evidence
of financial prosperity, increase In membership, and a zealous devotion to the interests of the Craft, which It Is believed has seldom If ever been attained in any preceding year. It is gratifying to know that throughout the jurisdiction the Craft; is
very prosperous. As a rule, peace and h1umony bas prevailed and the exercise of
Masonic discipline has not been necessary.
The meeting of the Triennial Conclave of Knights Templar in the city of San
Prancisco awakened a lively and meritorious Interest, not only among Masons but
among all and the best classes of citizens in the State; and that grand event was
one never to be forgotten as an exhibition of the universality of Masonry; that
fraternal and brotherly love which exists among the members Gf our Ortler, and as a
•triking evidence of ita power for good in the exercise of its most excellent tenetabr.other ly love, relief and truth.
The duties devolving upon your chief executive officer have not diminished during
the year; the station is no sinecure; its duties require constant vigilance and
unceasing attention. The official correspondence has extended to answering over

three hundred letters calling for information, advice and decisions upon nearly every

If the contingent expenses of the Grand t.lRster's ·office have undergone any
change during the year it has been for the worse instead of the better. With a firmness of purpoRe and a resoluteness prompted by the frequent payment of fares over
long routes of travel in pilgrimages to the temple, the repositories of corner-stones,
and in fraternal visitations, as well as perhaps by the prevailing progressive spirit of
the present age , I have fearlessly drawn from the ample stores of our treasury the
full sum of two hundred dollars, set apart as a contingent fuud for the office, believing that to leave any portion of it unappropriated would be an unwholesome precedent for those who may follow after.
My relations and intercourse with the various Grand Officers who have been called
upon to a3sist in the administration of the affairs and business of the Grand Lodge
have been most pleasant and agreeable. I fear not that I shall be charged with par·
tiality when I take pleasure in mentioning the fact that especial thanks are due from
me , and are cheerfully rendered to our Very Worshipful Grand Secretary and Grand
Treasurer, and the Worshipful Grand Lecturer.
The unlimited store of Masonic learning of our Grand Secretary, whose advice,
though frequently sought, has always been given with gentlemanly colll"tesy and
fraternal kindness, has materially asRisted me in the performance of my duties, and
will always be kindly remembered.
Our Grand Treasurer has also been ever ready to aid with advice and counsel,
made valuable by long experience and close observation, and the more so by a full
knowledge of the indisputable fact that his financial ability and undying love for this
Grand Body would prompt him at once to save it harmless from any possible disaster
which his keen foresight had failed to discern.
To the Grand Secretary and Grand Treasurer, and the liberality, untiring, unend·
ing zeal and industry of Bro. JOHN W. SHAEFFER, Worshipful Grand Lecturer, is due
in a marked degree whatever credit may be given this Grand Body upon the occasion
of the Imposing pageant on laying the corner-stone of the Garfield Monument at
Golden Gate Park.
To the efficiency of our Grand Lecturer and bis never-ceasing attention to the
duties of hie office, in lecturing Inspectors and Masters, and to his unbounded devo.
tion to the principles of our Order·and the welfare of this Grand Body, we are deeply
indebted.
Whatever credit may be given, if any, for the prosperity of the Craft during the
period of my administration, may be attributed to the zealous and faithful brethren
who have censtantly as's isted me with both advice and counsel.
With a heart overflowing with gratitude it becomes my. pleasant duty to once
more return to you my sincerf' thanks for the high honor you have heretofore con·
ferred upon me, in elevating me for the second time to the highest and proudest
station within the gift of this Grand Lodge. In the administration of its various and
manifold cares and duties, it has been my constant endeavor to execute the law as I
found it, keeping carefnlly and constantly within the bounds of constitutional
authority, and the rules, regulations , edict.~ and resolutions of this Grand Body, and
executing them· strietly, firmly and impartially and in a spirit of fraternal love and
kindness. That errors may have been committed is not doubted, for 'tis human to
err; but that each and every action was prompted by pure motives and executed
with such ability as I possessed, and under the ' guidance of such lights as were before
me, it Is confidently hoper! the love and charity of my brethren will concede. My
official intercourse with you as Grand Master will cease at the close of this Annual

()/ear Lake Lodge, No. 183, appears to have had an election of officers at the prop·
er time, but no certificate thereof was transmitted to this office. A letter ~rom ite
l:!ecret&ry, dated in.August last, states that, some two months after the election, the
Master elect "informed the Lodge that he would not be able to learn the work, and
the Lodge thought that, as it was so late to procure a dispensation to elect new officers it would be better for the old officers to hold over."
Hill's Ferry Lodge, No. 236 , apparently had an election at the proper time, but,
as will be seen in the foregoing list, sent no certificate·thereof until some four months
afterwards , and that certificate, while it announced the installation of the other officers, briefly stated that " B. D. NoxoN, (the previous Master) holds over-- no installation of Master."
In both these oases, the law appears to have been doubly violated. In the first,
because no certificate of election , &o., was eent to this office, and because , when It
was known that the Master elect could not qualify, the Lodge declined to ask for a
dispensation to elect another, and resolved to allow all ~he officers of .the preceding
year to "hold over;" and , in the second, because the imperfect certificate was not
sent within the proper time, and because that certificate states that the Master of the
previous year " holds over" and was not installed.

.Again it is reported, as it has been for very many years past, that, for the fiscal
year now written of, the annual reports of all the Lodges in the jurisdiction have
been received and all their dues have been paid in full. It has seemed somewhat
singular to the writer that, during a long period back, many Committees on
Correspondence of other Grand Lodges have expressed surprise, wonder, admiration, and other things to which exclamation pointa might be attached , at so simple
a statement as the foregoing. The only explanation is, if any be needed, that the
Grand Secretary takes not a little trouble to see that Secretaries of Lodges properly
perform the duty which the law prescribes for them. When a Lodge report is received, it is carefully examined and compared with that of the preceding year, or,
if necessary, of other years preceding ; and if errors are found the Secretary is at
once notified thereof and corrections are required. If they are not made within a
r easonable period, he gets another letter, and again, if necessary, another or others
until his report is properly corrected . If his report does not come within the time
prescribed by Jaw, he is notified of that fact , and, if necessary, again and again until
it does come. If the dues do not accompany the report, as required by our law,
the Secretary's attention is at once called to that requirement, and, if need be, aga.in

Proceedings of the

[Oct. 9,
1883.J

To the M.·. W.·. Grana Lodge of Oalifarnia:The undersigned herewith presents his annual report of the condition of the
Lodges in this jurisdiction. Relying upon the fidelity and well-known Masonic
knowledge and experience of the Inspeotors of the various Masonic districts, I have
not felt It incumbent on me to give much personal supervision to the Lodges. I
have, as heretofore, instructed such Inspectors and officers of Lodges as have applied
to me, in the work and lectures, and have been gratified to observe the earnest desire
and determination on the part of the applicants to acquire the work correctly.
The general condition of the Lodges throughout the jurisdiction, so far as I can
judge from the reports of the Inspectors, and from conversation and correspon·
dence with their officers, is in the main satisfactory. Rome there are which languish
and show unmistakable signs of decadence, and it would be better if such would
surrender their charters, and their membership be absorbed Into atronger and more
prosperous Lodges. A weak and spiritless Lodge is like a decaying branch upon a
healthy tree-marring its beauty, sapping its vitality, and bearing no fruit. A little
pruning Is an excellent thing occasionally in Masonry as in arboricnltore.
Our system of inspection Is perfect, if it conld only be thoroughly and consistently
carried out. A large majority of our Inspectors are careful, conscientious, pains·
taking officers, who understand their duties and appreciate their responsibilities.
Bntsome, I regret to say, accept this Important position without a thought, apparently,
of the important services required of them, and their resp,osibilities sit as lightly
upon their consciences as does the foam upon the billow's crest; and, for all practical
purposes, they are about as useful as that evanescent substance. I have brought
this matter so often to the attention of the Grand Lodge that I am wearied of the
subject, as, perhaps, my brethren may be also, bot the importance of the matter
induces me to make one more effort to remedy the evil. No brother should accept
the office of Inspector unless be Is able and willing to perform his do ties faithfully
to the best of bis ability. If he finds that he cannot do this, let him at once resign,
in order that the Grand Master may promptly seek another who can and will do bis
doty. It is important that every Lodge in the jurisdiction should be inspeoted at
least once during the year, and its condition reported to the Grand Master and
Grand Lecturer; and this inspection should be thorough and searching-not a mere
informal or cursory examination. It should not only include the manner in which
the work is done, but a careful investigation of the general manner of conducting its
affairs, the condition of the Lodge-room, the method of keeping Its records and
accounts, the charaoter of its membership, financial condition, etc. If this is done,
the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer will be able to present to the Grand Lodge,
annoally, a report of the real condition of every Lodge borne upon its roll; and
thus, if difficulty exists in any quarter, the remedy may be intelligently sought and
efficiently applied.
After all that bas been said in former communications, relative to the importance of
Inspectors sending their reports within the prescribed time, it is discouraging to
find this year so large a number of delinquents. I am at a loss to account for
this neglect of duty on the part of Inspectors, several of whom have hitherto been
very prompt. I have received reports from the Inspectors of the following dis·
tricts, viz.: Nos. 1, 3, 4., 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14., 15, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 2', 25,
· 26, 27, 28, S", 31, 32, and 38, and append the usual abstract therefrom for the infor· ·
mation of the Grand Lodge.

and that all work in harmony.

Inspector IRVING N. M0Gu1BE, of the thirtieth district, reports a very satisfaoto~y
state of atfairs in the five Lodges assigned to him. He says: cc The Lodges within
this district have never been so prosperous 88 during this year. There have been
many valuable acquisitions of new members by initiation; the officers of all the
Lodges have made themselves proficient in their duties, and perform them in a manner creditable alike to themselves and their Lodges."
Inspector JoN.lTH.rn D. HINES, of the thirty-first district, reports that harmony
prevails in the three Lodges under his Inspection; that their business is done aooord·
ing to the requirements of the Grand Lodge; and that their work, though not per·
feet, is fairly done.
Inspector GEOBGE HINDS, of the thirty-second district, reports that he had visited
each of the seven Lodges under his charge, and found the officers profloient, records
well kept, and business properly transacted. The report shows the condition of
each Lodge in detail, and, as is invariably lhe oase with this efficient and valuable
officer is well prepared and exhaustive. The Lodges in this district are generally
prosp~rous, and in some a decided improvement has been made since his last rep~rt
w88 submitted. Anaheim Lodge, No. 207, is indebted to the Masonic Board of Rehef
of San Francisco in the sum of five hundred and sixty-eight dollars. This debt rests
like an incubus upon the Lodge; the brethren acknowledge their obligation, bot
deplore their inability to pay. They have paid about three hundred dollars on ac·
count, but, 88 the revenues of the Lodge are barely sufficient to meet its onrrent
expenses, they can pay no more; and, in view of all the faots, Bro. HINDS recom.
mends that the Board of Relief be 88ked to cancel the Indebtedness.
Inspector JOHN C. KING, of the thirty·third district, make~ a r~port. m detail of
the condition of the four Lodges confided to his care. There 1s un1form1ty of work
in the Lodges of this district, so far as he had been ab le to examine them. Pomona,
No. 246, had no proper Lodge-room, and could not exemplify the work. ~ro.
KING found its members assembled in a little back room of a school-house, ~n a
"most deplorable condition," 88 he expresses It. He gave them some goo~ adv1oe,
and it is hoped that the Lodge will speedily procure a proper place of meeting. Of
San Diego L9dge, No. 35, he speaks in terms of warmest praise. "It was never my
good fortune," he says, cc to see the work better exemplified." All the Lodges, with
the exception of Pomona, No. 246, appear to be in a flourishing condition financially
and otherwise.
The districts from which no reports have been received are as follows, viz.: Dis·
trict No. 2, Bro. JAMBS VA.NOE, Inspector; District No. 6, Bro. J.a.us BRA.NH.llll, In·
spector; District No. 11, Bro. WA.LL.A.OE H. CHAPPELL, Inspector ; District No. 16,
Bro. ALBERT WRIGHT, Inspector j DistrictNo.29, Bro. DA.YID BROWNSTONE, Inspector;
and District No. 34, Bro. D.a. vrn K. FYFE, Inspector; making six districts not reported
upon, and leaving the Grand Lodge without inform~tion of the conditi~n of the
twenty-seven Lodges therein. It is hoped that the dehnqnent Inspectors will be able
to render the Grand Lodge some sufficient exonse for their neglect of duty.
In conclusion, I desire to suggest that the welfare of our Lodges wonld be gre~tly
promoted, and their efficiency measurably enhanced, by re-electing, when pract1ca·
ble, their Masters for a second term. In most cases, when a new :M88ter assumes t~e
chair he is Inexperienced in the duties incumbent upon him, not well grounded in
the ~ork and lectures of the several degrees, deficient In knowledge of Masonic law
and usage, aud nndecided, in many instances, how to act where the interests of his
Lodge and of the Craft in general are involved. During his first term he acquires
the knowledge necessary to make him an efficient Master, and he learns confidence
in himself as experience may have taught him that which enables him to rule and
govern liis Lodge with wisdom and discretion; but, just as the knowledge and exp~·
rienoe he has acquired might be made available for the benefit of the Lodge, he is
required to resign the gavel to an inexperienced hand. When a M88ter knows that

1883.]

Grand Lodge of California.

41

he has but one year to serve, there is not that incentive to study and etfort to excel
whloh would exist w.ere he assure~ of a re-election. This, of course, does not always
follow. If a Master is found to be mcapable, the sooner his successor shall be elected
the better f~r t~e Lod~e. But'. if he is . found to have the proper capaoity, it will be
well to re tam him until one eVJdently his superior can he found. The system of rota·
tlon in office, as practiced in many of our Lodges, is signally detrimental to their
lnte~ests •. Ambition to rise in ~88onry is laudable only when based upon proper
qual1flcat1ons; and the Lodge which elects a brother to the Master's chair simply
beoause he is a good fellow and wants the honor, not only does a great lojustioe to
ltae.lf, but also to the Fraternity at large. Merit, and merit alone, is the standard by
which Lodges should be governed in the choice of their .Masters.
I have to report that the following named Lodges have failed to forward the In·
1pector's certificate of qualification of the Master as required by law, viz.: Sotoyome,
No. 1~3; Hart'ley, No. 199; Freano, No. 20; and AUuraa, No. 248. Home explanation should be demanded as to why this plain provision of the law has In
these C88es been violated.
All which is respectfully submitted by
JOHN WERNER SHAEFFER,
Grand Leoturer.

ALABAMA.
The sixty·second Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Alabama was
held in the city of Montgomery, commencing on the fourth day of December, 1882,the M.·. W.'. RUFUS WILLS COBB, Grand Master, presiding, and the B.'. W.'. DA.N.
IEL SAYRE being Grand Secretary. One hundred and nlnety·nlne snbordinate
Lodges were represented at roll·call.
The first glance at the Address of the Grand Master conveys to us the sad Intelligence of the death of the talented Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence,
Bro. OLIVER STURGES BEERS. This distinguished brother bad for many years occu ·
pied the Chair of Oorrespondence in Alabama, and the earnest, decided and forcible,
yet courteous expression of his views upon matters Masonic, commanded the respect

1883.J

Grand Lodge of California.

49

even of those of his contemporaries who dilfered with him In opinion. Bro. BEERS
was born in Augusta, Georgia, on the tweoty-seventh day of January, 1819, and died
in Colnmbus, Mississippi, on the tenth day of November, 1882, aged sixty·three
years, nine months and thirteen days. He was initiated, passed and raised in How·
ard Lodge, No. 69, at Mobile, Alabama, in 1848. He served several years as Master
of that Lodge, and continued an active working member thereof until his death-a
period of thirty.four years and eight months. A shining light has been extinguished
In Alabama, and our brethren there have our sincere sympathy in the loss they have
sustained.
The Grand Master, after paying an eloquent tribute to the memory of Bro. BEERS,
takes the melancholy event as the subject of an earnest and well-considered dis·
course upon the moral teachings of Masonry, from which we clip the following
extract:If Masonry.was simi>ly an association for mntual pecuniary relief, it would long
sln_c e have ceased to exist. Its command to love one another-to share each other's
pams and sorrows? as weli as joys and pleMures-to afford each other mutual assist ·
ance and support 1~ all the relations of life-to respect the opinions and guard and
protect t~e reputation of a brother, and throw the veil of charity over his errors and
Hhortcomrngs: and, above all , its firm belief in the existence of a God and His Prov!·
dence, as well as t~e immort~lity of.the soul, has preserved and protected its exist·
ence as an B88oc1at1on, and will contmue to do so, as long as mankind shall inhabi t
the earth._ T_ben,_ my brethren, let me urge you to learn more of its moral precepta,
and practice its virtu~s ~ore, so that the standard of Masonic character may be elevated, the sphere of its mfluence enlarged, and its great moral teachings made more
.
.
popular, and therefore more observed among the brethren.

He reported the granting of dispensations to six Lodges to continue work and
elect omcers, their charters having been forfeited on varions accounts.
Decisions to the number of fourteen are reported, bnt t wo only call for special
mention. He decided that to embezzle the funds of the Lodge, or the property of a
brother Mason, was unmaaonic; and the Hrand Lodge sustained the decision. We
are glad to know that this matter is authoritatively settled in one jurisdlctlon, at
least; for, from the frequency of such occurrences, and the immunity extended to
the olfending parties, we had begun to believe that the embezzlement of funds was
looked upon as a rather creditable transaction.
He also decided, and the Grand Lodge concurred, that " a Lodge, or the mem·
bers thereof, are not bonnd to prefer charges against a brother for killing a pro·
fane." There are circumstances under which one man may be justified In taking
the life of another; but, if the slayer is a Mason, we believe the same course should
be taken in the Lodge as in the Courts of Justice. Let the brother be tried, and, if
the circumstances justify It, let him be acquitted and go forth to the world adjudged
gniltless by his brethren, as well as by the tribunals of his country.
The methods of Lodges in t he trials of offenders are " past finding out." .A case
is reported wherein a brother was tried upon charges containing nine specifications,
alleging the "challenging of a minor to combat; the use of filthy and vulgar lan?uage within the hearing of females; threats to shoot a brother Mason; qnarrellng
m a public place with an old man , and bringing false accusations against the same·
charging a brother Mason with falsehood, and ot herwise speaking evil of t he goo~
name of a brother Mason," eto. Upon five of the above speciflcatlons-1, 2, 4., 6 and
6-tbe accused was found gnflty, and sentenced to be reprimanded by the Worehlp·
ful Master. The Grand Lodge very properly reversed the aotlon of its subordinate
and indefinitely suspended the olfender.
'
A series of resolntlons, r elative to the establishment of a " Masonic Home and

In favor of their adoption, The r eport, together with the orig inal resolutions, was
referred to a special oommittee of five, with instructions to perfect some plan to
carry out the ideas contained in the resolutions, and report at the next Annual Oom-

munication. The representatives were also requested to present the matter to their
several Lodges for their action-the same course as that pursued by onr own Grand
Lodge in a similar case. We would advise our brethren of Alabama to make haste
slowly in this matter. The object seems to be a wortb,y 'one upon the surface, but
there are many difficulties in the way of itB successful aocomplishment. The experi·
ment has been tried in Arkansas and proved so unsatisfactory that measures have

.
In our own jurisdiction very little interest has been manifested in the proposed
"Widows' and Orphans' Home,'' as, out of two hundred and fifteen Lodges to whom
the matter was referred, only sixty-seven responded; and, although five hundred
and eighty·one widows and orphans resided within the jurisdiction of these Lodges,
very few of them would avail themselves of the privileges of the Home if offered
them. This report threw a wet blanket upon the scheme, and it went over until the
next Annual Oommunication. We have very little faith in the practicability of the
·
idea in California.
Past Grand Master HENRY CLAY ARMSTRONG was made happy by the presenta·
tion to him by the Grand Master, on behalf of the Grand Lodge, of an elegant service
of silver. The Grand Secretary regrets that he was unable to obtain copies of the
"brilliant aud effective " speeches made upon the interesting occasion.
Past Grand Master PALM.EB JOB PILLANS, having been appointed to fill the chair
made vacant by the death of Bro. BEERS, thus Introduces himself as Chairman of the
Oommittee on Correspondence:-The writer hereof having been requested to finish the report which it was presumed our lamented Bro. BEERS, late Chairman of the Oommittee, had nearly completed before his death-which occurred only sixteen days before the assembling of
the Grand Lodge-upon inquiry was unable to find that anything had been written ;
but, as the M.·. W.·. Grand Master still requested that a report should be made, he
~eluctantly undertook to _prepare a. hasty report, to be published with the proceedrngs. He approaches this labor with great apprehension, not only because of the
very large number of proceedings to be examined and the thousands of pages to be
perused, but also, because it is always difficult to follow in the footsteps of another
who had reflected credit upou the reportorial oorps, and be at all satidfled with one's
work. Trusting, however, to the generosity of the guild towards a fledgeling, be
will uudertake the task, promising to do the best he can with the time at his
disposal.
The term" fiedgellug,'' as applied to a tough old bird like Bro. PILLANS, is suggestive of Arciic coolness. We remember, when scarcely more than a boy, of the
pleasure we experienced in perusing the reports of Bro. PILLANS in other Masonic
Grand Bodies of Alabama, and .we know of no brother in that jurisdiction upon
whose shoulders the mantle of tbe lamented BEEBS could more gracefully and appro·
prlately fall. The preparation or such a report as he has given us in the brief pedod
of sixteen days, shows his eminent qualification for the position, and we congratulate
our brethren of Alabama upon securing the services of a brother in this Important
department whose experience, learning and research have already placed him in
the front rank of the Masonic writers of the day.
The proceedings of fifty Grand Lodges are reviewed in this report, among which
we find California for 1881. Be quotes liberally and approvingly from the report of
Grand Master DENSON, and heartily endorses his views upon the subject of death·bed
restorations. He gives in full the report of the committee upon the Widows' and
Orphans' Home, with the proposed Act o! Incorporation, and in this connection he
says:....,

Grand Lodge of California.

Gre.nd Lodges have tried the experiment of economizing In this particular, but have
•oon discovered that the paltry snm saved was but a poor compensation for the loss
of prestige that followed; and the popular clamor for "more light'' from their conatltuents soon induced tbem to seek retrenchment in some other channel.
A brief oration is published with the proceedings, but, as to when, where and by
whom delivered, we are left to conjectllre. The author, however, has no reason to
be ashamed of bis work, for it is a schnlarly, ornate and eloquent effort; beautiful
In conception and elegant in diction, and deserves a better fate than to be burled lo
the concluding pages of the proceedings, between the list of members and the index.
We extract the following as a specimen of the author's style:From the towering pyramids of the Nile, the stupendous palaces of Persopolis,
the stately temple at Jerusalem, down through the period when classic cnlture in
Greece had reached the zenith of its fame, when Pericles ruled supreme In the home
of genius, and every Athenian carried about him the halo of artistic conception,
down through the period of Roman grandeur and magnificence, when the Corinthian
columns were the acme of artistic excellence, and the sculptured fa9ade of Imperial Augustus fl.ashed and glimmered with all the gorgeous embla.zonry of pagan
ostentation, down through the era of Ohristianity, the rise and progress of Christian
faith, through the stormy P.eriod of iconoclasm, the dark ages, until the revival of
!otters awakened the spirit of the past and relit the fl.res of genius, through the
period of modern civilization, the foundation of modern greatness and power, the
oKtablishment of civil and religious liberty in the western hemisphere, down to the
present grand and magnificent period of law, order, intellectual culture, inventive
progress, and tbe rapid a~proach of that spirit of true inquiry and research which
wlll consummate the perfect blending of all the great principles of physical and
moral ethics; through all these changes and varied strata of social, political and
religious organization, running through ages of time, Masonry has remained
unchanged and unchangeable. ~'aithful among the faithless, firm among the faltering, steadfast in its purpose, sublime in its Integrity, grand, glorious and eternal in
its unostentatious devotion!
" The immortal gods
Accept the meanest altars that are raised
By pure devotion; and sometimes prefer
An ounce of frankincense, honey or milk,
Before whole hecatombs of Sabian gems
Offered in ostentation."
No grander ·motto could be inscribed upon the altar of Masonry than the simple
words, "I still live."
Draw the veil of secrecy, Bro. Grand Secretary, and let the author of these eloquent lines stand revealed to an admiring brotherhood.
The returns or the five subordinate Lodges show the total membership to be three
hundred and fl.v.e. The brethren of Arizona have our ardent wishes for the future
welfare and prosperity of their Grand Lodge.

ARKANSAS.
An Emergent Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas was held in the
city of Little Rock, on the tenth day of October, 1882, for the purpose of paying the
last sad tribute or respect to the memory or the Grand Tyler, Bro. JAM&S TuNNAB.
The Grand Lodge, escorted by Hugh dB Payem Oommandery of Knights Templar,
repaired to the late residence of the deceased brother, and from thence, accompanied the remains to Mount Holly Cemet&ry, where the solemn and Impressive bnr•
isl service of the Craft was conducted by the Grand Master, and all that remained of
one who, for many years had faithfully guarded the outer portais against the
approach of" cowans and eavesdroppers," was consigned to his kindred dlll!t.
The forty third Annual Commnnoation was commenced in the oity of Little Rock,
on the twenty-eighth day or November, 1882,-the M.·. W,•, GBOM& E. Dooos, Grand
Master, presiding, and the R.-. W.·. FAY HBMPS'r&AD being Gr11.nd Secretary. One
hundred and sixty-six subordinate Lodges were represented, and by subsequent

The Address of the Grand Master gives a good exhibit of the condition of the
Craft In that jurisdiction. He congratulates his brethren upon the favorable auspices
under which they assemble in Annual Communication, and says: "The past year bas
been one of general thrift and prosperity in all the various departments of material
iudustry." Be reports that Masonry bas shared in the general prosperity, and that
peace and harmony have prevailed throughout the jurisdiction, and regrets that
pressure of other matters bas prevented him from bestowing the time and attention
to the welfare of Masonry, which its importance demands. During bis term of office
be has received and answered about two hundred communications upon the sn)>ject
of Masonry, seventy-seven of which were answered by referring the seekers after
light to the plain letter of the law, which the intelligent (?) leaders of the Craft had
failed through indolence or indifference to consult, preferring to occupy the valuable
time of the Grand Master in rep.lying to questions whioh a brief reference to the
Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge would have at once set at rest.
Qneetlons, the most trivial and nonsensical, are sometimes submitted to the Grand
Master with all the gravity and earnestness which would surround a new problem in
mathematics or a novel theory in political economy.
We remember an instance where two lecturers in the ritual disagreed upon the
point as to whether the Grand Master, HIRAM ABIFF, shonld be characterized as" so
good and great a man" or" so great aud good a man." Failing to come to any sat.
isfactory conclusion, they submitted the point in dispute to our Grand Secretarv, who
replied, that " having diligently searched the Ancient Charges and Regulations, and
consulted the Constitutions and Edicts of most of the Grand Lodges in existence, be
had failed to find any authority upon the subject;" hut, in his opinion, any disposition they might choose to make of the adjectives "would not seriously affect the
reputation of our Grand Master, HIRAM ABIFF." Very many of the queries submitted to Grand Masters are of similar profundity and Importance. When Masters
and Wardens learn to read the laws and think for themselves, the poeition of Grand
Master will be relieved of an intolerable annoyance.
The Grand Master thongbt the installation of officers good enough work for
Christmas-eve, and therefore aeclined to grant a dispensation to hold a meetmg for
installation a week in advance. He also declined to grant a dispensation to confer
the second and third degrees upon an Entered Apprentice within the specified time,
the excuse being that said Apprentice bad sold ont and desired to" travel to the
Springs.'' He thought in this instance the "Entered Apprentice would keep."
A number of decisions are announced , most of which are covered by the plain
provisions of the law; one, however, is of such a nature as to call for our dissent.
The inquiry Is made as to the status of a brother under suspension for non-payment
of does to a Lodge now defunct, and whether his application for affiliation could
be received. The Grand Master replied, that the brother must apply to the Gr.and
Lodge for the removal of bis disabilities; he could not apply for affiliation in his
present condition. "His suspension being orily for non-payment of dues, individual
Masons may bold communication with him. His disabilities go no further than the
forfeiture of Lodge privileges and of the right to Masonic Relief. He ha.s no right
to visit the Lodge."
This is a new kind of snspension. Io Maine, Me.s~achosetts, and some other jnrisdictions, they have what is termed "suspension from membership," which simply
leaves a brother In the condition of a non-affiliate, bot otherwise in good standing.
In the case cited, the brother is depfived of Lodge membership, of the right to visit
a Lodge and debarred from Masonic relief; yet" individual Masons may bold com·
munication with him," but ·Lodges may not. We hold, that while the brother is
under the ban of suspension, whether for non-payment of does or for any other

1883.J

Grand Lodge of O<ilifm-n:ia.

nauae, no brother has the right to hold Masonic communication with him until he is
reatored to good standing.
The following, also, is contrary to the practice in this and most other jurisdictions.
The question was asked: "Can a dimit be granted a brother upon his paying up all
dae1, when it is known that he does not intend to move outside the jurisdiction of
thtN Lodge, nor connect himself with another Lodge?"
After stating that there was no edict of the Grand Lodge upon the subject, the
Orand Master responded" No" to the question. The general theory Is, that as 8
Mason enters the Lodge " of bis own tree will and accord," he should he allowed to
leave It in the same manner ; and if his dues are paid and no charges pending against
him, the Lodge cannot refuse him a dimit when applied for, and has no right to
question his motives In withdrawing bis membership.

Under the head of "Nevade.," he notices the case of a brother who belonged to
a Lodge in Michigan, bot who was temporarily residing in White Pine. The sum of
$442 was expended for his relief, he being destitute. Of this amount $172 was raised
by private subscription, and $270 was app~opriated from the Lodge fonds. White
Pine Lodge requested the Lodge in Michigan to reimbnrse them for the $270 ex·
pended by them, but were refused payment upon the ground that it wonld establish
a precedent which would result in their final bankruptcy. The Grand Master of
Nevada laid the matter before the Grand Master of Michigan, who advised hJs sub·
ordinate that, though the claim might not be legal, yet it was equitable, and they
- ought to reimbnrse White Pine Lodge to the extent of their ability. The Grand .
Master of Nevada, in his address, says:I have heard nothing further abont the matter, and, as more than two months
have elapsed, it is probably ended. I refer to this case, not to cast any reproach
upon our brethren of Michigan, nor to even intimate that you should in the least fail
to relieve distressed worthy brothers, wherever dispersed, but to caution yon that
if you expect to be reimbursed for any outlay made in behalf of' any brother hailing
from the other side of the Rocky Mountains, you must obtain authority in advance.
Of course, the brother might die while you are negotiating; but, unless you are able
to care for his wants without hope of fee or reward, there is no other way. This is
the law. The ways of our Eastern brethren are different from our ways, and we
cannot change them. I would recommend the use of the telegraph in snch cases.

We of California also appreciate the situation. We have been roundly abused
tor 11nggesting to the brethren of Eastern Lodges at least a partial reimbursement
tor the amount expended for the relief of their sick and destitute members. In some
oa11es t~e amount .is promptly and cheerfully refunded, but in others the reqoeat is
ungraciously received and not unfrequently denied or entirely ignored. During the
past year the Board of Relief of San Francisco expended for the relief of destitute
Masons,_ their wives, widows and orphans, coming from without the jurisdiction of
Oallforn1a, the sum of $6,781 92, about one-half of which was refunded. We do not
claim th~ reimbursement of this expenditure as a right; but we ask it to enable us
to meet more fully the constant demands upon us for aid from Masons from all parts
ot the world'. Since the organization of the Board of Relief in 1856, it has expended
•186,051 77 m charity, and we think it no more than right that those Lodges whose
members have been relieved, and who 11.re able to repay the amount, should do 110 ,
and thereby strengthen our hands to relieve still others who may call upon us
for aid.

The followinr;, under the caption of" Rotation in Office," meeti with our full concurrence:-

1883.]

Grand Lodge of California.

63

In more than one instance during the past year I have found that the refusal by
the Lodge to elect officers to a higher station than they had previously occupied, has
been the cause of discord, and in one case threatened the very existence of the
Lodge ; and on the other hand, I find the interests of the Lodges sntfering from the
election or incompetent officers. The prosperity, efficiency and harmony of any
organization, depends mach upon capable and efficient officers, and this is especially
true of Masonic Lodges.
The idea has prevailed, especially of late, that when a brother has been appointed
.Junior Deacon, it is only a question of time when he shall be seated in the Master's
uhair, and that whenever a vacancy occurs in any office above him, his claim to
advancement is superior to all others. In many cases this claim is conceded by the
members, until he is advanced to the highest office In their gift, and entrusted with
the government of the Lodge, a position for which he may be utterly unfitted. In
overy snch case, the interests of the Lodge will eutfer during his administration and
11erhaps for years afterwards. Brethren who have filled subordinate positions with
llredit to themselves, and profit to the Lodge, sometimes prove incompetent when
nailed to govern. The Master of a Lodge should be firm, courteoos, faithful to hi~
Lodge, moral, upright, and of good report before the world. All this he has proml•cd to be before he was installed, and if he add to these tact and sound judgment,
his administration cannot fail to be a successful one, and his Lodge be greatly benellted. Lodges should never forget, that the world will judge by the character and
uondoct of those who have been selected as officers, and it is perhaps just that they
"honld ; for the fountain can never rise higher than its head, I believe that officers
•hoold be advanced always, when capable ; not from the fact that they have held
•ome other position, but because they are capable. Perhaps it would be wise for
tho Grand Lodge to declare, that a brother acquires no right to any office, by reason
of having filled another, either in the Grand or subordinate Lodges. I submit this
for yoor consideration.

degree. In such a case we think the Grand Master was perfectly correct In his

adoption of some standard form, with all the necessary rules of forming, marching,
conntermarchlng, eto., deposjting the evergreen, Grand Honors at the grave, and
every minor point, would tend to a more dignified manner in performing these sad

nature should be conducted with order and decorum, and if there is any place where
it is absolutely necessary, It is at th~ burial of a deceased brother.
The following upon the snbjeot of non-affiliation is worthy of consideration:We think In the discussion of this subject, it should be borne in mind that the
Masonry of the present day is entirely different from that before the organization or
the first Grand Lodge, when such a thing as "fixed membership was unknown. Since
that time, however, the system of fixed membership has been recognized, and
Lodges are chartered on thRt basis; dues have been required for the support of this
system, and certain privileges acquired which were unknown, all growing out of,
and depending upon, one's membership in a Lodge. It Is right, therefore; that he
who neglects willfully to perform his duty as a member should be deprived of those
rights and privileges which accrue from membership. It is just, from a common··
sense standpoint, and in accord with the Divine Law, that the wicked shall perish,
while the righteous shall inherit everlasting life. In the church, even, the principle
is more forcibly portrayed, and we may safely draw a parallel in Its Illustration,
where for ages the inftuence of the church has been exerted to induce the wayward
to come within its sacred precincts, yet there are sinners in abundance to-day. To
use a familiar 1,>hrase, "the woods are fall of them;'' and, as asserted by Grand
Master WELLS, m his address regarding non·alfiliates, much the largest proportion
of the community is on the outside.
It follows. then, that any legislation of a coercive nature is fruitless, as has been
demonstrated time and time again, and the question presents itself: What shall we
do to retain our membership, and not what Is necessary to get back a large amount
of rubbish that can only" count,'' and who, unless they have reason for a better
opinion of onr privileges, wonld be as worthless a set as ever. We think, for the
accomplishment of this result. the objective point is within our Lodge-rooms. We
should cultivate more the social element of Masonry, designed from its inception,
else why use the benignant appellation of brother in our interoourse one with
another 1 We should as much as poBBible make our meetings attractive, and if work
does not present itself sufficient to occupy our evenings, let some other means be.
employed that will prove both pleasing and instructive, and tend to keep the mem·
bership uuited and interested-good and true advocates of "that divine attribute
which is the foundation of every virtue." To use the language of the ritual," let
hypocrisy and deceit be unknown among us, sincerity and Ria.in dealing distin~ish
us, and the heart and tongue join In promoting eac)l others welfare, and rejoicing
in each other's prosperity."
Above all, we should exercise charity, which is the bond of peace and the per·
fectlon of every virtue-yea, the foundation-stone of our fraternity, laid deep and
strong. It appeals to our sympathy, our manhood, and our Masonry, seeking
responsive chords to its supplications within tne repository of Faithful Breasts;
and when exemplified in accord with the true exposition of Masonic principles,
completes the typical structure adorning its principal arch with a crowning glory.
When Lodges begin to live up to such principles, they will find little cause for
complaint, and the annual stipena required of members for the purposes of charity
and snstenauoe, and social enjoyment, will be cheerfully donated, knowing that in
proportion as they give, in like manner shall they receive.

DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA.

The pamphlet containing the proceedings of the Grand Locli'e of the District
of Columbia at its Stated, Special, Resumed Special, Semi-Ano,ual, Annual and
Installation CoDl.Dlunications .for the year 1882, has been placed on our table. At
the Stated CoDl.Dlunication held on the eleventh day of January, 1882, considerable business was transacted, but it was entirely confined to m11tter11 of local
Interest.
A Special Communication was held in the city of Washington on the third day
of February, 1882, for the purpose of attending the funeral of Past Grand Master
0HARLES FREDERICK STANSBURY, who died at his residence in west w ashington,
on the thirty-first day of January, after only a few hours illness. We sympathize
with our brethren of the District of Columbia in the sad loss they have sustained
In the death of this distinguished brother. 'Prominent in all good works, active
and zealous in all that concerned the welfare of Freemasonry, his loss will not be
euily supplied.
A second Special Communication was held on the twenty-ninth day of Me.rob,
and resumed on the thirtieth, for the exemplification of the degrees, which was
done by the Grand Lecturer and his assistants.
The Semi-Annual Communication WllB held on the' tenth day of May, 1882,the M. '. W. '. NOBLE D. LARNER, Grand Master, preeidiDg, and the R. '. W. '.
WILLIAM R. SINGLETON being Grand Secretary. Nineteen Lodges were reprennted.
The Special Committee on the death of Past Grand Master STANSBURY made
their report and submitted a series of memorial resolutions, which were adopted.
A touching letter from Bro. DEWITT C. CREGIER, Representative of the
Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia near the Grand Lodge of Illinois, WllB
allo read. Action was had upon sundry amendments. to the Constitution and several coDl.Dlunication\ were received and referred to the proper committees.
The seventy-third Annual Communic.a tion was held in the city of Washington,
commencing on the eighth day of November, 1882,-Grand Master LARNER prellding. Twenty-three Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, in his Address, gives a very gratifying exhibit of the con·
ditlon of the Craft in that jurisdiction. The year had been a prosperous one; the
Lodges, with but two exceptions, had enjoyed 11 large degree of prosperity, and
pee.oe and h11rD1ony prevailed. Not a sound of discord had been heard in any part
of the jurisdiction during the year, and no case of grievance had been presented
for adjudication. The Lodie11 had never presented a more aatisfa.ctory condition

Proce,e,dings of the

[Oct. 10,

Georgie.. We endorse every word of it, and trust that the time is not far distant
when the demon Alcohol will be banished from our Lodge-rooms thronghout the
land, and the curse removed and the stain obliterated from the fair fame of Masonry.
He says:18th. Upon the question being presented to me I have more than once decided
that It is exceedingly Improper and unmasonlc in a subordinate Lodge, while called
from labor to refreshment, to have, or sulfer to be had, among such refreshments,
any kind of intoxicating drinks, malt or spirituous. I do not mean refreshments at
hotels or restaurants-where the respon.sibility, as well as the appetite and taste, is
purely individual. There, each one acts on his own sense of propriety-but the
carrying into ante-rooms kegs of beer, baskets of wine, ale, porter and the like, is
exceedingly oft'ensive to many brethren-at least soipe in every Lodge, and is a
reproach to the Fraternity! The time wu, and perhaps within the memory of some
here, when this practice, beginning in innocent mirth, ende<1 in drunken revelry,
and in the disruption and downfall of many a Lodge, in perhaps more jurisdiction~
than one, and brougb.t upon the whole Fraternity, not.unjustly, the criticism of good
men in and out of the Order. Now, in this enlightened day, when the good of every
Order, faith and persuasion have set tl!eir faces against this giant evil, drunkenness,
shall we who profess to be moral men; wb.o profess to walk in.the light and dispense
light; whose cardinal virtue is (professedly) temperance, shall we by ezample lend
our influence to this terrible curse? Think a moment. ·When we affirm ours ls a
moral institution-when we would by a word of exb.ortation or persuasion attempt
to save a fellow-creature from what must lead him to inevitable ruin-when we
would point the erring, it may be enthralled, one, to that great virtn.e, temperance,
and beg him to abstain-to be a man-he, they, the profane, whoever it may be,
will throw back into our very teeth, and in words that burn, mortify and crucify us,
our own (uuthoughted it may) immoral practice, and point us to the day--the
night-the honr, when he saw tb.e wine, beer, ale, porter and the like, carried into
our ante-rooms to be consumed upon our vitiated appetites, if not to excess, to
unbecoming hilarity. Thus are we j eered and taunted, because of our lntldelity to
the principles of our Orner. l have held, I repeat it, that to carry spirituous, lntoxi·
eating or malt drinks into Lodge and ante-rooms, to be used while at refreshments,
i• not right, and if allowed, will drive from our Order hundreds of good m!)o. If it
must be used, let it be elsewhere, when the Lodge is closed and where each acts
for himself, and not in Lodge-rooms or Lodge capacity. I present this decision
squarely to this Grand Lodge. It I am correct, so pronounce ; if wrong, say so.
We must know where we stand, and the outside world ought to know. Is onr
example nothing worth; are our professions sounding brass and tinkling cymbals!
Where is our influence in tb.is great struggle to free our race, of every age and sex,
of this the Q.eepest, darkest evil that ever cursed humanity!
The Committee on J nrisprndence, in their report, do not sqnarely meet the issue
on this question, and we cannot refrain from saying that there is much of sophistry
in tb.e following :The eighteenth ruling, touching tb.e use of intoxicating liquors in the Lodge.
room during tb.e business hours of the Lodge, is an important one. The Grand
Master very properly draws a distinction as to the time and circumstances nuder
which these are and are not allowable. We concur with him, that it Is improper for
a Masonic Lodge to enter upon such Indulgences as a Lodge. They should not be
partaken of until the Lodge has finally closed its meeting and the brethren are
resolved into their individual conditions as men and citizens. Let the business and
labors of Masonry be finally concluded before any indnlgence of tb.e kind referred
to i'.s allowed, and even then we regard it as highly Improper and unmasonic, and as
subjecting the parties thereto to discipline when they indulge beyond tb.at moderation which becometh a man and Mason. Tb.e car<linal virtue of temperance, while
allowing moderation, condemns, in the •trongest terms, any dep1uture from that
restraint which keeps the passions and aft'ections within due bonnds, renders the
body tame and governable, and frees tb.e mind from the allurement of vice. While
Masonry would not dictate what shall be the appetite and pleasures of her cb.ildren,
sbe likewise recognizes tb.e fact that there is a time and place for all things, and tJiat
everything should be done decently and in order.
·
Thus the doctrine is held that, while it is highly improper for Maso'ns to get
drnnk as a Lodge, yet, "when the brethren are resolved into their indi1'idual con·
ditiona a.s men and citizens," they may use the Lodge-room, dedicated to the sacred
purposes of Masonry, aa a place for wine-bibbing and carousal. The righteous
dennnciations of the Grand Master were directed against the use of the accursed

IDAHO.
The Grand Lodge of Idaho commenced its fifteenth Annnal Communication in
Boise City on the twelfth day of September. 1882,-tbe M.·. W.·. L. F. CARTEE,
Deputy Grand Master, presiding, and the R .·. W. ·• J.urns H. W1cKERSH.u1 being ·
Grand Secretary. Eight Lodges were represented.
The R. •. W. ·• Deputy Grand Master announced the illness of the M. ·. W•.•• FRANCIS
E. ENSIGN, Grand Master, who, later in the session, addressed the Grand Lodge,
ate.tin!{ the circumstances which had deprived him of health and prevented him from
performing the duties of bis olf!ce. The Deputy Grand Master made a brief report
of his official acts, but we find nothing of general interest which calls for notice.
The Grand Secretary rendered a very clear account of the transactions of his
office, and of the financial condition of the Grand Lodge. He acknowledged the
receipt of the proceedings of twenty-two Grand Lodges, but California does not
appear in the list. One copy of each was forwarded to Bro. E. A. BTBVENSON, Past
Grand Master, Chairman of the Committee on Correspondence, but they might as
well have remained in the hands of the Grand Secretary, for no Report on Correspondence appears, and no excuse for its absence is given.
The Grand Treasurer reports a balance 011 band of $1,909 29. This sum is divided
into four funds, viz: General F u11d, Orphan Fund, Interest Orphan Food and Reprereotative F11od. The sum of $412 43 stands to the credit of the General Fund.
A communication from the Grand Lodge of New Mexico announces the re-establishment of fraternal relations between that Grand Body and the Grand Lodge of
Missouri. The request of the Grand Lodge of Arizona for recognition was referred
to the Committee on Jurisprudence, who recommended that" the papers and correspondence be placed on file and that fraternal recognition be for the present withheld." No reason is given for withholding recognition, and we are at a loss to
account for this action on the part of our brethren of Idaho. The sum·of fifty dollars was appropriated for the _relief of ihe orphan daughter of a deceased brother.
A brother who bad be~n suspended by an Idaho Lodge, and since removed to Arizona, applied for restoration. His application was endorsed by the Master, Wnrdens
and Secretary of .d.ztlan Lodge, No. 1, of Arizona, and his restoration was recommended by Siloer Oity Lodge, No. 13, of Idaho. Fonr of the members of the Committee on Grievances recommended his restoration, but the fifth objected and moved
that the application be noi granted, which motion prevailed. This, taken in connection with the refusal to recognize the Grand Lodge of Arizona, would seem to indicate
some cause of grievance, but no ray of light is thrown upon the motive for nnfraternal action.
One dispensation was granted for the formation of a new Lodge. A Committee
on Correspondence was appointed wfth the same chairman as last year. We trost
he will find time to furnish a report for the next Annnal Communication.
There are nine chartered Lodges in the Territory, with a total membersnlp of

Under the caption of "Jurisdiction of Lodges," the Grand Master fully expresses
our ideas upon the absurd doctrine of " perpetual jurisdiction." He says:This baa been a long, troublesome an!l vexatioua question. I am aware that I
differ in my opinion upon this subject with able jurists, but I wish to enter my pro·
teRt to the doctrine of .perpetual Jurisdiction. It Is fraught with much inconvenience, trouble, and, to my mind, injustice. If rejection were proof that a candidate
was an unworthy man and could not reform, it might be well. Bnt tbe candidate
may have been in every way worthy of admission, and twenty-five out of twenty-six
members present may have voted for him, but one black ball was cast against his
lldmissioo, and hence rejected, and perpetual jurisdiction obtained over bim for all
time to come. I submit, is this in accordauce with the priociple11 of justice? It is a
well known tact that man,Y candidates for the mysteries of Masonry, "who were
W<Yl"thy and well qualified' to be made Masons, bave been rejected. They have
removed to other parts, perhaps several hundred miles away, and after a lapse of
five or ten years, "still entertaining a favorable opinion of Maaoory," desire to petition the Lodge where they now reside. But one man, ten years previous, opposed
bis being made a Mason, and now the consent of that Lodfr" must be obtained,
though it may have no knowledge of his present character. Some whom I know
personally have been rejected and afterwards admitted, who have done much to
•dvance the interests of our Craft, and are to·day burning lights In this Grand Jurisdiction. I believe the law, if it is a law, is wrong in principle and does not work
well in practice. At least that is my offtcial experience.
Again he says:There is another phase of Lodge jurisdiction I wish to present. It is this : In
Home quarters there is an Impression that territory is assigned for pecuniary be111!fU
only. A Lodge invades the jurisdiction ofa sister Lodge, and the onlyjdifficulty appears
to be the fe6 that has been collected. The Grand Master is written to and the question asked," How can we compel the offending Lodge to pay tbe fee collected, or a
part of it?" Io my opinion this principle is wrong. We should not, as Lodges, be
Influenced by mercenary motives any more than individuals. Let us be more particular as to Lodge courtesy, and the aouTLdne&!I of the material used in onr mystic
temple, and less as to who usea the material. A good Mason is a benefit to the
Craft at large, no matter where initiated, and a bad one is a disgrace wherever he
·
belongs.
With reference to Masonic trials, we desire to endorse the following:1 have been taught, as a Mason, that" truth. was a. divine attribute," and that to
reaob the truth was tba great and the ONLY OBJECT of a MASONIC TRIAL, and hence,
In all Masonic trials, no advantage should be permitted to be taken through technioallties, that justice may not be reached and a correct judgment rendered. Masonic
trials, I conceive, should be conducted in the simplest and le6Bt technical method
that will preserve both the rights of the accnsed and also the Institution, so that the
l,odge may reach a thorough knowledge of all the facts in the case.

P'l'oceeding& of the

Aga.in it is pleasant to say', as has been said, in effect, during some twenty years
past, tha.t, for the fiscal year now reported, the annual reports of all the Lodges in

The Grand Orator, R.·. w.·. Bro. OWEN ScOTT, delivered an eloquent oration
upon the subject of "Masonry-its ritualism, its realities, its results." We can only
find space for the following extract:The actual deeds, the noble results, are so numerous that were they but "~'er
named" the world would scarcely contain the books of their recital. Because our
society has for its chief purpose the development and establishment of truth and the
formation of character, is no reason why the more material should not be considered.
As a creature of circumstances, man is largely dependent upon his fellows. To·day,
he appears strong, rugired , needing no help; to-morrow, weak, helpless and deml\nd· ·
ing sympathy and assistance. To-day his head is erect, his footstep strong and
elastic, his eyes full of lustre, and the healthful lines of Heaven are beaming in his
face; to-morrow, in" his long home" he "sleeps the sleep that knows no waking."
But when disease, infirmity and death come and carry the Mason to that "undiR· ·
covered con·n try " fraternal hands minister to the af!lictions of the last hour, and are
ready to wipe away the widow's tears and relieve the orphan's needs. Without
ostentatious trumpeting, with no ConRtitutlon or by·law to enforce benefits, the
world has yet to know of a genuine .Mason, his widow or orphan, begging bread, or
being sent away hungry; but when gaunt famine stalks into the midst of the loved
circles of one who "meets upon the level, aeta by the plumb, and parls upon the
square," sweet charity drops down her blessings like the gentle dew, and silently
veils his hideous form nntil he disappears to wreak his vengeance upon those out·
side our mystic circles.
"In silence
Steals on soft handed charity,
Tempering her gifts that seem so free,
By time and place,
'Till not a woe the bleak world Ree,
But finds her grace."
In all our difficulties, tl'ials, and solicitnde for the future we can feel " what a
precious comfort '.tis to have so many like brothers commanding one another·s fortunes." We differ in our politics, in onr religion, knowing that
" In faith and hope the world will disagree,
But all mankind's concern is charity."
The Report on Correspondence is again from the pen of Bro. JOHN WABBINGTON
BBOWN, and is condemed within the limits of one hnndred and fotty·four pages. Last
year he favored us with some five hundred pages, dealing largely in extracts, but, in the
present report we get what pleases us better; the writer's own ideas and opinions
upon Masonic subjects, and upon the questions which now form the topics of dis·
cnssion among the Masonic writers of the day. Among these Bro. BnowN takes no
mean rank. His opinions are clearly, forcibly and boldly expressed, and his criti·
cisms, though incisive, are invariably courteous and fraternal. We do not hesitate
to say that the report before ns is one of the best that has come under our notice,
and we trust our brother will long continue to wield the quill reportorial for Illinois.
Hie notice of California, for 1881, is brief but kindly, and he has a pleasant compli·
ment for our Grand Secretary and Grand Lecturer. Bro. BROWN thus expresses his
views upon the question of "Grand Lodge Sovereignty" :When a man has a genuine warranty deed for a farm, which is based on an unclouded
chain of title, there can be no question that he is its lawful possessor. Likewise, when
a corporation has been formed by the assent of all participating in it, and has acquired
large possessions by strictly legal methods, there can be no doubt of its right to control
them. The question and the <loubt only come when the rights of title and the forms of
law have been violated, or when the principles of justice and equity have been disregarded. Freemasonry is eminently an institution devoted to truth, and the principles
of fraternal brotherhood. It recognizes the di vine law of right and equity, between
man and his fellow. It plants itself squarely on the GoLD&N R1JJ,i;;, and in the admission
of candidates to its mysteries, and in devising constitutions and regulations for the gov·
ernment of its votsries, conforms strictly to the divine MAGNA CHART A· It never usurps
power nor coerces allegiance, but obtains sovereignty by free-will and accord. Its
authority is acquired and maintained solely by assent; it thus is purely representative,
and true to the eternal principles of freedom. Its cement is brotherly love, and its

INDIAN TERRITORY.

The eighth Aoooal Communication of this Gr&od Lodge was held in the town of
Vioiia, Cherokee Nation, comme11ciog on the seventh day of November, 1882,-the
M.·. w.·. CHARLES E. GOODlllG, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. JOSEPK
S. MUBROW being Grand Secretary. Eleven Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, in a well-considered AddreBS, presented a clear exhibit of the
aft'aire of the jurisdiction. Be. reports the Lod.u:es to be in. good and healthy ooodi·
tioo; the only serious trouble having arisen from the noo·compliaoce of one of them
with the General Regulations of the Grand Lodge, lo admitting to membership one
J. D. B&NRY without a dimit and electing him Master of the Lodge, when it was sub·
sequeotly proven thBt he had been indefinitely suspended by a Lodge in Arkansas for
defrauding it of a large snm of money. The Grand Master, upon the fact being
made known to him, suspended HENBY from office and forbade bis meeting with the
Lodge. The facts became known through a quarrel between HENBY and his Senior
Warden who, It appears, was cognizant of the fact that HENRY was a suspended
Mason, yei 11at with him lo the Lodge and ~llowed him to be elected as its MB!lter
without making the facts known until the quarrel between them induced him to
reveal them. The Grand Master instructed the Lodge to investigate this feature of ,
the Cl\Be, and if the Senior Warden was guilty, be too should be punished. The
Senior Warden, however, went before the Lodge, acknowledged his fault, and
begged pardon for his error. The Lodge forgave him, and he has since had charge
of it. The committee to whom the matter was referred, as a matter of courtesy to
the Grand Lodge of Arkansas, recommended that a full statement of the case be
sent to the Grand Master of Arkansas with a request that, in case the Lodge lo
which he was suspended beld any claim upon said HENRY, that the Indian Territory
Lodge be allowed to prefer charges against him for · imposture and deception .i and
if no jurisdiction was claimed, then the Lodge which he had so grossly deceived was
directed to 'prefer charges against him, and, if foood guilty, to expel him from all
rights and privileges of Masonry. The Lodge is censured for its failure to secure
dimite, or certificates of good standing, f'rom Its members when applying for a dis·
peosatioo, and the Senior Warden, who, io our opinion, deserved expulsion as much
as the Master, was let oft' with a mild reprimand.
The Grand Master reported several decisions, but none of them call for special
mention. Be warns his brethren against the vicee of intemperance and profanity,
which, he says, some of them holding high positions in the Lodges of the Territory
have fallen into. Be says: "Drunkeuoess le a Masonic crime, and we have good
and wholesome la we against it, but we fail to execute those laws. If we were true
to our Jaws and true to our weak brethren we would have lees intemperance in our
Lodges."
A communication to the Grand Master from a subordinate Lodge says: "At the
last meeting of Oherokee Lodge, No. 10, we discussed three questions in order, as
follows: First-Is tht: introduction of ardent spirits into our country so serious an
et1il as to make It the duty of all good citizens to meet it with active opposition!
Second-Is it so serious an evil to the Masonic Order and our tenets, as well as to
onrselvee as Masone, as to make it the duty of all good Masons to meet it with active
opposition! Third-What methods are feasible and practicable?'' The first two
questions were decided in the affirmative, and with reference to the third, it was
agreed that the matter should first be tnoroughly agitated, and a committee was
appointed to communicate with all the Lodges along the Arkaneas, MiBBourl and
KaoB1Ls borders, as well as within the Nation, and secure their cooperation. It was
·also decided to bring the matter before the Grand Lodge and ask for its influence in
aid of the object in view. The communication was referred to the Committee on
"Good of the Order," who reported that, while they respectfully insisted upon the
enforcement of the lawa iover:niug intemperance and profanity, they did not think
