IOWA.

The pamphlet containing the tra.nsactions of this Grand Body is a modest volume of 590 pages, beautifully printed in large type; in the highest style of the
"art preservative," with illuminated headings, etc., for which Bro. PARVIN is
famous. The volume is a credit both to compiler and printer, and although, as a
rule, we are not particularly in favor of ma.king a picture-book of the proceedings
of Grand Lodges, we must confess that the specimen before us has an exceedingly
attractive
appearance.

The fortieth
.Annual Communication was held
the fifth day of June, 1883,-the M. ·• W. ·.GEORGE B. VANS.A.UN, Grand :Master,
presiding, and the B. •• W. •. THEODORE S. PARVIN being Grand Secretary. All
the Grand Officers were present save the Senior Grand Deacon, who had removed
from the State. Three hundred and fourteen Lodges were represented.
The Address of the Grand :Master is lengthy, but well prepared and interesting,
showing deep thought and an earnest desire to promote the welfare of the Craft by
wise legislation and judicious amendments to existing regulations. " Our institution," he says, "has prospered even more than we dared to hope for, or could reasonably expect ; and yet there is room for a still greater growth -yea, a necessity
for a continued advancement-in exemplifying the beauties of the true :Masonic
life."
Fifteen Lodges, chartered at the last Annual Communication, were duly constituted and started on their career of UBefulness. He had drawn orders on the
Charity Fund for $300 for the relief of sufferers by the cyclone at Grissell, $100
for sufferers by a cyclone at :Malcom, and $65 to assist the widow of a deceased
.
brother to remove with her family to California.
Eighteen _cjispensations for the formation of new Lodges were granted during
the year. In this connection the Grand Master stated that notwithstanding his
desire " to go Ind sl<Ywly " in the granting of dispensations for new Lodges, yet from
the wants of the brethren at many thriving towns on new lines of railways, ha had
felt it''.t o be his duty, and for the best interests of the fraternity, to grant this ·
number. An increase of thirty-three Lodges in two yea.rs certainly does not look
as if :Masonry was retrograding in Iowa to any appreciable extent.

rehearing, on the ground that the Report of the Committee on Appeals was b&Bed
upon outside testimony and not upon the transcript forwarded by the Lodge.
Upon examining the papers relative to the case in the Grand Secretary's office, he
became convinced that their claim was just, and ordered that the action of
the last Grand Lodge be held in abe)'ance for further action, and that all parties in

The Representatives of the Grand Lodge of Iowa near other Grand Lodges are
furnished with golden jewels, and the honorary title of Senior Grand Warden is
conferred upon them. Past Grand Master TITUS, being the Representativ.e of
Iowa near our Grand Lodge, will thus ha.ve an opportunity to outshine his brethren
of the diplomatic corps in the splendor of his decorations and the formidability of
his titles.
The Committee on Appeals.reports a case wherein the accused party was introduced and testified as a witness in his own behalf. The committee, thereupon,
submitted the following question, which was referred to the Committee on J urieprudence : Is it the rule ar practice in Masonic tria~ to receive testivwny from
defend.amt& on trial 1 The committee reported that "the accused cannot testify in
his own behalf, but that he should be permitted, when the evidence is concluded,
to make a statement of his case, which should be heard, leaving its value to be
determined by the proper tribunal." Such is the practice in California.
· In two cases where brethren had been tried and convicted of unmasonic conduct
in matters shown by the testimony to have been purely business transactions, the
action of the Lodges was reversed and set aside, and the accused restored to all
their Masonic rights and privileges. This is right ; a Lodge should take no note
of business transactions among its members where no moral turpitude is involved,
nor should Lodges be made a medium for the collection of debts, unless the debts
are incurred under a Masonic pledge.
The Board of Custodians reported that the revised work had been completed,
and five schools of instruction had been held at different points, which were so well .
attended as "to plainly show that the old-time desire for instruction in the work
had been revived." They recommend the continuance of appropriatfons to enable
them to prosecute the work, and that the sum thus appropriated be sufficiently
large to enable them to secure the services of a competent Grand Lecturer. The
Grand Lodge of Arizona was recognized, and fraternal correspondence invited.
The Report on Correspondence by the Grand Secretary, Bro. PARVIN, covers
two hundred pages and comprises a review of the transactions of forty-five Grand
Lodges. It is a model report. From beginning to end the interest of the reader
never flags, for there is intellectual food, well spiced, in every sentence. Bro.
PARVIN throws his scissors into the waste-basket, and makes this a report of the
pen. He reviews the proceedings of California for 1882 in pleasant and fraternal
style; praises the address of Grand Master TAYLOR, and, in commenting upon the
numerous queries usually propounded to Grand Masters in general, pertinently
asks : " Why will Grand Masters continue to be mere private secretaries of the
ma.ss of subordinate Lodges, to hunt up the refe1-ences for them!" He concurs in
the decision of Bro. TAYLOR, that charges may again be preferred &glloinst an
offender for the same offense, and the same and similar testimony introduced.
"In this respect," he says, "the Masonic differs from the criminal law of our
country." Very true ; Masonic investigation is intended to elicit the truth, while
a judicial examination too often serves to cover up or pervert it. He praises the
act of the Grand Master in exempting from the discipline visited upon a recreant Lodge, all.members who did not participate in or directly uphold or approve
the course pursued by the Lodge. We presume that none will deny that the innocent should not be made to suffel' with the guilty. He thinks the report of Bro.
ABELL, that all the existing Lodges in this jurisdiction--some two hundred and
twenty-had made their annual reports and paid their dues in full within the prescribed time, is "astoni8himg." As the <.'Onstant dropping of water will wear away

right to grant a dimit to a member against whom charges are preferred , provided

What right bas a Lodge to issue such a certificate to one against whom charges of
uomasonic conduct have been preferred, which, if beard and determined, may place

•
The second decision is, we a.re aware, in a.cco.rdaoce with general usage; but why
an installed officer may n1Jt resign his position under certain circumstances., is a
problem which we have never been able to solve; nor have we ever heard an Intelligent, or even plausible, reBl!on given why soch should be the case. It is urged that
Masters and Wardens promise, upon their installation, to perform the dnties of their
office fa.ithfnlly, to the best of their ability, during the term for which they have
been elected. Granted; but suppose they no longer have the ability to perform
their duties ; wha~ then? A man may become paralyzed, insane, or incapacitated
in many ways from discharging the duties he has promised to perform ; must he still
retain his office, when he can no lona;er attend to 8 single linty appertaining thereto?
The exigencies of business may require an instslled officer to remove permanently
from the jurisdiction; must he retain an office, to the actual detriment of the Lodge
perhaps, when he cannot be present to attend to its duties? One of the first lessons
impressed upon our minds as Ma.sons is, that "Masonry is not to interfere with our
usual a.vocations, for these a.re on no account to be neglected.'' TbArefore we a.re
of the opinion that, when any officer of a Lodge finds that, for any reason, he has no
11Jnger the ability to perform the duties appertaining to his office, he should be per·
mitted to resign, and allow some one to be elected or appointed who can do justice
to the position and to the Lodge. We think our California law is a wise one, viz.:
"Vacancies in office, either in a Lodge or in the Grand Lodge, may occar by death,
deprivation, rellignation, rem01Jalfrom thejurildiction, suspension or expulsion."
Decision No. 3 we think is correci, as the petition is rejeoted and not the candidate.
Decision No. 4. involves a belief in the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction, which
we utterly repudiate.

The truth is, Masonry was not instituted solely f~r the mutual protection,. assistance
and social improvement of its members. Such duties are owed to all ma.nkmd, for all
mankind are brethren, and these duties a.re, therefore, to be practiced in all climes, and

It covers two hundred and nine pages of the Annual, and reviews the proceedings of

stantially ihe same as that of the Canadian official quoted below. Under the head
of "Canada," Bro. BBoWN says:The following strikes a Mason of the United States as rather abnormal, to say the
least. One of those District Deputy Grand Masters decided as follo~s : ".A broth~r
is entitled to his dimit, notwithstanding that t~e~e are charfteB aga1~st him .. He ~s
11till amel!able to Masonic trial, and, on conviction, penalties, notw1thstandt0g his
withdrawal."
Whereupon he animadverts as follows:What do you send out a brother with a clean record, and thus enable him to affiliate with' a Lodge no matter where, and yet reserve certain charges against him, on
which proof being made, you cau, and may, expel him from all the rights and privi,leges of Masonry? . This may be good law in Ontario, but everywhere else, repud~·
'a ted. No brother should be dimitted unless all dues are paid and no charges are or
can be preferred against him : otherwise his Lodge is party to a fraudulent misrep·
resentation to other Lodges, and the Fraternity at large.
The Canadian brother might with propriety retort, that this" good law in Ontario" wa.s not" everywhere else repudiated," as it is the law of ·Kansas to·day, the
Grand Master having so decided ; the Committee on Jurisprudence having approved

The following abstract of & para.graph of the Address we give to show up the result

Lodges in that city. Removing a.gain to the District, he petitioned for affiliation with a

"Now, what?" asks the advocate of the doctrine that a Lodge which has rejected a
"andidate, never loses inrisdiction over him, however frivolous or unfounded the obiection may be--however worthy he may be of Masonic honors.
First, any such claim or pretense is at war with the very spirit of Masonry, which, in
all its teachings, inculcates the broadest measure of personal IiberJy, and the enforce·
ment of such claim is nothing more than an act of petty tyranny. The longest period a
1,odge can claim its so-called jurisdiction over a reiected candidate, is the period fixed
by the Supreme Lodge of its jurisdiction, at the end of which he may present a new
petition for the dogrees. .For such a period the jurisdiction of the candidate may prop·
orly enough be left to the rejecting Lodge; when it expires, as he is free to prefer a
new petition to said Lodge, he should, of right, have the privilege of preseotmg it to
any other, if he so choose to do. and his previous rejeotion should not bar its reception
nor action thereon ; of course, in applying to another Lodge for the degrees he should
state the fact of his rejection, which would incite the Lodtre. or its committee, to make
n more searching inqniry into the habits, character and merits of the petitioner, when,
if found worthy, he should be admitted, without regard to the previous rejection.
But who does not know that three-fourths of tho rejeotions are the result of captious
or sinister motives? Who is not aware that mere petty malevolence. or detestable
oovy, has shut out from the Lodge many a good and true man? Indeed, one of the
most experienced Masonic writers of our country estimates the num her of candidates
thus excluded at ninety per cent.; this may De too high, but there is no doubt that the
num her will exceed fifty. perhaps sixty; per cent. of all rejections. So long as this
evil- and a (!'rowing one it is-prevails, such cases as the foregoing will recur. Candi·
dates. koowmg that their exclusion from the Lodge was prompted by perversity, or
do1vori~ht meanness, will suppress the fact on making a second application, and run
the risk of beinl!' deemed and treated as Masons irregularly made.
But as all Ie111slation which works unfairly, generating evil rather than good, can be
amended so as to bring about the contrary result, so can this, without more cost than
repealing a few lines of the Regnlations.
Again, it occasionally happens that a petitioner is rejected throuirh a mistake of
facts. or upon false information. yet, after a thorough investigation, he 1e found worthl,
and, when the time fixed has elapsed, on sending in a new petition, he is admitted. t
is granted such cases are not common, but enough so to influence Masonic legislators to
a more just and lenient couree. More of them would be h eard of. were petitioners,
when thus rejected, not disgusted with the ha.r•h. unbrotherly treatment received, and
wore Lodges more ready, more anxious to right a wronged applicant, when the error of
a committee, or R member or members, was disoovered. 'fo send a fair man from the
outer gate, branded with rejection, when the ballot which caused it was ca.st by some
ignorant, captious or malicious hand, is bad enough; bnt to claim jurisdiction over such
a one is unjust, and ill becomes an Order which inscribes Justice upon its banners. To
maintain it is simply to say," You cannot enter our Lodge, and the gate of every other
shall be barred agamst your admiesion."
We trust that Bro. BROWN will not rest until these absurd lawij are eliminated from
the Code of Kansas. His review of California le kindly, conrteous and fraternal. He

KENTUCKY.
The Grand Lodge ot Kentucky held its eighty-third Annual Communication in the
city of Louisville, commencing on the seventeenth day of Ootober, 1882,-the M.·.
W.·. Wu.LIAM HENRY Me:FF.BRT, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. HIRAlll
B.i.sse:'lT being Grand Secretary. Several subordinate Lodges were represented,
bot how many is something that" no fellow can find out" from the report. The
number of delegates in attendance, however, is stated as four hundred.
In commencing his Address the Grand Master ~ives this timely admonition : "To
those who are here for the first time, I give this special caution : Be constant in
attendance at our meetings and faithful in the discharge of duty, and may a spirit of
harmony, forbearaoce and brotherly kindness animate us in all our proceedings, and
may it be the constant care of every brother to see who can best work and best
agree." Several decisions are reporte{I, but they pertain to local matters of no particular interest to the general Craft.
Jn regard to the question of non-payment of dues, the Grand Master thinks their
-present mode of procedure, that is, making it obligatory upon the Lodges to notify
delinquents for dues, then summon them to appear before the Lodge, then prefer
formal charges and proceed to a regular trial, works a great hardship upon the subordinates, and we folly agree with him. We think our California rule much the best.
When a brother is six months in arr~ars he is notified of th6 fact by the Secretary,
and at the same time notified that, unless his dues are paid at the next stated meet·
ing, or some good and sufficient reason given for his failure to pay, he will be sue·
pended from all the rights and privileges of Masonry. Thus the brother bas due
notice of his delinquency, and if he fails to appear at the next stated meeting and
pay his arrearages, or give some reason which will be Patisfactory to the Lodge for
his failure to pay, he can blame no one but himself if be is suspended.
The Grand Master resorted to a shrewd device in order to aBcertain what members attended regularly to their duties in the Grand Lodge, and how many, while
receiving mileage and per di.em, shirked their duties in the Grand Body and spent
their time upon the street• in attendance upon their private business. He caused
the chairs of the delegates to be tagged, so that all were seated in accordance with
seniority, and the Grand Marshal, Deacons and Sword Bearer were instmcted to se8
that none but delegates occupied these chairs. Thus, those who attempted to receive wages when none were their doe, if any there should be, would at once be
detec«.d. The sum of $520 was contributed by the subordinate Lodges and forwarded to the sufferers by yellow fever in Florida.
The Grand Master makes an urgent appeal for a more liberal support of the
Widows' and Orphans' Home, and suggests that the festival of ST. JoHN the Baptist
be utilized throughout the jurisdiction in its interest, as is usually done in the city of
Louisville. Having made a thorough inspection of the buildings and surroundings,
he says:1 unhesitatin~ly assure you that I found nothing from cellar to attic that did not
indicate the utmost care and cleanlineMs, the highest. regard for health and happi·
ness. And I am fully convinced that in all its appointments, its local management
and general discipline, it has never been In a more satisfacfory and prosperous condition than during the present administration.
It is to be hoped that the appeal of the Grand Master will have the effect to stimulate the Craft in Kentucky to more earnest efforts in be halt' of this noble charity.
He announces the death of three Past Grand Masters during the year ; one having
reached the good old age of eighty-three years, one eighty, and the youngest sixty·
eight. Bequiescat in pace.
The Grand Treasnrer reports a balance, cash on hand, of $2,509 80, and the total
resources of the Gra.nd Lodge, $23,858 80.

The Report on Correspondence, by Bro. JAMES W. STATON, covers one hundred
and forty-eight pages or the Annual, and contains a review of all the Grand Lodges
in the United States except that of Washington Territory, and all in the Dominion of
Canada except Manitoba. The Grand Lodges of England, Ireland, Scotland and
New South Wales are also included, making a very complete, interesting and valua·
hie report. California, for 1881, receives a generous share of his attention, and his
notice of us is courteous and fraternal. He concurs in all the decisions of Grand
Master DENSON, which he says are in conformity to sound Masonic principles. He
quotes from the report of our "venerable Secretary" relative to the library, upon
which he comments as follows:Now Craftsmen of Kentucky, what do you think of that report? Here is a Grand
Lodge organized just fifty years since the Grand Lodge of Kentucky, and by the
energy of its distinguished Grand Secretary, liberally aided by the Grand Lodge,
has collected one of the finest libraries on the Continent. While we have been frit.
tering away our opportunities, other jurisdictions have been active, and can now
boast of magnificent collections of Masonic literature, while we must be satisfied
with oar little pile of Grand Lodge Proceedings only, with not even a complete file
of oar own proceedings. -It is all wrong; we ought to get out of the ashes and try
and recover some of the lost ground. It is a shame that the Mother Grand Lodge
of the Mississippi valley, should be so far behind in library matters. It is not too
late to recover some of the lost territory yet, but we should not lose a moment in
getting to work.
He also extracts that portion of our Grand Lectare·r's Report relative to funeral
ceremonies, which he fully endorses. Of Bro. HILL'S Report, he says:Bro. flILL is slightly mistaken when he says "the Grand Lodge reduced the dues
of subordinates to tile Grand Lodge to fifty cents per member, instead of one dollar,
as before, and then resolved to meet hereafter only once in two years." The Grand
Lodge did neither, and I trust will never do so foolish a thing as to fix biennial meet·
ings instead of annual meetings.
Referring to some remarks mnde by Bro. Moanrs on the Past Master's degree, it
would seem that in California, as in some other jurisdictions, a Past Master made in
a Chapter, mast be re-obligated before he can be installed Master of a Symbolic
Lodge. If we were called upon to re-obligate a newly elected Master, we could
make it no stronger or more pertinent than that in a Chapter; hence we are wholly
nnable to see the necessity of such a course, unless it would be for the same reasons
given by Bro. HILL, when he says, " We felt, like the curtailed fox of the fable, that
we should like to have the same sauce served oat to all others."
We do not believe in mixing blue and red Masonry. The Lodge is supposed to·
know nothing of the Past Master's degree in the Chapter, and should insist npon the
observance of its own ceremonies. We are strongly tempted to make farther ex·
tracts from this excellent report, but time presses and we mast on to the next.

HIRAM BASSETT was re-elected Grand Secretary. There are several Lodges in thisjnris·
diction, but we have no time to count them. The total membership is reported at
fifteen thousand four hundred and ninety-three-five hundred and fifty-nine being
ministers of the gospel.
LOUISIANA.
The seventy-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana was
held 'in the city of New Orleans, commencing on the twelfth day of February,
1883,-the M.·. W.·. WILLIAM RITCHIE WHITAKER, Grand Master, presiding, and the
R. '. W.-. JAMES C. BATCHELOR, M. D., being Grand Secretary. Fifty-eight chartered
Lodges, were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master, although principally confined to local matters,
is not without interest to the general reader. It is a carefully prepared paper of
thirty-two pages, and gives an excellent idea of the condition and workings of the
Craft in that jurisdiction. The "loved and lost" of his own and other jurisdictions

Grand Locbje of California.

are not forgotten, but to the memory of each a fraternal tribute is given. He expresses warlll thanks to the brethren of Pennsylvania for their gratuitous offers of
aid to the Masonic sufferers by the late overflow, bat, fortunately, their kindly proffered assistance was not needed. A somewhat novel phase of the Representative
question is presented: The Grand Lodge of Vermont, by edict, limited the term of
its Representatives near other Grand Lodges to three years ; and, in 11 communi·
cation to the Grand Master of Louisiana, the Grand Master of Vermont informs
him that, in accordaooe with this rule, the commission of the Representative of the
Grand Lodge of Louisiana near the Grand Lodge of Vermont had expired by limitation, and nominated a brother to succeed the preeelit incumbent. The Grand
Master of Louisiana, while conceding the right of Vermont to make such rules as
she might deem proper for the government of her own Representatives, could not
see that the edict in any manner affected the Representative of Louisiann, and he
politely informed the Grand Master of Vermont that, should any cause exist for a
change, it would be promptly considered, bnt the commission of its representative,
until revoked by the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, would remain in full force and effect,
In this ruling he was sustained by the Grand Lodge; correctly, in oar opinion,
In answer to a question, he ruled that "Masons in Masonic regalia (clothing)
cannot join in the procession of a secret organization not Masonic, and that each an
association cannot participate in any Masonic ceremony.'' He saw no impropriety,
however, in Masons performing the ceremony of laying a corner-stone, while at the
same time other societies were in the procession in regalia, so long as they took no
part in the rite ; or at a funeral, so long as the Lodge had full control of the ceremonies.
During the prevalence of the yellow fever in Florida, he directed the Grand Secretary to draw from the" Overflow Relief Fnnd" the sum of one hundred dollars in
aid ot the sufferers by the epidemic, an act of charity which was doubtless duly
appreciated by the stricken brethrtm of Florida. He calls attention to the meagre
snpport given by the Lodges to " Louisiana Relief Lodge," and says that, had it not
been for the aid extended to it by his order from the Overflow Relief Fund, It would
have been compelled to suspend its beneficent labors. This Lodge of Relief expended
daring the year the snm of el,076 85 for the relief of distressed brethren from the
various States and from foreign countries, none of whom, we are pleased to say,
were from California. A resolution was adopted appropriating one thousand dollars
to the funds of the Relief Lodge.
·
In the matter of joint occupa.ncy of Lodge Halls, the Grand Master intimates
that the Lodges themselves might be safely entrusted with the regulation of such
matters, and suggested the repeal of all legislation upon the subject. The Oom·
mittee on Jurisprudence, however, could not agree with the Grand Master's view of
the case, and reported against any repeal of the restrictive law, and their report
was adopted. As a general principle, we think Masonic Halls should be used for
Masonic purposes only; but there are sometimes cases where this is inconvenient,
if not impracticable, and in such instances we see no impropriety in a Lodge occupying a hall in common with other societies until able to procure one for themselves.
The Grand Master says : - "There are many evidences of a generally improved
condition of the Craft throughout the State, manifested in awakened Interest, greater
attention to Lodge dntiee, and more earnest effort to revive the standing of weak
Lodges. There can be no doubt of the fact that there i~ a solid reason for anticipating a decided and substantial advance in the standing and beneficial influence of
Masonry in Louisiana."

.MAINE.
The sixty-fourth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Maine was
commenced in the city of Portland on the first day of May, 1883,-the M. ·. W. ·.
MARQUIS F. Kum, Grand Master, presiding, and the R. -. W.-. !RA BERRY being

The Address of the Grand Master gives evidence of zeal, fidelity and culture.
He pa.ye a fraternal tribute to the memory of several of the brethren whom death
had removed from their circle during the year, one of whom, Bro. lsAAC DOWNING,
Pa.st Senior Grand Warden, had been an active Mason fifty-five yea.I'll. Be
reports that the venerable Grand Secretary, while arranging some books in the
library, fell from a step-ladder and broke a leg. Much anxiety was felt for a time
on account of his advanced age, but "thanks to a vigorous constitution and a pure
life," he had recovered; .. the bones of forescore years knitted a.s readily as those
of youth," and he was again diligently a.nd patiently attending to his duties. We
are rejoiced to learn of this favorable result. If we mistake not, Bro. BERRY is
the oldest Grand Secretary no~ living in the United Sta.tee. The Grand Master
states that during one of his visits to the Lodges "an invitation from the Grand
Secretary, to accompany him on a short walk of nine miles to the top of an adjacent mountain, was respectfully but firmly declined." W e presume that· Bro•
BEBRY, having been Grand Secretary when the aforesaid mounts.in was a hole:in
the ground, was anxious to inspect its summit in search of relatives in the vegetable kingdom. We echo the pioue ejaculation of the Grand Master : " Spa.re him,
0 Lord." One dispensation was granted for the formation of a. new Lodge. The
claims of Maine to Masonic precedence are asserted in the following :It is a pleaaure to note that returns have been received from every Lodge.
These show that eight hundred and five have been initiated, an increase of one

reinstated, an increase of thirty-eight. The visits of the angel of death have been
unusually frequent during the year- two hundred and sixty-five ; one of ea.oh
seventy-two have been transferred to the celestial Lodge. Our present member"
ship is (19,469) nineteen thousand four hundred and sixty-nine, a. gain of four
hundred and seventy-eight. Maine stands first of all jurisdictions in the world in

new Grand Lodge was formed by eight Lodges holding under the Grand Lodge of
Scotland, and four of Irish origin; twelve in all-being scarcely more than onefourth of the Lodges interested. This small minority determined to set up housekeeping for themselves ; and accordingly assembled in Convention, adopted a
Constitution, elected Grand Officers, and proclaimed the Grand Lodge of New
South WaleH duly established and organized, with exclusive jurisdiction over all
"the territory of the colony of New South Wales. This claim is decidedly Arctic
in its coolness. Had a majority of the Lodges, existing in the Province of New
South Wales, concurred in the establishment of the new Grand Lodge, we would
have had no hesitatation in considering their claims to independence; but, when
so small a minority claim absolute sovereignty, the Grand Lodge of California
cannot consistently disturb the relations of amity existing between herself and her
sister Grand Lodges of England, Ireland and Scotland by recognizing them as a
sovereign Grand Lodge.

The Grand Lodge of Maryland was convened in Special Communication in the

The ninety-sixth Annual Communication was commenced in the city of Baltimore
on the twenty-first day of November, 1882,-the M.·. w.-. JOHN S. TYSON, Grand
Ma•ter, presiding, and the R.-. W.'. JACOB H. MEDAIRY being Grand Secretary.
Seventy-two Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master commences a very brief Address by the following fraternal
tribute to the memory of our late brother, the Rev. THOMAS GUARD, Grand Chaplain
or the Grand Lodge of Marvland :It becomeR my melancholy duty to inform you, officially, of an event which haA
been announced by the entire press of the country, and has everywhere excited the
most profound sorrow. Rev. dro. THOMAS GUARD, Grand Chaplain of thiM Grand
Lodge, and who had formerly held the same office in the Grand Lodge of California,
departed this life on Sunday, October 15th, 1882, aged fifty-one years, at his residence, No. 160 Park avenue, in this city. His death is a loss, not only to this community, but to humanity. His fame as an orator and as a minister of religion, was
known throughout tbe United States. By special invitation of the authorities of
Mount Vernon Church, of which the deceased was pastor, the installed officers of
the Grand Lodge attended his funeral in a body, and also attended the memorial
services of the church on the following Sunday. I suggested that a. special committee be appointed to prepare a suitable memorial of oor distinguished and
lamented brother, for record in our proceedings.
Nowhere was the loss of this distinguished and eloquent Minister of the Gospel
more sincerely monmed than In California. During his brief residence among us,
by his earnest piety, his genial social qualities, his surpassing eloquence, and his
liberal charity, he won his way to the hearts of our people of all classes and denominations. His Masonic experience was a brief one, but It was sufficiently long to
carry to our hearts the conviction-when the sad news of his death was ,heralded to
our shores-that Masonry, as well as the Chnroh, had sustained a loss which It would
be difficult to repair. His memory Is enshrined in our hearts; his labon on earth
are ended. May his reward in the celestial Lodge be abundant.
The official acts of the Grand Master were few, and he was called upon to render
no decisions of sufficient importance to be reported to the Grand Lodge. One dispensation for the formation of a. new Lodge was granted. He closes his Address with

Hands were joined, "Auld Lang Syne" was sung, and thus ended the one hundred and forty-ninth Stated Communication of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts.
Since the above was written we have received the proceedings of the Quarterly
Communication, held in the city of Boston on the fourteenth day of March, 1883.
One hundred and fifteen Lodges were represented. A communication from the
so-called Grand Lodge of Peru, proposing fraternal relations with the Grand Lodge
of Maseachasetts, was referred to a special committee.
'l'he committee to whom the Annual Address of the Grand Master was referred,
say, in their report :Inasmuch as the Grand Lodge has already taken such steps as seemed necessary,
in regard to those subjects presented in the Addrees of the Grand Master which
a.ppear to require action, it only remains for your committee to congratulate the
)fraternity of the Commonwealth. on its prosperous and happy condition, and to
join in the general and hearty ex\)ressions of b'Tl>titude to the Most Worshipful
Grand Master for the arduous and mcessant labor on his part which has so largely
contributed to bring about that condition, and for the very interesting and instructive, as well as modest report of his valuable services during the past year.
Two members of a subordinate Lodge were expelled; one for burglary, the other
for a fouler crime. In Massachusetts, the Graml Lodge alone expels, at the
recommendation of a subordinate or of its own motion.
Two interesting presentations were made ; one being a portrait of the Hon.
J osIAH BARTLETT, third Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts after
the union in 1792. He served two years, viz.: 1798 and 1799, and was again elected
in 1810. He died March 5, 1820. 'l'he other presentation was a portrait of Past
Grand Master MOSES MICHAEL HAYS, who 0<.'Cupied the Grand Master!s Chair
during the years 1788, '89, '90 and '91, and who died on the ninth day of May,
1805. TJ:.ese valuable relics of the past were gladly accepted, and the thanks of
the Grand Lodge were returned to the donors.
It was stated that the charter iesued to St. John's Lodge, .of Boston, in lieu of
the one destroyed by fire in 1864, did not correctly describe the precedence of that
Lodge, and as the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of its organization would
occur during the present year, it seemed an appropriate time ~ make the proper
alteration. It was therefore moved that the Grand Master be authorized to issue
to this venerable Lodge a charter, with such corrections from its present form as
he might deem proper. Which motion was unanimously carried. After some
further unimportant business the Grand Lodge was closed in ample form.
The proceedings of a Quarterly Communication held in the city of Boston on
the thirteenth day of June, 1883, have been placed in our hands since the foregoing
was sent to the printer- the M." W." SAMUEL CROCKER LAWRENCE, Grand Master, presiding, and the R. '. W. ·. SERENO D. NICKERSON being Grand Secretary.

One more decision claims onr attention, as it touches a matter which bas already
caused some controversy between this and other jurisdictions. A brether from
Michigan found himself in Nevada sick and destitute. A Lodge in Nevada came to
his relief, paid his doctor and board bills and famished him with money in all
amountin&' to several hundred dollars, to enable him to return to his home in 'Michigan. The Lodge in Nevada applied to the Lodge of which the distressed brother
was a member, a.eking to be reimbursed for the amount expended, which said Lodse
refused to pay on the ground that they are "unable to meet such expense and are
not liable for said claim.'' The Grand Master decided, that:'
. The L.od~e to which this brother belongs is not liable for this claim. 1'he quest1.on of ~id is not a compnleory one. Each Mason is bound to give to tile extent of
his ablltty-no more. The brethren of Nevada simply performed their Masonic
clnty.

The following idea of the pre•emioence of Freemasonry, as compared with other
organizations, is well conceived and felicitously expreS&ed :

.
·~· .

Viewed from the exterior, Freemasonry presents no marked excellencies which
are not possessed in common with numerons other associations. To the profane, it iR
simply an organization which professes to practice virtues which e.Jl mankind are under like obligations to perform; but to those who have entered within the most
secret apartment of the temple, and beheld the cherubim whose outstretched win~s
shield the ark of the covenant, and who have studied its symbols and read their
hidden meaning, it exhibits peculiarities which distinguish it from all other bumat
organizations; and to him who has been so fortunate as to receive the true ~pirit of
the inspiration which it breathes in its every teaching, it must always remain without
a peer in bis affections. We speak this in no spirit of self-approbation or of vaunted
superiority, for while it must ever retain to it;ielf the peculiar field it occupies, it also
imposes a. greater and higher measure of duties upon its initiates. This is not an .
occasion which calls for an expo•ition of tile nature or extent of those duties. Yon
woold not be here if you did not already understand and appreciate them, and yow
also know whether it is worth the expenditure of time and labor which is demande!J
by the efforts to make it the mea.ns of doing a ~reater and ever increasing measure
of good, not only to ourselves, but to all mankmd. Such i~ the great purp o~e of our
assemblage once more aronod our sacred altar. Let us humbly and reverently pray
that the incense which we ~hall bum at this time, shall prove grateful to Him to
whom our thanks are doe for the social and fraternal intercourse we enjoy at those
annual reunions, when not the least among the privileges they confer, is the renewal
and cultivation of old friendships and the formation of new ties, which, we trnst, will
endure so long as life itself she.II le.st.

We recommend the following to all Grand Masters " whithersoever dispersed: '•
I refused to grant any dispensation which required a suspension of any law of the
Grand Lodge-such as to take the ballot at the same meeting at which the precedlngo
degree was conferred; to transact business with a less number than seven members;
to elect a Treasurer to fill a vacancy; to initiate a temporary sojourner: also one who
hRa not resided within the jurisdiction of the Lodge twelve months ; also a non-resident ;
also a young man in his non-age ; to confer two degrees on the same ca11didate at the
same meeting ; and to install a brother as Master who has not served as a Warden. I
know of no warrant or authority for the suspension of a written law by the Grand Master.
On the contrary, I think that he is under a double obligation to enforce the rules which
the Grand Lodge bas established. I am well awe.re that it has been claimed by many
eminent Masons, that dnring the recess of the Grand Lodge, sole executive power is
vested in the Grand Master, and that he may, of his own pleasure, set aside its laws.
To such an extent has this practice gone, that I might have claimed the force of pre·
cedeot to justify me in so <loin(!", but my installation obligation contained a clause,
that in whatever light I may view the claim of Grand Masters to be possessed of
certain undefined, and perhaps I may say undefinable, prerogatives, in my judgment
utterly forbid its exercise by me.
It is often claimed by certain moss-grown Me.sonic antiquaries and delvers among
the ancient landmarks, that the Grand Master ie above the law ; a Masonic autocrat
in ract, whose hereditary prerogatives and privileges no ~tatutory code may set aside
or disturb. This absurd theory is rapidly being dissipated under the strong light of
common sense, and we are glad to see so intelligent and learned a brother as the

1883.]

written constitutions, Grand Masters were doubtless invested with plenary powers;
but when Grand Lodges were organized, and Constitutions adopted for their government, the Grand Master became as firmly bound by their provisions as the humblest
worker in the quarries. Every Grand Master promises, upon his installation, to obey

""Grand Master,save those which the Constitution prescribes. In some jurisdictions,

quarters for what Is termed her uncharitableness in suspending members for nonpayment of dues. We claim the.t we a.re not obnoxious to this charge, and that we

the Lodge, and is therefore unworthy of Masonic consideration. We have never yet

Alas! those "twin vices." When will Masons give heed to the lessons so solemnly impressed upon their minds upon the threshold of the temple? That "Temperance is that due restraint upon our passions which renders the body tame and
governable and frees the mind from the allurements of vice," end that the Sacred

there is no excuse. In no case can he who takes the name of God in vain be benefited, physically, morally, or intellectually, by his profanity. In the mouth of any
man, it is disgusting; in that of a. Mason, it is hideous. It shows that he has forgotten, or is indifferent to, the first leseons taught in Masonry ; a.nd the Ma.son who
is guilty of habitua.I indulgence in it, commits an oft'ence age.inst ~he institution,
which should subject him to discipline.
The resolution forbidding the joint occupancy of halls, adopted a.t the last Annual Communication, was rescinded. We a.re in favor of Masons owning and occupying their own halls when practioa.ble, but, in small communities, this is not a.lwa.ys
possible; and, as &matter of convenience or necessity, we can see no objeotion to a
joint occupancy. The various Orders, organized for fraternal and benevolent pur·
poses, though operating upon &plane essentially differing from that which Masonry
occupies, a.re each, in their proper sphere, doing a. good and beneficent work. They
can learn nothing by meeting in a. Ma.sonic ha.11, which is not free to public criticism
every da.y in the week; and we can gain no knowledge of their esoteric workings by
holding our meetings in the halls which they have occupied.

How must that Grand Body have been shocked when, on the following day,
after having installed the newly elected Grand Officers, their venerable ·Paet Grand
Master WM stricken down by a severe attack of pneumonia, of which he died four
days afterwards. A sad realization of his own presentiment. He WM buried with
appropriate Masonic ceremonies at Deer Lodge, by the Grand Lodge, in Special
Communication, on the fourteenth day of October. A page is devoted to an obit·
ua.ry notice and memorial resolutions.
By a neat resolution, the Grand Lodge welcomes our youngest sister, Arizona,
a.nd by another, full of the proper spirit, commends the action of the Grand Lodge
of Utah in excluding Mormons from a participation in our privileges.
Many of the inconveniences and embarrassments complained of in the Report
of the Grand Secretary will be measurably removed, now that so much railroad
communication ha.s been opened between the settled portions of the Territory.
Montana, until within a few years, has not only been practically isolated from
other portiQns of the Union, but its own towns and settlements, by the long distances separating them, and the precarious modes of travel, have been isolated
from ea.ch other. It is now rapidly filling with settlers, and must speedily become
one of the largest, as it has ever been one of the most intelligent and active, Ma·
sonic jurisdictions in the northwest. Masonry there has been something more
than ceremony and pastime. In early days it was a nucleus around which an
incongruous people gathered, harmonized, and adopted plane for personal protection against gangs of robbers and murderers. Then it was law, society, religion,
charity and benevolence. It has succored the needy, fed the hungry, clothed the
naked, buried the dead, and bound up the wounds of the afflicted. It ha.s grown
and strengthened on this broad basis of Masonic principle ever since, and we can
but unite with all our hearts in the dying prayer of Grand Master POHEBOY, that
the " choicest and richest of Heaven's bleeeings" may be showered abundantly
upon the Grand Lodge of Montana.

The taicing of members of the particular Lodge to create a fund to be expended
in some work, however good, and which may never come, is to anticipate' and com·
pel members to bear a burden not called for by the present condition of the Lodge
or its members, and is beyond the scope of the principle upon which the true Masonic work is founded.
'l.'he action of the Grand Master in forbidding the lottery, before referred to,
and his decisions were sustained by the Grand Lodge.
In a case wherein the Master of a Lodge ruled that a brother, against whom
charges were pending, had no right to vote upon the application of a candidate for
the degrees, the committee reported that the brother, at the time alleged in said
charges; was a member of the Lodge in good and reguliU- standing, and entitled to
participate in the ballot; "that, as a matter oflaw, the preferring of charges cannot so affect his standing in the Lodge as to deprive him of his right to vote-evet"Y
brother being presumed to be innocent until he is proved to be guilty. Aliy other
view would place it in the .power of an unscrupulous party, by filing charges with·
out foundation, to overthrow the safeguard of a nnanimous ballot ; or even, as has
been attempted, to elect the officers of the Lodge against the will of the majority
of the members." The committee call attention to the "weakness and unmasonic
conduct of the Master in permitting an appeal to the Lodge from his decision."
Perhaps the brother had been reading the proceedings of a certain Grand Lodge
wherein the rulings of the Grand Master are appealed· from and defeated by a
majority vote of the members.

'l'he centennial anniversary of the organization of the Grand Lodge of New
Jersey will occur in 1886, and a special committee was appointed to mature plans
for its proper celebration. Warrants were granted for the formation of two new
Lodges, and the petition for a third was referred to the Grand Master to grant
111 dispensation if, in his judgment, such a course was desirable.
The Committee on History does not appear to have been signally successful in
Its operations, and at its own suggestion was relieved from further services, and a
new committee of three appointed.
The reports of the District Deputy Grand Masters show that those officers
have been faithful in the discharge of their duties, and that the L odges generally
are in a prosperous condition.

Under the head of "District of Columbia,'' Bro. NoRt'ON discusses a question
to which we have given ·some attention in another portion of this report, and we
are pleased to find that our ideas are in harmony on the point at iBSue.
The Committee on .Turisprudence of the Grand Lodge of the District of Columbia held that a Lodge has no right to discipline an affiliated Muon of another
jurisdiction without the consent of the Lodge of which the brother is a member.
In commenting upon this report, Bro. NORTON says : From the opinion of the committee we most emphatically dissent. Two years
ago we had occasion, and gave our views quite fully upon the question. The question
was at the time brought into prominence by the action of a Lodge in Tennessee
towards a Kentucky Mason (one T. OLIVER), to which the Grand Lodge of Kentucky took exception. The same points were raiaedW e assent , as before, to the proposition that Lodge courtesy should impel a
·Lo~e, having jmisdiction where an offense is committed, to notify the Lodge to
whiCh the offending brother may belong, but that is all that can be expeuted of it ;
the welfare of the Fraternity _requires that measures should at once be taken to
vindicate the good na.me of Masonry by the punishment of brethren who deserve
punishment, and we have never been able to find any justification for awaiting the
action of the Lodge to which the brother belongs. 'l'he point to be settled in any
given case is, which Lodge first commenced proceedings. Whichever did has
exclusive jurisdiction. The principle laid down in the quotation from Mitchell's
Common Law of Masonry which the committee characterizes as the "just and correct rule,'' is rejected by the bulk of Masonic authority an(l hy the best living Masonic jurists; indeed, so far as our information extends, by nearlr. all.
It seems to u~ that nothing but sensitiveness over the possibility of an invasion
of sovereignty could ever have induced Grand Lodges or Masonic jurists to consent
to debate the question.
We could not have better expressed our own opinion. The report covers one
hundred and fifty-nine pages, and is a thoroughly good one.

He says:-

In 1873 new regulations were adopted by the Grand Lodge, providing a pena.11f'
for the non-payment of dues. I am forced to the conclusion that these regulatiotll
do not properly protect the interests of the subordinate Lodges. So long as theGrand Lodge requires payment of a stated sum from the subordinate bodies, it
must of necessity permit those Lodges to collect dues from members, and as their
existence depends entirely upon their ability to pay to the Grand Lodge each year
the moneys demanded, they should have the authority to compel payment of the
dues provided for by their by-laws. Every Maaon, when he becomes a member of
a J,odge, signs his name to the by -laws, and by his own act enters into a contract
to pay into that Lodge each year the amount therein stated as dues. Any failure
on his part to do this indicates a want of integrity, and is a clear violation of a
solemn compact. And as the Lodge enters into obligations based upon the agreement of each member to pay a certain sum each year, the ne~leet or failure to pay
often proves a source of embarrassment to the Lodge and bnngs scandal upon the
Fraternity. There has been, in my opinion, a great deal of mistaken sentiment
brought into the discussions of this subject heretofore. If the neglect or refusal
to pay was confined to our indigent brethren all this might do, but experience
demonstrates that it is not. The representatives of Lodges here present will, I
think, bear me out in the aBSertion that at least three-fourths of those unaffiliated
by Lodges for non-payment of dues are those who could well afford to pay if they
chose so to do. 'l'herefore, my opinion is the neglect or refusal to pay by members
who can do so without injury to their families, should subject the delinquent to a
loss of his Masonic privileges, and that the penalty should be suspension from all
the rights and privileges of Masonry until payment be made of the amount due at
the time of such suspension. This .penalty should only be infticted in accordance
with such regulations as the Grand Lodge may prescribe. Nor upon any who may
show to the satisfaction of his Lodge that by reaaon of indigence he is unable to
pay. This course would be entirely in accordance with Masonic usage, and would
enable Lodges to deal out to delinquent members something corresponding to that
which they receive, if they fail to pay Grand Lodge dues.
We have been roundly abused in some quarters for what is termed our uncharitable custom of suspending members for non-payment of.dues, and we are glad to
Hee that New York, in her one hundred and second year, has awakened to the
necessity of adopting some such meaaure. In California the rule has worked well.
There is no uncharitableness in it, bec!'use no brother who is really unable to pay
his dues is ever suspended, if the fact be known. Every brother receives due
notice of his indebtedness, and, if he fails to pay, or submit some good reason why
he has not done so, he cannot claim to be unjustly dealt with if the penalty is
inflicted. As the Grand Master truly says : " There baa been a great deal of
mistaken sentiment brought into the diacuBSioIIS of this subject heretofore." Each
party should comply with the terms of the compact, and one of those terms is,
that each member shall pay a stated sum, monthly, quarterly or annually, as dues.
The Grand Master mentions an in~tanoe where two Masons who had been unaffiliated by their Lodge for the non-payment of dues, applied for membership and
were accepted in a Lodge in another jurisdiction; they each owing twenty dollars
to the Lodge from which they had been dropped from the roll. The case was
referred to the Grand Master, who replied, that, "as non-payment of dues was
not considered a Masonic offense by the Grand Lodge of New York, the action of
the subordinate Lodge was legal and proper."
This portion of the Grand Master's Address was referred to the Committee on

upon it. The Grand Master answers the question, " What iR a legal summons?"

be handed to him or sent through the post-office to his last known addreBB.

The report of the Board of Relief of San Francisco is a remarkable document.
The amount to the credit of the fund in January, 1882, was about 812,000, of which
nearly $3,000 were due to money refunded by Lodges and individuals, which to us
is marvelous, because after many years' experience in like work we have seen nothing approaching it. Out of this sum nearly $9,000 had been expended, inoluding
seven applicants from New York, and the burial of fifteen brethren from various
jurisdictions. All honor to that Board of Relief.

NORTH CAROLINA.
The Grand Lodge of North Carolina held Its ninety-sixth Annual Communication
in the city of Raleigh, commencing on the fifth day of December, 1882,-the M.·. W.·.
HENRY F.GBAINOll:Jt, Grand Master, presiding, and the R:. w.·.DoNALD w. BAIN being
Grand Secretary. One hundred and eleven I,odges were represented.
'fhe Grand Master delivered a well-prepared Address, in which he appeals strongly
to his brethren for an increased manifestation of zeal and energy in advancing,
upholding and enforcing the teachings of Masonry. In this connection he rves
some excellent advice, which, if heeded, cannot fail to produce a beneficial result.
He says:Make your Lodge meetings as social, instructive and pleasant as possible. En·
deavor to make them &pecially attractive j.so much so that every member, ln~tead
of dreading or forgetting the time of Loage meeting , will look forward to it with
pleasant anticipations, and feel himself wiser and better for !laving attended. Have
some object in view and accomplish some good in your collective c11pacity as a
Lodge at every meeting . If you have no distressed brother or the family of such
asking relief, perhaps tbere are others within your jurisdiction in need, whom you
can relieve without injury to yourselves or your Lodge. While you are bound by
special ties to those of our own household, every human being has a claim upon ou1·
kind offices. Do good unto a.11, is the injunction. Ont of the Lod~e let every Me.son
practice the duties and high moral lessons taught in it. Let his hfe and conduct be
squared by the square of virtue and morality.
If every :Mason would heed these suggestions, how !loon would the complaints of
want of interest and lack of attendance in our Lodges ce11se. The secret of succeKs
is to make our Lodge meetings attractive and Interesting. The mere routine of
ritualistic labor, after its novelty has pa.BSed, soon becomes monotonous, and fails to
attract. Something more is needed to a.waken the interest and fix the attention of
the members. Introduce discussions upon questions of :Ma.sonic law and usage;
such discussions tend to create an interest in the subject, and induce brethren to
search farther and deeper for more light; and thus many will be prompted to study
the jurisprudence of Masonry and to inform themselves more fully relative to its bis·
tory and objects, thus storing their minds with useful knowledge, and preparing
themselves, when called upon, to take those official positions in the Lodge which, in
order to be successfully filled, require the incumbent to be something more thane.
mere talking ma.chine, wound up to :cepee.t a certain formula of words, with, in many
ins~nces, about as much appreciation of their real meaning as the parrot who glibly

He quotes, approvingly, portions of Grand Master DENSON's Address, and also that
portion of Grand Lecturer BBAEFFEa's report relative to funeral ceremonies. He
thinks the decision of Grand Master D1111so11 relative to the rights of contributing
non-affiliates" quite original," and makes e. somewhat lengthy argument iu favor of
equal right.• for this class of brethren. We are willing to concede e.11 he claims for
non-affiliates whli are Masons in good standing, but we have no sympathy for that
class of non-affiliates who, having the ability to contribute to the general purposes
nf Masonry, elect to sever their connection with the Lodge for the purpose of evading their share of the labors and responsibilities inseparable from t.hat connection,
and who, when trouble comes upon them, are quick to claim Masonic sympathy and
aid. They are drones in the hive ; dead branches upon the Masonic·tree; leeches
upon the body of the fraternity. The race of this class is short in California; six
months are given them to affiliate, or at least to make the attempt to do so. If they
try and fail, it is not·their fault, and, in that case, six months more are given them;
and thus the attempt to do their duty, even if abortive, preserves them in good
standing. It is the duty of every Masou to be a member of some Lodge, that he
may assist iu caring for the sick, in relieving the dis ~ressed and in burying the dead,
and he who is not willing to do this, has, in his heart, none of the true spirit of
Masonry.
He appropriates that portion of Bro. HILI.'S report rPlative to Foreign Grand
Bodies, giving due credit therefor. Bro. CHADWICK closes his interesting and valuable report with a long article upon "N on-afllliates," in which there is much food
for reflection ; but our limits wlll not admit of a discussion of the question at this
time.

of Pennsylvania at its Quarterly, Extra, and Annual Communications, is before

One hundred and thirty-five pages are devoted to the Seaqui-Centennial Celebration. The record is very interesting, but, as the main features of this grand
pageant have been published in nearly every public journal in the land, we reserve

was held in the cit"y of Philadelphia, commencing on the twenty-seventh day of
December, 1882. Sixty-seven Lodges were represented.
The Stewards of the " STEPHEN GIRARD Charity Fund" report an expenditure
for purposes of charity of $2,770; $2,405 of which was for the relief of members of
their own'jurisdiction, and $365 to Masons bailing from other jurisdictions, none
of which were from California.
The Almoners of the Grand Lodge Charity Fund also report an expenditure of
$2,933; relief being granted in 257 cases, 233 of which were from Pennsylvania,
and twenty-four from other jurisdictions; California again not represented. This
makes $5,703 expended for charity during the year, which leads us to believe that
our Pennsylvania. brethren are by no means remisa in their practice of the greatest
of the cardinal virtues.
A list of nine Centenary Lodges is given, the oldest of which was constituted
in 1758, and the youngest in 1785. The records of the Lodges from 1730 to 1767
are unfortunately lost, but the Committee on Library are confident that they will
yet be found among some cast-aside papers, and caution their brethren to carefully
preserve any old Masonic papers that may be discovered, and forward them to the
committee for preservation.
The Grand Master, in an able and happily worded Address, sums up the rooord
of his two years' service. He reports that the year pa.st has been one of unabated
prosperity to the Craft in Pennsylvania. "Throughout the whole jurisdiction,"
he says, "we have the most gratifying evidences of the lively interest felt by the
brethren in the institution of Freemasonry." He calls attention to two events of
the year whkh he deems of special importance, viz., the celebration of the one
hundred and fiftieth anniversary of the formation of the Grand Lodge of Penn1ylvania, and the sale of the Chestnut Street Hall for $225,000, all of which amount
hu been placed in the sinking fund for the extingui.shment of the debt upon the
present Grand Lodge property, which amounts to $1,026,850. The annual interest
upon thiR sum is $63,975, which is offset by the amount of int erest received upon
Investments held by the sinking fund. H e expresses his great satisfaction a.t the
Jlresent condition of the finances of the Grand Lodge; its credit is now strong,
and the sinking fund has been augmented till now it is in a condition to afford the
oancellation of a large amount of the bonded indebtedness at an early day. H e
lllJlresses his admiration for the "continuous devotion to their duties which has
•o markedly characterized the Committee on Finance," and says they " deserve
tlie confidence and respect of the members of the Grand Lodge." We congratulate
our brethren of Pennsylvania upon their present brilliant prospects, and hope the
tlnrn may soon come when they may sit under their own "vine and fig tree," free
from encumbrance, and enjoy the fruits of their enterprise.

He is strongly in favor of two yea.rs' service on the part of Masters of Lodges, as
the experience they acquire in the first year renders them much more efficient in
the second ; and in this opinion we fully concur. He strongly urges the brethren
to put. a stop to the growing disposition to electioneer for Masonic stations, and to
select their officers for their qualifications alone, regardless of personal friendships
or prejudices; advice which may well be heeded in other jurisdictions than Pennsylvania.
The Deputy Grand Master delivered a good AddreBS, in which he warned the
brethren to be watchful of a growing disposition to violate the le.ndmark regarding
the physical qualifications of candidates ; and, from his remarks, we infer that
nothing below the standard of physical perfection will be accepted by him.

conceived. He says:Reviewing ~he proceedings of the Grand Lodges with which the Grand Lodge

?f Pennsylvania holds fraternal relations, and discussing those questions of general

interest to the Craft which thus arise, is a duty both responsible and important.
It ~e~a'!ds a clear perceptio!1 of the subjects; a comprehensive knowledge of Ma8?mc Juns;prudence; an unbiased judgment; a devotion to the fundamental principles of Freemasonry ; a calm and generous spirit ; an earnest desire to discover
truth; the courage of enlightened convictions; and that true courtesy which restrains dogmatic criticism, and acknowledges that infallibility is not the attribute
of human reason. It is, then, rather a judicial than a critical examination or
b.etter t~ express it, a judicial, rather than a mere critical treatment of the ques'.

A case was adjudicated which, under the laws of California, never could have
occurred. A dispensation was Issued to certain brethren to form a new Lodge. A
oharter was subsequently granted, and Union Lodge, No. 10, granted dimits to such
of its members as desired to remain members of the new Lodge, among whom was a
brother named MINER. At the constitution of the new Lodge, said MINEB was
present and was elected one of its officers. For some reason he did not sign the
by-laws, and afterwards refused to submit to the lawful requirement& of the Lodge
and to obey the by-laws thereof.
·
Held, that said M1NEB fs a member of the new Lodge, and the Lodge was directed
to proceed with him as with any other member who neglected or refused to comply
with its laws. In our jurisdiction, applicants for a dispensation to form a new
Lodge, must present, with their petition, their dimlts from the Lodges of which they
last were members. Thus no such complication as the foregoing oould possibly
occur.
An interesting report relative to non-affiliation and Its causes, was presented by
Past Grand Master DoYLB. He attributes the troubles and difficulties which grow
out of non-affiliation to the modern system of dues. The report is somewhat lengthy,
but as it treats of a subject that has long occupied the attention of Masonic writers,
11nd is felt as a crying evil in every jurisdiction, we of,t'er no apology for reproducing
It In this report, He says :We use the term modern system, because the matter ofdues is, so far as oan be determined, as old as the institution itself; it is very certain that with the establishment
of the oldest Lodges in this State dues were instituted, and they were paid not only
by the membere of the Lodge, but also by visiting lirethren, and they were cheerfully
and willingly paid, because each brother received an actual equivalent therefor.
There were dues, but there wdre no troublesome questions therewith, such RB now
affiict the entire Fraternity of this country. In the former days the " social element "
prevailed throughout the Lodges, and the brethren were t hereby drawn to the Lodge·
room at every Oommunicatlon. The call from labor or refreshment meant somethlog,
and the office of Steward was no sinecure. When the convivial bowl was banished
from the Lodge-room, does were no longer required, and the custom fell Into disuse.
The fathers seemed to !'eel that because the social glass was banished there was no
need to provide a substitute therefor, and so Masonry came down to us robbed of the
1ocial element which had characterized it.
Your committee use the two terms' • social glass" and "social element" advisedly,
because it does not believe that they are synonymous or need to be. The social
element can exist in the Lodge-room to-day, and be as produotive of harmony and
brotherly love as it ever was in the olden time, without a drop of wine or punch, or
other intoxicating stimulants being used in connection therewith. The troubles arising from the modern system of dues are, In the opinion of your committee, cbietly
attributable to the fact that the brother does not feel that he is receiving a return
for the amount he is called to pay. The Lod11c demands his money, and what doe1
it olfer in return? Masonry Is a sociRI, charitllble Institution: it is not a ben(llo'al
organization which promises a certain specified, fixed return for a certain, specified,
ftxed sum paid Into the treasury of the Lodge by her members. The province of
lllasoory is to bind man to his fellow man, and to bring toj!ether in a common
brotherhood men of every" country, sect and opinion." This is its mission, and its
members should seek to accomplish ito purpose by every means at their command.
Instead of driving members out ofa Lodge the effort should be to retain them within
Its influence. That the pre1ent,,.y1tem does not do this prompts the Inquiry as to
where the defect is, and why the number of unaffiliated Masons is so rapidly Increasing. The committee unhesitatingly declares that the trouble Is mainly within the
Lodge·room, and In the manner in which the alf11irs of the Lodge are conducted. In
a jurisdiction so small as this there ought not to be any difficulty in ohanging the exlstiug order, and the committee deems It proper to suggest a mode which it believes
to be worthy of trial. The principal object which a Master of the present day seems
to have In view, is to add to the permanent funds of bis Lodge rather than to increase

At a recent annual meeting of a Masonio body, the report of the Treasurer
showed ao increase during the year io the uermanent fonds of several hnndred dollars, and an expenditnre for· refreshments· of less than sixty dollars. Far better
wonld it have been for Masonry if the items had been reversed. The Masters of
Lodges seem to fear that those who are to come sfter us will not be able to take care
of themselves, and hence every effort must be made to provide funds for their main·
tenance. The dues are used to pile np fonds for posterity, while the Lodge-room is
made as cheerless as can be, and the members tired of climbing up to the meetinl(S
only to find a cold and unsociable assembly-ask for a dimit, aud abandon Masonry.
The committee urges upon the Craft the necessity of trying a change of tactics, and
it earnestly begs that the Masters adopt as a role that the work of the Lodge shall be
so arranged that there may be, at each sLated Communication, an hour of social lnterconrse about a table on which shall be some simple refreshment, aod where the
members may be made acquainted with each other. Let there be, three or four times
each year, a meeting at which the members with their families may be present, with
such invited guests as the Lodge may select. At this meeting provide mosic, reading,
aod if possible brief speaking, with some slight refreshments, at the expense of the
Lodge. When this is done there will be created an influence for the Lodge in the
home circle, and the mem her who should attempt to dimit, to save his dRes, will find
that he will have a force to fight against that he cannot resist, and to which be will
be compelled to yield. A Lodge based upon this plan is in operation In this city,
and your committee are satisfied that the day will be far distant when its members
will lose their interest in the Lodge or their love of Masonry. Shonld the method
of this Lodge become universal throughout the jurisdiction, no tutnre Grand Secretary will feel compelled to call the attention of Grand Lodge to the nnmber of unaffiliated Masons, audit is very certain that the record books required for them will
be of little use.
Your committee does not wish to be understood as placing a higher value upon
the social thau upon the moral element or Masonry; but it is of the opinion that by
the cultivation of the former the members of the Institution will more surely be
brought within the influence of the latter, and made to realize that they do not live
for self aloue, but are bound to their fellow-men by ties which they cannot break
and by obligations from which they cannot escape. The fathers could attend upon
the worship of God, and sit, io the coldest days of a New England winter, upon oncushioned benches, in a cold church, while sermons two hours in length were droned
out; but their descendants cao only keep their faith alive by having ao elegant
ehurch, comfortably warmed, luxurious seats, a fine choir, an eloquent minister, and,
io addition thereto, church parlors and kitchen for the cultivation of the social element. Just what the churches require to-day is what Masonry needs. The one is
the handmaid of the other and both need the same elements to secure and retain
their members.
In some of our California Lodges this social feature bas been introduced with
gratifying success. When the labors of the evening are concluded, the Lodge is
called from labor to real bona fide refreshments, no reason-destroying wines or
liqnors, but good substantial food, with tea or coffee for beverage, and, after the
brethren have refreshed themselves, the remainder of the evening is enlivened by
mosic, songs, recitations and speeches by the members and their visiting brethren.
Lodge meetings are looked upon as occasions of real enjoyment and anticipated with
genuine pleasure. It would be well if this example were more generally followed.
Soch Lodges always prosper, and suspensions for non-payment of dues and applications for dimits rarely occur.

The financial condition of the Grand Lodge appears to be a matter ·of serious
import to the brethren, and a considerable portion of the address Is devoted to the
discussion of the pecuniary situation. It appears that the debt of the Grand Lodge
is twenty-three thousand dollars, ($23,000) for which bonds are issued at eight per
cent. per annum, interest, and secured by mortgage upon the Temple. An effort to
reduce the rate of interest was unsuccessful, and the officers are now endeavoring to
negotiate a loan in New York, but with doubtful success. In this emergency the
Grand Master recommends that the communications of the Grand Lodge be held biennially, and thus a saving of some three thousand dollars per annum would be
effected, and the debt could be extinguished in eight years. The Idea is a good one,
for as the Grand Master truly says: "No circumstances can more surely conduce to
the prosperity of Masonry, or of any other institution, than its.financial independence."

Bro. lNGLESBY is a warm advocate of the doctrine of perpetual jurisdiction,-&

1883.]

Grand .Lodge of OaUfornia.

167

doctrine which we never did and never can endorse. The idea that because a man
has once been rejected by a Lodge, he Is forever debarred from making application
to another Lodge without the consent of the Lodge which rejected him, is a little too
autocratic to suit our republican taste. He cites a case in Indiana, where a man
was made a Mason who had previously been rejected by a Lodge in New York. The
Grand Master of .New York desired an explanation, and was informed that the law
In Indiana permitted the Lodges to receive petitions from candidates rejected by
other Lodges, provided one year has elapsed since the rejection. The Committee
on Jurisprndence of the Grand Lodge of New York, to whom the matter was referred, say:We do not see that any action Is necessary, further than the suggestion that our
Indiana brethren wheel into line as soon as may be, in a matter so necessary to the
peace and harmony of Masonry throughout all jurisdictions.
More than Indiana wonld be required to " wheel into line" if the peace and harmony of Masonry depended upon the general adoption of this rule. In California, as
In Indiana, Iowa and many other jurisdictions, the doctrine of perpetual jurisdi<rt.ion
i1 repudiated, and the candidate Is only required to state in hie petition that he has
not been rejected by any Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons within a period of
twelve months. Bro. INGLESBY attempts to answer an argument of Bro. PABVIN, of
Iowa, on this question, but we think with poor success. He says:He (Bro. PARVIN), thinks that the landmark quoted by us as sustaining the
perpetual allegiance doctrine, i. e. " none shall discover envr. at the prosperity
of a brother, nor supplant him, nor put him out of his work 1f he be capable of
finishing the same," does not and cannot refer to the rejection of a candidate by
another Lodge. He asks, "How can a Lodge be put out or Its work when it has no
work in hand ? " To this we answer that Bro. MACKEY, in his work on Jurisprudence,
has taught us that when a petition for Initiation has been presented to a Lodge, it
cannot be withdrawn, nor can the petitioner, after rejection, apply to any otlrer
Lodge, because the petition becomes the property of the Lodge. The petition and
tile petitioner, says Bro. MACKEY, are the material for the work of the Lodge, and
cannot be passed on for further examination. Each Lodge is constructing its portion
of tbe spiritual Masonic Temple, and no Lodge can properly use the rejected material of another Lodge without discovering envy, supplanting it and putting it out of
Its work. The rejection of improper material is as much and as important a part of
the speculative work or Masonry, as is the conferring of degrees.
Has our good brother forgotten that "the stone which the builders rejected became the head of the corner?" One would naturally suppose that when an article
le rejected or thrown away by one party, another may be justified in taking and
making use of It. .Bro. INGLESBY says: "Each Lodge is constructing Its portion of
the spiritual Masonic Temple." Very true; and a stone that may not fit one portion
of the Temple may be very nicely adjusted in another. But he goes further, and
says : "No Lodge can properly use the rejeoted material of another Lodge without
discovering envy, supplanting it and putting it ont of its work." This is a bad case
of 71on sequitur. How can we envy them that which we want not? or how can we
1upplant them in a position they have not taken? It is undeniably true that many
good men are rejected simply through prejudice or personal motives, for Masons are
but human, and, notwithstanding the salutary teaohings of our charges and leoturea.
will sometimes allow themselves to be influenced by a personal pique, strongly akin
to malice, in balloting for a candidate, who, for some reason entirely disconnected
with his qualifications for the Masonic connection, is inimical to them. We have
known cases where good and true men have been rejected by the vote of one who
was unworthy to loosen their shoe Iatchet, and, were the doctrine of perpetual juris..
diction to prevail, such men might be forever debarred from uniting with the Fraternality, through the malicious spite of one who has no more Masonry in his heart than a
Dead Sea apple. Suppose a man, who thirty years ago, was rejected by a Lodge in
South Carolina, and immediately thereafter removed to California, should now apply
to a Lodge here for degrees? All those years he may have lived in onr midst a pure

Under the head of Mississippi we find the following doctrine, beside which that of

families a pecuniary return for the money they invest in it,-witl sooner or later
learn that they do not understand the first principles of Masonry, and have joined an
institution, which for their purposes, is not comparable to the Knights of Honor or
any other real Mutual Benefit Association. Ma~onry is an institution organized for
the promotion of Friendship, Morality and Brotherly Love-in doing this, it necessarily promotes all the moral and social virtues. Its shrines and temples are
asylums where all meet as brothers and members of one family, free from the cares
and troubles of the world. The worthy Mason feels, or ought to feel, that when he
enters bis Lodge, he is surrounded by those who are ready to sympathize with bis
sorrows or share in bis joys,-that here no selfishness, hypocrisy or aeceit can touch
him. That strong and friendly arms are around him ready to sustain him when
falling, or to support him in well doing. To keep Masonry on this high plane, it has
ever been held necessary to exclude from her portals, business, politics,-even discussions or declaration~ of religion, beyond the belief in the G. A. o. T. U. Business,
with its varying fortunes, its heartburnings, its contentions, its over-reaching and
selfish schemes and purposes, would soon destroy all fraternity and harmony in
Masonry.
