The vexing qneetion of non-affiliation will never reach a solution under a system
that countenances dropping from the roll for non-payment of dues. Being dropped
from the roll cBrries with it no particular disgrace ; it simply leaves tbS' brother
unuftilfated, and entitled to the same rights as any other unaffiliated Mason. Many
are only too glad to escape the duties and burdens consequent upon Lodge member·
1hip upon terms so easy, if their general standing in the Order le not affected. They
are perfectly willing that others shall relieve the distressed, minister to the sick, and
bury the dead, so long as &bey are not called npon tO perform their portion of the
labor and pay their quota of the expense. They can afford to dispense with the
privileges that accrue from Lodge-membership ; these are placed in the balance
with Lodge duties and expenses and "kick the beam." They are Masons at large.
contributing nothing to the charities of the Craft, bearing no portion of the burdens
imposed hy the Masonic connection, and almost forgetting that they are Masone,
until poverty and misfortune overtake them, and then, bow quickly they remember
tt, and how promptly they clBim Masonic sympathy and aid. These are Masons
only in name; not one iota of trne Masonry ever existed in their hearts; they are
decayed branches upon a healthy tree, neither use nor ornament. The only thing
to do in order to relieve the tree of their unsightly presence is to cut them off and
throw them among the rubbish. We think the California rule is the trne one; give
them every opportunity to do their duty as Masons, then if they refnse, show them
thu.t, if they will not work neither shall they eat; that the Masonic hive will tolerate
110 drones, and if they are worth saving, the remedy will be effectual; if not, they
drop from our eight flnd we are well rid of them. If we have brethren in onr
1.odges who are unable to pay their dues, let us aid and enoouraa:e them until better
limes enable them to meet their obligations. If there are those who can, and will
not pay, cut them otf from all the rights and privileges they have proved themselves
unworthy to enjoy. This le the policy pursued by California, and we believe it to be
the correct one.

Thanks, Bro. FRIZZELL ; we wish all were as just in their criticisms. The Masonic
Boe.rd of Relief of San Francisco has been severely scored in some quarters for presuming to ask of Lodges, whose members have been benefited by its benetlcenoe, a
partial return of the am.ount expended. We do not claim this. remuneration as a
right, but we ask it in justice to our peculiar position. San Francisco is the temporary abiding place of all creation. Masons of every nation, kindred and tongue
congregate here. As a matter of OQurse, many of these sojourners lind themselves
without means and without friends in a strange land, and naturally apply for relief
to those from whom, if found worthy, they are sure to receive it, viz. : the Masonic
Board of Relief of t)an Francisco; and this Board has disbursed to this class of
brethren, since its organization, about $190,000. Not one dollar of this sum has
been given to a member of a Lodge in this city ; each Lodge takes care of its own
members, besides making liberal contributions for the sapport of the Board~ We
claim, therefore, that 'we cannot justly be charged with covetousness or uncharitableness if we ask from the Lodges whose members have been relieved the return of
at least a portion of the amount expended, in order that we may continue the good
work and act well our part as the almoner of the Masonlo world.

We have sometimes heard the remark, made by thoughtless. and inconeideratt
brethren, "Masonry is good enongh religion for me." The remarks of the Grand
Master on this subject have our fullest endorsement. He says:Let no man for a moment believe that Masonry is a substitute for the religion oJ:
God. Such it is not-such it cannot be. It has been well said that "Christianitf
and Masonry are of different origins-the one being of divine-the other of hum8*
origin." Masonry being merely of hnman origin, can only hope, by the blessing of
God, to be an humble handmaid of religion, doing Its duty in the different epher~
and upon the lower plane, where man could only place it-seeking to ameliora
man 'e condition in this life, but with no claim or hope of bettering his soul's cond
tion In the world to come. Let not then any brother teach, believe, or act upQll the
idea, however vague or remote, that M.asonry can be a substitute for the religion of
God.
Masonry, as a "beautiful system of morality," leads the seeker after truth up to
that point where religion takes him by tlie hand and conducts him into the presence
of Him who alone can give that perfect peace which coinee from repentance and
forgiveneee of sin.

In all these decisions we concur, save the fourth. We believe that, under certain
circumstances, an installed officer may resign and dimit. We know that the hands
of the ancient Jandmarkers will be raised in holy horror st such an announcement,
bnt there iR an ancient landmark called common sense which is too frequently vio·
lated in decision• upon Masonic law and usage. An officer upon bis installe.tion
promises to do his duty to the best of bis ability during his term of' office, but, when
his ability to perform his duty cee.ses from any cause, we bold that be has a right to
resign-sud, if he haR a right to resign, be has a. right to dimit. Suppose an officer,
after his installation, was called by the exigencies of business to reside in a dtstsnt
jurisdiction. To perform his duties as an officer of his Lodge is simply Impossible.
He may, perhaps, never visit it again. Why can he uot resign and give place to Rome
one who can and will discharge the duties of the office? We are taught In the very
outset that Masonry is not to interfere with our usual avocations. Must a man neg·
lect his business in order to discharge the duties of an office to which he has been
elected? By no meanR. A man who would do so would be denounced instead of
applauded. We will again .suppose that an officer, after his installation, is stricken
with paralysis, or permanently disabled by some untoward accident from ever again
visiting bis Lodge; is his station to remain vacant to the end of the term, or be filled
from time to time pro tempore? We have heard this question discussed often, but
we never yet heard a satisfactory reason given why an installed officer could not
resign when circnmstanceR prevented him from performing the duties of his office.

ence was inRtrncted to limit its reports to fifty pages. Now when we consider that
the Committee on Foreign Correspondence have to review the proceedings of over
fifty American Grand Bodies, it must appear plain that the committee cannot do
justice · to itself nor to the various snbJects under consideration. These reports
become every year of greater importance on account of the many innovations
attempted to be introduced into Masonry in these days of progress, which, without
an opportunity of a free and thorough discnBBlon would soon throw our Ancient
Le.ws into a state of wild confusion. It is claimed that the pro11eedings of tho Grand
Lodge and these reports are hut lltt.le read. This is a very great mistake. While
perhaps not all members of Lodges bave an opport1mity of reading these reports,
there are always some, if not many, who eagerly devour every sentence pnblished'
therein. The expressions of each of the fifty or more Committees on Foreign Cor·
1·espondence, the decisions and views of the Revera) Grand Masters contained thereto,
afford the most valuable information to the MMter of a Lodge, sod considering the
sound condition of our treasury, tho mature and discreet judgment of our Committee
on Foreign Correspondence, I earnestly recommend that the Grand Lodge authorize
said committee to use as much space in our proceedings as in their opinion may be
deemed necessary.
This recommendation had its effect, for the Committee on Finances, in their report, recommend that the Grand Secretary be directed to have the Report of the
Committee on Correspondence, not to exceed one hnndri:d and fifty pages, printed

These reports form an epitome of Masonic information more usefol to the intelligent
anP, knowledge-seeking Masons than digests, manuals or encyclopedias, for they dis·
cuss the current Masonic events of the day, and in them are found the Ideas, opinions
and constructions of tbe most celebrated Masonic writers and jurists, as WiJll as the

cruder ideas of leBB experienced theorists.

Under the head of Louisiana, Bro. REED quotes from the report of Bro. FL!!MING
the following relative to the organization of new Grand Lodges:This matter of organizing new Grand Lodges in what is called unoccupied territory, is of prime importance, and deserves candid and dispassionate treatment in
argument. We should not busy ourselves tn finding pretexts to bolster up inconsiderately expressed views, but should come directly t.o the question-what is fairest? We venture a suggestion-to originating it we lay no claim--that when a
sutlicient number of Lodges, say three, in " unoccupied territory," unite in calling
together in general assembly all the Lodges of such territory for the purpose ot'
organizing a Grand Body, each Lodge being invited to!articipate, and a ma,iority
of the Lodges, three or more, decide in favor of propose organization, their action
should be held binding on the minority, and the new Grand Lodge should be reooguized and upheld by all other Grand Lodges. This majority rule prevails in the
legislation of our constituent and Grand Lodges. In them tile minority must yield
for the common good. We do not there regard the rule as oppressive, but tending
rather to the preservation of order and the security of individual rights.
The value of this principle, the authoritative position of the majority, is illustrated in the history of our country, and the stability of its institutions. Its general
recognition would render impossible such a state of affairs as that which E'Xisted
between New Mexico and Missouri.
To this Bro. REED responds :We fully agree with Bro. FLEMING that sur.h "should" be (if it is not clearly so
now,) the law on the subject; and that this is the generally received opinion among
our" Reporters" and able Masonic jurists, who have given expression to their views
on the question, we have no doubt. But there ih one question in connection, collaterally, with this subject, upon which there seems to be more diversity of opinion,
and that is: Uan a newly-organized Grand Lodge c<Jmpel the allegiance of a 1·ecu1ant
Lodge who hold its authority to work from another Grand Lodge possessing" SO'(·
ereign" authority? We think not. But the question is an important one, and we
would like to receive "more light" thereon from brethren of the "Guild.'1
It is a well settled principle of American Masonic law, that each Grand Lodge ia
sovereign in its own territory; therefore, when a new Grand Lodge is legally organized and recognized, no other Grand Lodge has the right to maintain a subordinate
Lodge within its jurisdiction; and, in our opinion, the new Grand Lodge has the
right to "compel the allegiance of a recusant Lodge " existing within its jurisdiction, no matter from what authority it may derive its charter. We fc{lly concur
in the views of Bro. FLEMING as above expressed.

The eighteenth Annual Communication was held in the city of Wheeling, commencing on the fourteenth day of November, 1882,-the R.'. W.', WILLIAM H. H.
FLICK, Deputy Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.-. 0DBLL S. LONG being
Grand Secretary. Bevent-y-tllree LodE,<es were represented.
•
A letter was read from the M.'. W.·. Grand Master, JOHN H. RILEY, announcing
his removal from the jurisdiction and the regret he experienced at the necessity
which caused even a temporary interruption of his social and friendly relations in
the jurisdiction where he first saw the light, both natural and Masonic. His Address,
which is very brief, was read by the Grand Secretary, and is simply a recital of his
official acts. He bad granted three dispensations for the formation of new Lodges,
and issued his proxy for the constitution of two Lodges under dispensation. He
reported· a number of decisions, from which we select as of general interest:First. A former member of an extinct Lodge, in good standing at the time the
Lodge became extinct, is a non-affiliated Mason, eligible to membership in aay Lodge
that may desire to receive him.
This, in our opinion, would depend upon the manner in which the Lodge became
extinct. If by a voluntary surrender of its charter, we concur; but, if the charter
has been revoked for misconduct, each i:.ember not specially exempted i>y the Grand
Master or Grand Lodge should oocupy tile position of a suspended Mason until law
fully restored,
Second.. A member ibdefinitely suspended by the Grand Lodge on appeal, may
be rein•tated by a subordinate Lodge without further aotlon by Grand Lodge or
Grand Master.
We dissent. The subordinate Lodge has no power to discipline its members,
except that delegated to it by the Grand Lodge. In the trial of a brother it acts as
the agent of the Grand Lodge, and its findings are subject to approval, amendment
or reversal by the Grand Body. A subordinate Lodge cannot in any way di11turb or
interfere with tile edict of a Grand Lodge.
Third.. Giving a suspended Mason notice of the action of the Lodge Is proper,
and is not such communication with a non-member as is prohibited.
'fJlji. we think, would depend entirely upon tile nature of the communication.
Jf it were simply to inform him that the Lodge had suspended him, we do not know
that it would be particularly objectionable, but even this had better be left to the
proper officor of the Lodge. Rev~aling the transactions of the Lodge Is a Masonic
offense, and is a fruitful source of discord and difficulty,
The olosing words of the Grand Master show that distance does not wean his
love from his Masonic alma mater. He says:A great river, forming the line between States and Grand Masonic jurisdictions,
may flow on and separate us, but tile "cable tow" of affection and filial regard shall
extend from the other shore, and, being electrified bye. grateful heart, shall ever
I: iar to this jurisdiction greeting and assurances of' good will and fraternal regard.

We have came together, not merely to speak to and shake hands with each otber,

There Is something else to be done besides the election of officers. The election
is not the Alpha and Omega of our meeting, although important, and, in the dicharge
of this duty, great care and caution should be exercised. The sncceas of Masonry
depends largely upon the character and qualifications of the officers of this Grand
Lodge; but a Mason's zeal should not be so abundant as to permit him to prepare,
and distribute by the handful, printed or written ballots for his favorite candidate,
long before the hour of election arrives, and then, as soon as election is over, take
the first train home, as if hie mission to the Grand Lodge were ended. Such conduct obviously smacks a little too much of' the King Caucus System which prevaila
. i~ 'political nominating conventions of •he day, and ought not to be encouraged ID
Grand Lodge.

11ll the Grand Lodg.,s in correspondence with each other on the face of the globe." He

In California we elect the best man to the office of Worshipful Master irrespective
of former service. We do not believe in the idea that, because some incompetent
brother has slipped into the Warden's chair, he moat perforce become Worshipful
Master. If a brother proves to be Incompetent in the Warden's station, he la quietly
Mhelvcd and one better qualified la elected to succeed him. Thus we are not often
troubled with Incompetent Mastera, yet many will say that by doing this we are
pulling the "ancient landmarks" up by the roots.
We dissent from the following: " In the absence of a con&titutional provision,
three Master Masons, members of the Lodge, one of whom is at least a Warden,
may open a Lodge of Master Masons, and when so opened, may tre.naact buaineas."
As seven, or more, are required to form a Lodge, we think no Lodge can lawfully
transact bus,ineaa with less than seven mem bera present.

The Grand Master recommended that all the Grand Officers and permanent members of the Grand Lodge, In actual attendance, be paid the same rate of mileage
and per diem as that received by the senior representatives of subordinate Lodges.
A. similar recommendation last year was defeated, and this year the committee to
whom it was referred reported against it; but a .Lamb--like brother submitted a
resolution in accordance with the Grand Master's recommendation, and it was
adopted. We think the recommendation a just one, for among the permanent members of a Grand Lodge may be found its most valuable workers-Past Gro.nd Masters
and other Past Grand Officers-whose experience renders their services of great
value to the Grand Lodge, and it is right that they should be paid for their attendance
as much as any of the representatives.

The financial condition of the Grand Lodge is by no means satisfactory. The
Grand Master complains that the funda have heretofore been distributed with a
too prodigal hand, regardless of income, leaving not a "moiety for charitable purposes." Thia is unfortunate- unwise. Masonry cannot afford to bear so wide a
reputation for charity, and perform so little of it. We have often thought that
the money expended for banquets (" spreads"), would be much better applied if
appropriated to the relief of the widow and orphan. Too much, we fear, is wasted
in feasting that should go to swell the charity fund.

* Only a few extreme fanatics, not counted by thousands, etc.

the first Grand Master of Masons in that jurisdiction. Subsequently he was appointed Agent of the American Colonization Society, and removed to Indianapolis,

The Address of the Grand Master is very brief and simply reciteR his official acts.
He appears to have discharged his duties with zeal and fidelity, for he visited, officially, every Lodge in the jurisdiction, in some instances being obliged to travel a
rough and rugged road to reach them. One visit involved a wagon ride of four
days; the road, leading up the precipitous sides of mountains and•anon diving dow·o
into the depths of dark canons, often obliged him to walk, as the horses were unable
to haul more than the empty vehicle over the primitive pathway. Think of that, ye
Grand Masters, who, with all the facilities afforded by palace cars and palatial
steamboats, can find no time to visit your nearest Lodges. He was everywhere
received and entertained with genuine Masonic hospitality, as he well deserved, and
his detailed report of the condition of the sever.al Lodges is very encouraging and
satisfactory. He congratulates the Grand Lodge upon the steady and promising
growth of .the Order, its general prosperity, and the manifest advancement of its
members in all that constitutes true Masonry.
The Grand Lodge was convened in Specie.I Communication oo the sixth day of
July, 1882, for the purpose of laying the corner-stone of the Morris Presbyterian
Church at Rawlins. At the conclusion of the ceremonies, the Grand Master dellv·
ered a brief oration appropriate to the occasion. We give the concluding pare.graph:Although Freemasonry has lived through ages of dim uncertainty, during which
time empires have been crashed, thrones have crumbled, and 'dynasties he.ve fallen;
gone through vicissitudes, we.rs and revolutions, and has witnessed the rise e.nd
growth of all the civilized nations now on the face of the earth, yet its eye Is not
dim nor its strength failing, as is evidenced by this le.rge concourse of friends to-day.
No, it has come out from the smoke of conflict stronger, brighter and more lasting
by the fiery ordeal through which it has passed. It has no known Alpha, and its
Omega will only be when the tromp of Gabriel proclaims the funeral ol' the human
race and sounds the dirge of time. Therefore, my brethren , let us to-day renew our
pledges to this grand old institution, which has for its motto," Glory be to God on·
high, and on earth peace and good will to man.''
The Report on Correspondence by the Grand Seorete.ry, Bro. JOHN H. SYMONS,
is a well prepared paper of seventy-five pages. Comparatively brief, as it i~, Bro.
SYMONS .contrives to condense within that limit a goodly amount of interesting information. California, for 1881, is pleasantly reviewed. Grand Master DENSON Is complimented on his Address, and Bros. ABELL and SHAEFFER receive a generous meed
of praise for their interesting reports. Bro. SYMONS' style is descriptive rather than
commente.tive, but he is judicious in his selections, sod gives a very good synopsis
of the doings of tlle Grand Bodies he reviews. We infer, from the endorsement of
the remarks of the Grand Master of Maine, that he Is not in favor of the doctrine of
perpetual jurisdiction, and we are pleased to see that this absurdity is being so agi·
tated in various quarters, that we believe the lightning of common sense will soon
strike it from the Masonic Code in all jurisdictions.
Wyoming has five chartered Lodges, with an aggregate membership of three
hundred and eighty-four. The M.'.

merits of this brother and his prominence in Masonry had been already honorably
mentioned at the session of the Grand Lodge October 25th. On the present occasion he desired to direct attention to the nature and design of an aaaociation to be
formed for the purpose of honoring the memory and name of the departed brother1
and furthermore with the view of not losing sight of the object to which he haa
devoted the best energies of his life. The membership in this aaaociation is not to
be limited to Masons only. A call for the formation of the association was signed
by a la.rse. number of prominent men in America, Belgium, Denmark Germany,
England, the Netherlands, Austria, Rusaia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.
" The prospectus issued," he continued, "states that it is proposed to establish
the BLUNTSOHLI Asaociation by voluntary m oney contributions for the purpose of
carrying out the life-long plan of the deceased, whose earnest endeavor it was to
encompaaa the whole field of political economy, who labored for the promotion of
peaceful relations between nations by the adoption of methods based upon science
for the management of State affairs, and who _was ceaselessly active in the work of
the international law branch of the acadamy which he aided in establishing.
"It is the object of the BLUNTSCHLI Association to extend the study of political
economy beyond the boundaries of particular States, and to induce the production
of works of sterling worth on (comparative) political and international law by the
offer of premiums or in some other suitable manner. The national character of
this association is to be preserved by permitting in the publications the use of all
great modern languages of civilization, or for the prizes that will precede them ;
the use of the Latin l~ is not tu be excluded. The expenditure of the
money of the aaaociation 1s to be regulated by the united action of the International Law Asaociation_,,and the three faculties in which BLUNTSCHLI had successively taught (Zurich, Miinchen and Heidelberg).
"In modern times it is sought to preserve peace among nations by the .introduction of an international code of laws binding_ upon all nations. It is ?enerally
known that a short time previous to his death Bro. BLUNTSOHLI, in his Es8ays,'
entitled 'Short Treaties,' proposed a new plan for the formation and functions of
a European confederation of States. As vice-president of the society known as
the 'Imtitut de droit I nternatimial,' he took the most lively interest in its efforts to
ameliorate the condition of the law of war in Europe. This Institute numbers
among its members the most honored names of science of all countries, and its
influence as well as the number of its members is constantly increasing. Ravid
vrogress would be made in the im_provement of international intercourse, if the
lofty mission aaaigned to man by T. G. A. 0. T. U., 'w love each other,' waa oon11tantly carried out by civilized nations. If, therefore, the solution of the problem,
t o disseminate the laws of nations as the laws of the world, devolves upon them,
it follows tliat the efforts made in that direction must be recognized as being eminently philanthrol>ic and consequently more particularly Masonic.
"The institut10n of Freemasonry cannot, therefore, from principle remain
indifferent to a participation in an association with such humane tend1Jnciea,
because the questions involved are neither purely political, nor are they of a nature
to exclude them from discussion in our Lodges according to our fundamental laws.
Viewed in this light the BLUNTSOHLI Association can be commended to the Fratel'nity. "
The praise bestowed in the foregoing upon the illustrious Mason and eminent
teacher of international law, the late Bro. BLUNTBCHLI, is well deserved and will
be warmly indorsed ·by all who posaess any knowled,,ae of his character and services. But since his worth is so well appreciated and his views and opinions
deservedly held in so high esteem by our brethren in Germany, might it not re

And again, at the same sesaion of the League, when speaking_of t"he French

Body can never admit that, for instance, the Grand Orient of France shall institute subordinate Lodges in Germany * * * W e cannot allow that Foreign
Grand Bodies can constitute subordinate Lodges in Germany."
In our opinion a decision of this question by the proposed International BLUNTSOHLI Asaociation would not be reqmred, if, M proposed, the association is to carry
out ~e ideas of its great exemplar.

At the session of the Grand Lodge, Ariril Hi, 1882, which our brethren of the
Eclectic Union designate F1·i!lfnqs Laye (the Spring Lodge)1 Grand Master VAN
DER HEYDEN addressed the Gram! L odge at length. The suoject selected by him
was : What are Lodges of Instruction ? In his answer, he says that according to
the views and inclinations entertained by different brethren, vurious opinions were
expressed in answer to the question. Some expect to r eceive, in these Lod!{0a of
Instruction, information on Masonic symbolism, perho.vs ulso on Mwmuic history,
and may be even on Mat1onic law. Others, whose clnef aim it iH to follow the
practical objects of Masonry, desire information on t hnt point; and finally, some
are imi;>ressed with the idea that these L odges of Instruction are for the purpose
of cultivating the liberal arts and science. Which of these is the correct view?
Who is in the right? In part all are in the right, but not one exclusively. It is
self-evident that Masonry is to give instruction am! impnrt information. MMonry
is called the Royal Art, and to acquire an art talent and ability are necessary.
Masonry requires this of its votaries inasmuch as it demands of the :profane a certain a.mount of culture, a desire for self-imJ.>rnvement and an ideal mmd. For the
acquirement of an art a large amount of labor is neoe88ary. Freemasonry, in a
certain sense, embraces in itself all arts and ecieuoea • therefore Freemasonry is &n
art, and to teach it to its votaries is the object of the Lodge of Instruction. To
become master of an art, It is necessary to become, first of all, u. mMter of its
forms ; the essence of an art is, to cause the min<! to work through. these forms.
To acquire these forms must be the first study of a Mnson. 'l'he forms of Masonry
are contained in symbols, symbolic discourses nrul symbolic arts; to learn to
understand these forms &nd to acquire their meaning, iH, what may be called, t o
learn them. In Freemasonry therefore, the stucly of tho form calls for the study
of the hilitory of the form. 'fhis ngain requirtlll tho stu1ly of the history of Freemasonry, because from the latter alone can the former be tletluced.

It does seem singular that thosa Masonic Ura.ml Bodies, oppOlled to the socalled right of jurisdiction when claimed hr other Grand Lodg_es, become zealous
advocates of the right, when it affects their own territory. To this the Grand
Lodge of Italy is no exception. With the declarntion on its statutes that it
reserves to itself the right of constituting Lodges where it plelllijls, it now threatens
excommunication to all Grand Lodges who would r ecognize the body obnoxious to
it in its own territory. It is so with other European Grancl Lodges. We cite as proof

the case of the two Grand Bodies in Hungary, the Grand Lodge for the three symbolic degrees and the Grand Orient for the Scottish Rite, between whom a compact
exists by virtue of which they claim the sole right of jurisdiction f'!r themselvi;s _in
Hungary. Fearing, however, t~at some Grand Lodge of freebo~tmg pr~pens1t1es
might select to charter a Lodge m Hungary to the contra.!Y !lotwithstandll!g, they

Europe are similarly situated.
At the session of the Grand Lodge, September 9, 1882, termed the " Fall Festival Lodge" (Herbst-Festloge), the Grand Master announced that the Grand
Lodge would celebrate the anniversary of its centennial existence March 18, 1883.
After an Address by M. ·. W. ·.Bro. VAN DER HEYDEN, Bro. REGES, Dep~ty
Grand Orator, delivered an interesting discourse on the reforms through which
Masonry is now passing in Germany.. He describes graphically wh!'t hn.s ~n
done and what is proposed to be done m that respect, and thus furnishes a v1VId
picture of the reform movement II\ade prominent by the p_ublication .of an Addr6!19
to the Lodges in Germany by six brethren, a translation of which appears m
another part of this report.
·
Speaking of the politically stormy year 1848, to which ll!anY of the old traditions in the life of the people had to succumb, he says that voices have made themselves also heard here and there demanding reforms in our institution and
expressing th~ opinion that Masonry in it~ pres~nt fo~ was no lo~er adapted for
our time. This reform-movement still contmues m poht1cs as well as m Masonry. A
criticism of our institution by the profane world, can affect us but little, but when
discontent in regard to existing arrangements manifests itself in our own circle, it
sets us to thinking. This should convince us that with us also all is not perfect,
a.nd that every call for reform must have some justification, while on th_e ~ther
hand experience teaches us that we cannot please everybody, and that the hmit to
which im:ero~ements may be carried is easily overstepi:>ed.
If we begin to reform Masonry we are in danger ol finally turning_it into som.ething which it was not originally. He did not want to say that ancient Masonry
must remain for ever as it is. It may be adapted to the necessities of the times
and particular circumstances, but its fundamental idea must be preserved. Our
efforts should be directed to its pllrification where degenerated and to its restora·
tion to the original intention. We must stand firm, examine without prejudi~
and adapt or reject as may be best.
He speaks of the successful struggle by: the Grand Lodge Eclectic Union ~
place ' every religious creed upon a:n equality !1'fld ho':" other Grand Lo~es. had
since followed the example. A desire had mamfested itself, however, to elimmatf'
not only all that is sectarian, but also all that is religious, and all that alludes tt

GRAND LODGE LEAGUE OF GERMANY.
By the kindness of a brother we are placed in J>?BBession of an official copy of
the protocol of this body, the annual session of which occurred at Berl~'!~ Ma:y 28i
1882. 'l'he eight Grand Lodges of Germany were represented; Most Wol'!!htpfu
Bro. REHRIG, Grand Master of the Grand Lodge Royal York, Berlin, presiding.
The principal business brought before the L eague was the diHcus•ion and adoption of a uniform balloting law for all L odges under the obedience of the eight
Grand Lodges of Germany. The proposition originBted with the Grand L odge Zur
Sonne, at Bayreuth, during the session of the L eague in 1880. A committee was
appointed in 1881 to frame the new law and report at the session of 1882, when it
was discussed at great length and approved with some changes. It was then recommended to the eight Grana Lodges for adoption. Since then it has been submitted
by them to their respective daughter Lodges, and if sanctioned by a majority of
them, it will become the general law. :From information received, it seems to be
l(enerally looked upon with favor, and the prevailing opinion is that it will be
finally adopted at the session of the League of the present year. No amendments
can be proposed to the law as it now stands; it must be either rejected or adopted
118 a whole. T o us it appears too diffnse and complicated. In many points it differs essentially from the halloting laws generally practiced by the S~bolic L odges
of the United States. The title of the law is : "General Ballotm~ J,aw for the
Lodges belonging to the German Grand L rnlge League." It contains thirty-five
aections, and its principal features are embodied in the following synop11is :Section 1 provides that the applicant for initiat ion must be a free mal!.o etc.; the
age at which the candidate may be initiated is reirulatecl by each Grand Lodge.
Uniformity on the last-mentioned point is unattainable in Germany, for by law
the three Berlin Grand Lodges can receive candidates only when arrived at the _age
of twenty-five ; the Grand Lodge Zur Eintracht, Darmstadt, at twenty-four, while
the rest of the Grand L odges may initiate at the age of twenty-one.
A peculiar feature of this new law is the opportunity it affords for the with.
drawal of the na.me of the petitioner at various •tages of the proceedings. Thus
according t o section five, the brother recommending the petition is at liberty to
withdraw it, if, previous to its presentation to the Lodge, objections to the candidate are raised b;y the College of L odge Officers. The same privilege is accorded
him in section thirteen, if the Master, upon consultation with his officers arrives
at an unfavorable conclusion in reg;ard to the candidate's character, of whlch the
brother recommending the petition ta to be informed.
Section 19 again provides that rrevious to a ballot being taken the Master lays
before the assembled bretheen al information obtained by him in regard to the
petitioner. If objections still continue to be made, explanations must be entered
ni;>on at once, at the close of which the brother recommending the petition may
withdraw it, or move for a postponement of the ballot.
All this is contrary to the laws and customs observed by the L odges in the
United States. A petition presented to and received by a Loage becomes its prop-

It seems, however, that the amount thus far/laid in, as above •tated, would be

the building alone, even if of modest proportions, would largely exceed the amount
paid in, and there would be no means on hand for the supfort of its inmates.
Other serious objections present themselves to the execution o the plan first suggested. It will be for the league, holding its session in June next, to decide on the
course to be pursued.
The Masonic Reform Movement in Germany.
The Address which we herewith give, issued by six brethren, has attracted much
attention and caused considerable excitement and discussion among the Fraternity
in German~. It is said to have been written in August last, but was distributed
among the Lodges at a much later date. We also add some of the answers it has
evoked from Grand Lodges, and as both addresses and answers speak for themselves, comment seems unnecessary.
The subject now brought prominently before the Fraternity is by no means a
new one ; it has had its advocates as well as adversaries for years, and has been
extensively discussed from time to time in the Masonic journals of Germany.
That the ideas promulgated therein are extending cannot be denied1 but that they
will remain unacceptable to the Fraternity at large is equally unaeniable. Perhaps they will have the effect of purging some of the Masonic systems of Europe
of the incongruities in which they abound. A careful reading of the Address has
left the impression on us, that its aim is to oppose sectarianism in Lodges and open
its doors to those whose ideas of the Supreme Being and morality are not in consonance with those accepted as orthodox by the institution.

[Oct. 10,

The Address is well written and conciliatory in tone. That the seven principles laid down therein are not offered as the ultimatum is evident, for it invites
propositions for improvement, for which there is ample room.
The following is the Address :" To the Lodgf,8 of ·Gerrru;iny :

masonry needs a clear explanation of its problems, and the Masonic Union a.n
internal renovation.
.
"It is acknowledged that Masonry must abandon the closely confinin!f princi·
pie of creed, which is not only undermining the most important foundations of a
Union encircling the world but also freedom of conscience and universality.
"It must remain open to the influences of the times, absorb new strength from
them, and diffuse them again in society. To those who puraue the history of our
Union attentively and without prejudice this task will not be difficult; we must
return to the old sources of Masonic knowledge, which, in the course of time, have
been disturbed by erroneous interpretation or international falsification.
"An attempt for this return and a revival of the Masonic Union we will make
in the annexed declaration, in which we lay down our conviction of the purport
and ol:Jject of our Art.

tion that in order to influence civilization, the aims of Masonry should be clearly
stated, and that the Masonic Union requires an internal renovation. They also
consider it indispensable that Freemasonry should be kept in harmony with the
progress of the world's knowledge, and that for the purpose of accomplishing thiis,
it is necessary to return to the 01d Charges.
"The Union Directory considers it proper not to leave the Grand Lodsce and its
daughter Lodges in uncertainty as to its opinion of the points in the Address, and
feels assured of a general assent thereto. To enter upon a full examination of
these points, would be investing them with too much importance. I will not omit,
however1 to draw attention to the inconsistency, that while Freemasonry is to be
kept in narmony with the progress of knowledge, this progress is to be found in
the period, long gone by, m which the so-called Old Charges were adopted. It
was as far back as 1870, that the United Grand Masters came to the unanimou*
conclusion in regard to the so-called Old Charges, that their claims were no longer
in accord with the spirit of the age, and that they should be preserved only as an
historical monument. Concerning the contents of the principles laid down in the
Address, they differ materially in one point from the general principles heretofore
contained in the Constitutions of the German Grand Lodges, and in this is found
the true tendency of its authors. It is to separate Freemasonry from its religious
basis and steer German Freemasonry into the channel in which French Freemasonry has been found since the time when the Grand Orient of France declared
that the principle of a belief in God was no longer required for admission into a
Lodge. For that reason the Address speaks of intellectual and moral education
as the objects of the Union, but not of religious education and improvement. In
France, the declaration spoken of, finds some excuse in the fact that the view upon
which it is based, is connected with the somewhat extended philosophical tendency,
the so-called PoBitivism. That, as is proclaimed, desires practically to eirt.ablish a
morality with-Out religiun, because the latter is met with in no other shape than the
frightful form of the Roman Church with its Jesuit morality. But the wish of
transplanting the doctrines of Positivism into Germany, even with the best intentions, is a sin against the spirit of our great philosophy and can only be occasioned.
by that wicked and generally prevailing confusion of conception by which Christ\antheology and Christianity, religion and churchdom, religion per se and in appearance, are arbitrarily mixed up. But German Masonry, unless it wants to abanda
itself, is too profoundly planned to lay aside religious culture and improveme
with humane moral perfection. It is one of the greatest errors of our time to insis
that a belief in God, in moral liberty, in the invariable laws of nature and in the
personal infinity of the Spirit, are dogmas that have sprung from a reflecting intellect or from abstract speculations; they are rather the profoundest ideas of the
mind, of which we become directly conscious in our feelings, will and imaginations,
and, therefore, the most positive that exist. Morality and religion can only be
separated _b_y abstract thought.
"The Union Directory (Bundes Directorium) has clearly expressed itself in the
circulars i&sued on St. John's day for the last few years on the problems and posl·
tion of Freemasonry of the present time. In the last circular, also, has it directed
attention to the inseparabihty of religion and morality. In this we are entirely i1J
harmony with the general Masonic principles established by the Grand Lodge
Diet, the lawful organ of the Grand Lodge League. A change of the same in tilt
sense of the Address would only be a weakening of their deeply moral and religion»
worth as laid down in our ritual and in the symbols of our Royal Art. We have
confidence in the enlightenment prevailing in our Lodges, that the brethren will
recognize this with ourselves and act accordingly."
The Grand Lodge fully assented to the explanations made by tha Deputy Grand

"Thi8, beloved brother, i8 the pith of the wh-Ole explamation, and it is remarkable

" W e do not want to make Freemasonry atheistical ;· that has never entered our

'' W e want fresh, cheerful intellectual life in our Union, and the banishment of

Whether this manifests itself in opposition or approbation is a matter of indifference; it is only carried on in fraternal forms, and these we have not disregarded.

more than we had hoped or. We never anticipated any other result, and never

and we intend to proceed quietly and fraternally, line im et atudio, as soon as the

"4. The Grand Lodge of Hungary for the Aymbolic degrees agrees to constitute

" 5. The brethren of the higher degrees are treated aa Master Masons only
when visiting Symbolic Lodges.
" 6. Previous to the union a Constitution and ritual are to be prepared far the
Symbolic Lodgee."
The Grand Lodge has twenty-four daughter Lodges, with one thousand t.wo

newspapers:.
"The Legislative Assembly, in confirmation of resolutions adopted by former
ASBemblies, declares that the supreme Masonic authority in Italy and its colonies

49, which is authorized to protect the rights and integrity of the national Muonic

A call for the assembling of an International Masonic Congre88 at Rome is proposed, also a revision of the ritual and the participation by women in Masonic
work..
The supreme authorities are embodied in the Grand Orient, namely: the Grand

to the rite which they practice. It is, therefore, incumbent upon every Italian
brother visiting Lodges in foreign countries to present his di'j'loma as a Master
Mason.

ROUMANIA.
Great disorder and strife prevails among the Masons of that country. France,
Italy Hamburg and Portugal have chartered Lodges there, and it also has a socalled National Grand Lodge, established by one Mornorn, in September, 1880.
It seems, however, that this Captain Mornorn, who fought in the Russian-Turkish
war, has, during that campaign, conferred degrees upon his friends ad /ibituni. He
was, as it is asserted, expelled by the Grand Orients of Portugal and France, and
also by two Lodges at Bucharest, for unmasonic conduct. The Lodge Le P1·og1·es
de la DoW-UU!cha, workin_g under the Grand Orient of France, is particularly severe
on Mornorn, while the Lodge L'Etoile du Danube defends him. Murnorn himself
has issued a circular in his own defense, which he has sent to all Grand Lodges.
We have no interest in this little family unpleasantness, which, to say the least,
is not creditable to the brethren of that country. It is stated that Lodges there
spring up like mushrooms over night.
A letter dated June 10, 1882, was received by the Grand Lod!fe Eclectic Union,
at Frankfort, from seven Lodges in Roumania, declaring their mtention to establish a Grand Orient for the purpose of uniting all Lodges of that country now
working under the different Grand Lodges, including the one founded by MoIROIU.
Tbe Eclectic Union has referred them to the Grand Lodge League of Germap.y . .
CONCLUSION.
Our task is completed, and we arrive at the jurisdiction of " Conclusion " with
feelings in which pleasure and regret are mingled ; pleasure, that our weary brain
and cramped fingers will find needed rest ; and regret, that we must bid adieu to
those with whom, in the spirit, we have spent so many hours of pleasant and profitable communion. We entered upon the performance of the duty assigned us by
the Grand Master with many misgivings. It was our first adventure in this flold
of Masonic literature, and we fully appreciated the disadvantages under which we
labored, both from inexperience, and from the fact that our immediate predeceBBor
was a brother whose reputation as a Masonic writer was world-wide, and we feared
that, compared with his brilliant reports, our own humble effort would appear
" flat, stale and unprofitable." However, inspired by encouraging words from th~
Grand Master, as Cassius says, "Accoutred as I was I plunged in" to the vast
mass of Masonic volumes, whose formidable proportions were aufficient to daunt a
stouter heart than ours, and, as we read, we became interested, then earnest, then
enthusiastic in the labor before us. In short, we fell in love with our work, and
the pleasure derived from perusing the written thoughts of th011e enga.ged in similar
work has sweetened many a weary hour of toil. In our journey through the wide
field of Masonic literature before us, we have found the way lined with flowers of
rhetoric, and studded with gems of eloquence, and we have plucked here and there
a flower, and gathered a few of the brightest gems for the delectation of our brethren of this jurisdiction; and to these we would say that, having honestly endeavored to collate and place before you that which we deemed most interesting and
instructive, we trust you will look only upon what is good in our report, and pass
its imperfections by.
,
In discussing the topics which now are prominently before the Masonic world,
we have given our opinion freely, but we trust in no case offensively. The object
of these reports, as we understand it, is to give and receive information; to reveal
the truth ; and by a courteous and fraternal interchange of thoughts and ide&11 to
settle ~ooted points, and bring about & unanimity of feeling. It is plea.eant to
note the peace and harmony which prevail universally among the Fraternity
throughout our land. All sounds of strife are hushed, and, from those jurisdictions
which but lately were in ill accord, come words of fraternal love and kindness
which are as "apples of gold in pictures of silver."
To our Grand Master our thanks are due, first, for the honor conferred in our
appointment, and secondly, for kindly encouragement in that which at first

1883.J

Grand Lodge of OaUfornia.

appeared an insurmountable task.

225

To the Grand Secretary, Bro. ABl!LL, our

~hanks are also due for advice and oouns~l. To our brother reporters we metaphar-

ically extend the right hand of fellowship in parting. In reviewing the proceedings
of their respective jurisdictions we have endeavored to do justice to all and if we
have unwittingly said aught to injure the feelings of any brother we'assure him
the intent was farthest from our thoughts, and ask his pardon here. ' We trust thiS',
our first and somewhat crude effort, will be received with that courtesy and
forbearance which is born of charity.
.
I~ India the young maiden fills a shell with oil, and lighting a wick within it
sets it afloat upon the broad bosom of the Ganges, watching with intense interest
i~s wayward course 118 it floats on freighted with her prayera and messa.ges of affection to loved ones in the Spirit Land. We have fteighted our little bark and
launched. it upon the sea of Masonic literature, with its dim light burning. We
shall &ruuously watch its coune. '.l'reat it kindly, and the undersigned will ever
pray; otherwise not. Finally, my brethren, "may the blessings of Heaven rest
up~n us. and all regular Masons; may brotherly love prevail, and every moral and
social virtue cement us." So mote it be.
All which is respectfully submitted by
THOS. H. B. ANDERSON,

Your committee, to whom were referred sundry papers from Guadalup~ Lodge,
No. 237, relative to the case of PATRICK McABDLE, a Fellow Craft who was expelled
by that Lodge on the twenty.fifth day of April, 1881,-which action was reversed and
1ot aside by the Gra.nd Lodge in October of that year on the sole ground that jurisdio·
tlon of the accused had not been acquired, and further proceedings ordered to be
hld,-have had the whole subject under consideration and report as follows:At the laat Annual Communication the Grand Secretary reported t.hat "no such
further proceedings have reached this office, nor has there been any information
received as to why they should not have been sent." Under those circumstances your
oommittee then reported. that "The officers of Guadalupe Lodge are censurable for
their inaction in tll.is matter," and, by a resolution reported and adopted, the Lodge
was directed to proceed at once to carry into effect the order made at the previous
Annual Communication • • •,if the same had not already been done, and to report
Ill! Roon as may be all its action in the premises, with the reasons, if any existed, for
the long delay.
It now appears that, in pursuance of said order for further proceedings, on the
twelfth day of December, 1881, the Master of said Lodge speoially convened it, prooeeded regularly to the election of trial~commissioners, and submitted to them the
original charge of gross unmasonic conduct with three speoifications. thereunder.
The second specification was that on a certain date the accused was guilty of "expos·
Ing the secret signs of the Order while in a beastly condition of intoxication; eto., to
persons not connected with the Order." The third specification was" that his con·
duct is generally immoral and that he Is addfoted to the vices of drunkenness and
profanity."
The accused, by his attorney, demurred to the jurisdiction of the Lodge over the
person of the accused, as well as to the insufficiency of the specifications. The first
ground of demurrer was one over which the Master had control a.nd which he prop·
erly overruled, as the Lodge of which a Mason is a member has jurisdiction over him
wheresoever he may be. The Master erred in sustaining the demurrer and dismiss·

228

PrO(;~e,dings of the

[Oct. 10,

ing the charge and specifications on the other ground stated-their alleged insufficiency. They a.re grave and serious charges, and could not well have been made more
specific; but, if they were not, the rule is that when a. charge and a~fl.aa.ti~ne are
presented to the Master, before he proceeds to call the Lodge in special meeting for
an election of commissioners, he shall "carefully examine the same." The meeting
should be called only after the Master blfs passed upon tile primary sufficiency
ff the charge and specifications. If they are found i_nsu~cient, no notifi_cation
or summons should be directed to be prepared for hie signature or be Bigned,
i saned, or served. All this was done, however, and with apparent correctness,
the charge and specifications seeming to have been found to be sufficient in the estimation of the Master.
It would appear that the Committee on Grievances of 1881 did not find the
charges insufficient, but reversed the judgment for insufficiency of the service of
summons alone. To dismiss the charge and specifications under those circumstances, and to dissolve the commission, was erroneous, and that a.otion of the
Master must be condemned. There is no doubt that the action of the Grand Lodge in
1881 restored the accused, and that be was properly reported in 1882 upon the roll
of the Lodge.
The Master's letter to the Grand Secretary, of January 12th, 1883, excusing the
long delay, is not satisfactory. The Grand Secretary reports that ·the trial-record,
or more properly the record of the proceedings as certified by the Sec.retary of the
Lodge, showing the dismissal of the charge by order of the Master, 10 Deoem:i>er,
1881, was not received by him until January, 1883-a. full year intervening. It dooiJ
seem to us that a. Master, taking the responsibility of dismissing snch serious
charges and epecifl.ca.tiws as are here presented, should have been eepeoia.lly anxious
to have had his action reported to the Grp,nd Lodge, and should not have delayed the
transmission of the transcript as wae done; and the a.lleged absence or neglect of the
Secretary of the Lodge does not appe.r to be a sufficient excuse for the delay.
Your committee do not feel that they will have fully dieoha.rged their duty in disposing of this now somewhat celebrated case if certain statements of the Master, in
his Jetter to the Grand Secretary attempting to excuse the delay, be overlooked. In
speaking of his action in sustaining the demurrer to ihe sufficiency of the speoilloatione, he says:-" I held the point well ta.ken and dismissed the case, as all but one
who had any grievance have left our Lodge, and I do not think would prefer any
charges." He also says that he thought other charges would be immediately preferred, and yet further says that he "has, at all times since, been ready to raise the
accused."
•
It is hardly possible, in the same space, to crowd so much misunderstanding of
Masonic law as is here presented. A Masonic offense is not personal. A charge
properly preferred becomes a case in which the Lodge pr?secutes the 11oo~aed. To
permit an unworthy man to remain in the Order because his accuser or accusers hne
dimitted from the Lodge, would be an inexcu1111ble offense of the Lodge against the
body of Masons. To dismiss charges for want of certainty only, and when other
charges are expected to be 'Preferred, and not directing such action to be ~ken by
the Junior Warden, js a dereliction of duty by the Master , and an error which .y our
committee are pleased to think never before oocurreq in this jurisdiction, and which
they hope will never be repeated. The Master, however, presents some extenuating
circumstances for his conduct. He confesses his inexperience and Ignorance, an
anxiety to be set right, and a willingness to receive instruction. It is hoped that _he
may profit by his experience in this case. Your committee recommend thea.dopt1on
of the following resolution :.Resolved, That the action of the Master of (Juadalupe Lodge, No. 237, in dismissing the charge of unmasonic conduct against PATRIOK MCARDLE, a. Fellow
Craft, preferred by two members of said Lodge, be and is hereby reversed; and that

.,. he approaches the end of his allotted three score years and ten. That Faith
which animated his youth Is almost lost in sight; Hope, which inspired his manhood,

usa.iied, his fortitude yields, the lessons of prudenoe which he so thoroughly learned
11nd has so often taught, are hushed and forgotten, he faUs, and justice, with her
Inexorable exactions, overtakes him. His advancing footsteps are arrested when the
last round of the theological ladder is almost yielding itself to bis possession, and he
11 expelled. Ia tlae summit of the ladder never to be reached? Is Charity-Masonic
Charity-not te be extended to him ?

been his punishment. Reason has resumed its sway. Struck with remorse a.t the
11reatness of his offense against Masonic law and teachings, he comes to you with a

To the M. •. W. •. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia 1 A minority of yonr Committee on Grievances has failed to agree with the majority
thereof upon the case of CHARLES Lours WIGGIN, heretofore expelled by ,"\fount
Moriah Lodge, No. «; and, as such minority, I beg leave to offer the followini
report:I have carefully considered the petition, as also the recommendation of the
Lodge of which the petitioner was formerly a member, for his restoration to the
rights and privileges of Masonry, and I have also examined the transcript of the
trial-record now on file in the Grand Secre~ry's office. From this I learn that the
petitioner was dnly expelled on the fourth day of September, 1878, for unmasonic
conduct and malfeasance in office. Although properly notifled,he never appeared before the commission elected to investigate his case, either in person or by connselnot having offered any defense in any manner whatsoever. His guilt was plain and
indisputable. The commissioners were unanimous in their verdict as to the ques·
tion on both charges; while but one of their number opposed the enforcement of the
severest penalty known to Masonic law.
You have listened to the only plea made by the petitioner and urged by the
majority of this committee, In all sincerity and truth I would that the oase were of
such 11 character that I could conscientiously concur with them. But, after due
deliberation, and with a sense of the duty that rests upon me, I am forced to say,
emphatically, that I cannot. While I am free to admit that charity, the gracious
mother of all virtues, can and should cover a multitude of sins, yet we, the representatives of this model institution of morality and virtue, should exercise due care
that this greatest of virtues should be dispensed devoid of riRk that the result will be
pernicious or baneful In its etrects.
The case before us is 11 serious one-one among the gravest of Masonic oft'enses_,
The plea offered in its extenuation might suffice If the offense had simply been com·
mitted in an hour of desperation, or was the result of 11 false step in an unguarded
moment. Such is not the evidence that confronts us in this case. For 11 period of
over five years the deficits of the petitioner gradually grew, as was alleged, to a
total of $6,804 87. When we contemplate the extended period through which these
deficits grew to such proportions, and consider the plea of Intemperance which has
been offered in extenuation, it makes the heart sad. The commission of a great
wrong, while in open violation of one of the great oardinaliiirtues of :Masonry, should
be a solemn admonition to the rational and thinking mind, in the honr of reflection,
to thenceforth steer clear of the rocky shoals that will inevitably lead to sure de·
struction, And when it becbmes plain that the same offense has been time after
time repeated, it certainly must suggest premeditated wrong.
·
I believe that the opinion among men deservedly prevails that the magnitude of
offense becomes greatest where most confidence has been reposed. That the petitioner was in full possession of the confidence and esteem of his brethren Is indis·
potable when we remember the fact that he held an honorable trnst in three of the Masonic Grand Bodies of California. Rather than that my action should be tortured into
a semblance of persecution of 11 fallen brother, I would cheerfully tear up this report
and remain forever dumb as regards the issues of the case. But, with conscientious
rrgard for the interests of Masonry rather than of individuals, I ask, if we concur in
the majority report, will it not be offering 11 precedent that will prove pernicious in
its effects? Will it not be offering 11 premium for similar offenses in the future?
There are times when sympathy may be aroused for the veriest criminal bronght to
justice; but can we afford to allow sympathy to subvert reason-to burst asunder
the bonds that bind our social system? If so, abolish codes, destroy courts, and
reap in remorse the fruits that will inevitably result from such rashness. If such
argument is possessed of merit in the first instance, how much more will it apply in
an Order "professing nothing but the purest principles of morality and virtue?"

Grand Lodge of California.

1883.J

241

Brethren, my simple appeal comes from an honest heart. It is not prompted by
malice or anything pertaining thereto, and is entirely free from the remotest inten·
tlon of doing an injustice. I am, on the contrary, full to overflowing with sympathy
for the petitioner in his penitence and contrition of heart, who, nevertheless, by his
wayward, reckless, and unwarrantable career, has brought disgrace npon himself
and shaken the few grains of faith that even the misanthrope might entertain in poor
fallen humanity. While I applaud the sentiments so beautifully expressed In the
majority report, I nevertheless claim that it is a duty we owe to the great instituti?n
of Masonry that our solemn vows should be B11credly fulfilled. Unless we do this,
worship at its B11cred shrines will be but sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal. With
these suggestions, I take leave to offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:.Re8olved, That the petition for restoration to the rights and privileges of Masonry
of CHARLES Louis WIGGIN, who was expelled by Mount Moriah Lodge, No. 4.4., on the
fourth day of September, 1878, be and is hereby denied.
All which is respectfnlly submitted by
HIRAM N. RUCKER, Of the Oommi.ttee.

occasion may also well excite humility and anxiety. We live in times of preter·

the Craft.
It is difficult to be original in the treatment of Freemasonry. Its external aspeots,
its ~eth~ds and its objects, have been explained and illustrated in every language in

and its antiquity demonstrated, nntil it has been connected with the origin of estab·

broadly unfolded, and their practical effect in promoting the growth of civilization
conspicuously exhibited. Its ~ymb olism and its ritual have been described to the

wb1cb, while they attest its universality, insulate and protect its institutional struct-

I am not a scientist nor a philosopher, and there may be serious defects in my

In the first place, then, individuals, communities, nations, races, the world, are

taken in its broadest sense, Is the perfection of man. The means by which that
object is to be attained, which comprise the substance and essence of all true prog·

one eternal pnrpoRe that moves the successive generations of men, that do not leave

These generalizations, though a faint outline, are all I need to introduce the second

ject, yielded up our deepest secret, delineated the Masonic character? If this be

deals solely with the individual, with bis character and conduct in the parenthesis of
mortality, and there in those particulars only concerning which there can be no
honest and rational disagreement. It requires physical completeness at the outset
of a Masonic career, as a presumptive guarantee for the equal performance of Masonic

limits of moderation. He is also Instructed in that kind of equality between men
which forbids jealousy and protects every substantial right., while it does not attempt
the Impracticable task of controlling the accidents and clrcumstanceR of life by com·

tionslism. He perceives, too, that uprightness and integrity are the basis of ordinary
success as well as of memorable achievements, and that men were created to wqrk

In regard to the proposed amendment of the Constitution, by striking out the
words " one dollar'' in the second line of the second claase of Section 4, Article
VIII, Part I, and inserting in lieu thereof the words " seventy-five cents "-so that
that clause shall read "For each Master Mason borne apon its roll at the date of its
annual report, the sum of seventy.five cents "-your committee report as foJ.
iows:The result sought to be accomplished by this amendment is the reduction of the
tax levied for the sapport of the Grand Lodge. The amount received into the treasury from this source during the last fiscal year was some $13,000. The adoption of
the amendment would reduce that sam by twenty-five per cent., and, wh!le making
I serious inroad upon the aggregate revenue of the Grand Lodge, would afford relief
to the individual membership of the Lodges lo so small a degree as to be scarcely
appreciable.
.
Your COmIDittee have given the proposition their serious consideration and do
not believe that the relief to be obtained by It would compens11te for the loss of so
large a portion of our revenue. The condition of our jurisdiction is fiuancially
healthy, the tax referred to Is not burdensome, and the rellef to be afforded, ff this
11mendment were adopted, would be scarcely perceptible.
B~sides, your committee are impressed with tb.e propriety, if not the duty, of
.keepmg oar receipts at such standard as will not only afford an abundance of fonds
when ~eed.ed in our own jurlsdictlon-io the event of a visitation by fires, fioodM,
epidemic diseases or other unforeseen calamities-but which shall enable us, with
rraternal gratification, to aid In relieving the dMresses of our brethren elsewhere
when misfortane shall have overtaken them, as it has been our happy fortune to d~
more than once in the past.
In view of these and other similar reasons they recommend that the proposed
amendment be not adopted •
.All which is respectfully submitted by

Bro. WILLIAM C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports :To the M. ·. W. •• Grand Lodge of Oa1ifomw:Dnring the yea.r, the Grand Master, upon applications made to him, has issued
sundry special dispensations for the purposes named in the report of the Grand
Secretary, all which were authorized by the Constitution. These are mattel'll p.roperly left to the discretion of the Grand Master, and it appears to .your committee
that in each of the cases named his discretion has been wisely exercised.
Your committee have given careful consideration to the question proposed by
Bro. GBORGB J. HoBE, ''whether it is competenl for e. Lodge to vote by ballot npon
a resolution for the restoration of one of its members who had been 6nspended for 1
unmasonic oondnot."
In the case presented it appears that, a resolution having been introduced for the
purpose above named, e. member of the Lodge !JlOVed that the vote th~reon be taken
by ballot, and another moved that i~ be taken viva vooe upon the calling of the roll.
The motion to take the vote by ballot was pnt and carried; whereupon one or more
members of the Lodge presented the objection that a vote upon such a question
should be taken viva vooe, and that it was not competent or proper that it should be
taken by ballot. The Master decided that it was within the discr~tion of the Lodge
to determine how the vote should be taken, directed that the vote m that case should
be by ballot, and the vote was so taken.
The Constitution provides that the vote upon e.ppl!oe.tione for degrees and for
membership, and in certain other cases, must be by ballot, but it does not direct in
what manner the vote upon such a case as this shall be taken. The usual manner
of voting is vi11a oooe, or by show of hands, but your committee see no reason why
the Lodge may not determine for itself that the vote upon any particular matter be
taken by ballot, in the absence of any law forbidding it.
Your committee have examined the papers relative to the ooneolidation of
Mokelumne Lodge, No. 81, and Oalaverae Lodge, No. 78, and, finding that the ~ro­
ceedinge in that matter conform substantially to the requirements of the Oonstita·
tion, offer and recommend the adoption of the following resolutions:Resolved, That the proceedings of .Mokelumne Lodge, N.o. 31, and Oalaveraa
Lodge, No. 78, looking to the consolidation of those Lodges into one Lodge under
the name and number of Cala11era1J Lodge, No. 78, be and are hereby approved, and
that such consolidation take effect at the stated meeting of Calaveras Lodge, No. 78,
in December next.
.

preside, and that all the members of both the foregoing named Lodges, shall have
the right to participate in all the proceedings of such meeting, and shall, from that
date, be members of the consolidated Lodge.
.
Be1olv11d, That the by-laws of Calaveras Lodge, No. 78, be and are hereby

Your committee have examined the papers referred to them, relative to the proposed consolidation of Neln'aska Lodge, No. 71, and Ione Lodge, No. 80, and fin~
them so imperfect that no action can be taken by the Grand Lodge e.t this Communication to carry into effect the wish of those desiring such consolidation.
The papers do not show that either of the Lodges has taken any action in the
matter at all, but only that, at some time in November last, certain action was proposed by thein . It appears to be probable that some action was taken, but no
certificate of that fact from the Secretary of either of the Lodges has been presented.
Section 11, Article II, Pari III, of the Constitution prescribes generally the manner
ln which consolidations of Lodges may be effected; and, in a report presented by this
committee in 1874., to be found at page 681, Vol. XI, of the bound proceedings of the
Grand Lodge-in the matter of the consolidation of Marysvil~ Lodge, No. 9, and
Corinthian Lodge, No. 69, at Marysville-the proper proceedings for a consolidation
of Lodges were stated explicitly and at length for the information of such Lodges as
might then or theree.fler desire to consolidate. The attention of the applicants in
this case is ca.lied to that report, a.nd its general purport iB again presented for
their information and for that of others, as follows:lst. There should be adopted by each Lodge e. resolution to the effect tha.t e. consolidation iB expedient and that a committee from each Lodge be appointed to
arrange and report the terms upon which such consolidation may be eft'ected,
2d. These committees, when appointed, must meet and agree upon the terms of
the consolidation, and ma.ka their reports to their several Lodges ; and their report.
must be received and concurred in by their respective Lodges.
3d. When the Lodges aha.II have thus concurred in the reports of their commit.
tees, and the terms of oonsolirla.tion shall have been agreed upon, notice must be
given by the Secretary of each of the Lodges to all its members, that, at a stated
meeting to be holden on a day named In the notice, which must be more than three
months eubRequent to the date thereof, a resolution for ooneolidation will come up
for final action.
4th. Meanwhile, e. paper or papers, either written or printed, substantially in the
form which follow~, should be presented to the members of each Lodge for their
1igna.tures :" In pursuance of certain action of
Lodge, No. --, and - - - - Lodge, No. ---, tending to the oonsolida.tion of said Lodges into one Lodge, under the
name and number o f - - - - Lodge, No. --, we, the underefsned, members
o f - - - - Lodge, No.--, do hereby express our a.seent to and our desire for
such proposed consolidation:"
Which paper or papers must be signed by at least thre&ofourths of the members
of each of the Lodges desiring to consolidate, prior to the time of fine.I aotion.
5th. At the stated meeting for which notice shall have been aiven, as above,
these papers must be presented, each to Its proper Lodge, showing that at lea.st
three-fourths of the members of each of the Lodges have expressed their aBSent In
writing, and thereupon the resolution may come up for final a.ction and adoption;
and when these proceedings shall have been had, the papers and the action of the
Lodges must be certified to the Grand Secretary by the Secretaries, under the seals
of their respective Lodges.
6th. When all the proceedings shall have been completed, they should be entered
upon tho records of each. of the existing Lodges, and the transcripts sent to the
Grand Secretary should contain full copies of such records.
The language of Section 11, Article II, Pe.rt III, of the Constitutfon, is explloit
in its declaration that "no such consolidation shall ao into effect nntil a.II the proceedings relative thereto shall have been submitted to and approved by the Grand
Lodge;" and your committee are therefore compelled to recommend that the present
application be dismissed.

All which reports were concurred in and the several resolutions
accompanying them were adopted.
Bro. WILLIAM C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudencd,
also presented a report upon the petition of Bro. JoHN H1LLHOUSEan Entered Apprentice of Vesper Lodge, No. 84, who, after having
received that degree, had suffered a physical injury which caused that
Lodge to decline to confer upon him the remaining degrees without
special authority from the Grand Lodge-praying that such authority
be given to said Lodge. The report of the committee was concurred
in by the Grand Lodge; but the chairman thereof, who was the
writer of the report, requests that it be not now published, as he
deems it desirable that the subject should receive further consideration.
Bro. CHARLES A. GARDNER offered the following resolution, which
was adopted by an unanimous vote :.Resolved, That this Grand Lodge expre•s its appreciation of the kind, able and
impartial manner in which it has been presided over by our retiring Grand Master,
the M.·. W,•, CLAY WEBSTER TAYLOB, qualities displayed alike during the Commu·
nications of this body and in the administration of its affairs throughout the year;
that in him we recognize one of the many illustrious leaders with which this Grand
Lodge has been honored, and that we would not willingly part with him, after two
years faithful service, without placing upon record this. testimonial of our appreciation, esteem, and brotherly love-sentiments which we feel assured move the hearts
of every member of the Grand Lodge of California.

presentation to him at the next .Annual Communication of our Grand Lodge.

Somo forty bands were distributed through the procession, and
yet, from its exceeding length, there was an apparent scarcity of
music.
From the Masonic Temple to Conservatory Valley, in Golden Gate
Park, where the ceremony was to be performed-a distance of about
three miles-the windows and roofs of all the buildings, the sidewalks,
temporary constructions for seating spectators upon every vacant
apace, and all the room in the streets and roadways permitted by the
police, were crowded with inhabitant.a of the city and visitors from the
adjacent country, who came by thousands upon thousands to witness
a procession such as never before had been seen in this city, and
which perhaps, owing to the peculiar circumstances of the occasion,
had rarely ever been elsewhere seen.
At the place in the little valley above named, surrounded by untlnlating elevations covered with verdure and flowers, an artificial
mound had been created, and upon it had been erected a platform on
a level with and surrounding the corner-stone to be laid, sufficiently
large to accommodate the Grand Officers of the Grand Lodge, the
various Office-bearers of that Body whose duties wore connected
therewith, the Masonic choir, and the musicians necessary for the
occasion .
The Grand Master was seated in front of the centre of the platform, immediately accompanied by the Grand Officers and Officebearers of the Grand Lodge.
Upon a table before him, properly draped, was placed by their
several bearers the Holy Writings, the Book of Constitutions, the
Golden Vessel containing Corn, the two Silver Vessels containing
Wine and Oil, the Three Large Lights, the five Orders of Architecture, the working tools of the Principal Architect, and the Casket
containing the deposits to be placed beneath the corner-stone.
All those for whom seats upon the platform had been provided
having taken their places, and general order and quiet among the
great concourse surrounding it having succeeded, the band played
that beautiful and impressive piece of music, the Prayer from " Moses
in Egypt."

Special, Oommunication of the

[Aug. 24,

The following prayer was then offered by the V. ·. R. ·. WILLIAll(
FLETCHER Co!dl'TON, Grand Chaplain of the Grand Lodge:0 God, the Mighty God, whose throne is in tne heavens, but whose glory and
majesty fill the ·universe, vouchsafe Thy gracious recognition of this imposing a~sem·
blege of Ancient Craftsmen , and command Thy divine blessing upon the object con·
templated by this convocation.
Here are those who represent the Ancient Order of Free and Accepted Masons,
from all parts &f our glorions commonwealth. May tbeir hearths and homes be
blessed witb the mild radiance of domestic peace ; may their lands be fruitful of the
rich reward of honest toil; and may the visions of heroic achievement cheer their
hearts in the onward march to ultimate triumph in all the great enterprises of life.
Bless our conntry with wise and judicious legislation, honest executives, and aJ
loyal people. Bless all benevolent institutions having for their object the ameliora·
tion of human conditions and the elevation of our race in the scale of moral, social,
and religions development.
Especially may Thy divine benediction signalize our ancient and honorable Order,
as foremost among the distinguished instrnmentalities now at work to harmonize the
discrepancies of humanity, unify the race in one great brotherhood, and hasten the
consummation of millennial glory.
Help us to emulate the virtues of our great hero, whose memory we this day
shrine in our hearts and transmit to posterity and monumental fame. May the
silent but eloqnent lesson of this structure, when completed, hold, as with the magic
of invincible logic, the heart of this great nation eqni·distant from the Rpirit of
fanatical usurpation and the stroke of fratricidal madness.
With the casket which we this day deposit in imperishable stone, never more per·
haps to see the light, may the American people bury In eternal oblivion the spirit
that culminated in the untimely death of our Chief Magistrate and worthy brother.
And, when the Universal Lodge shall rendezvous at last within the lofty battle·
ments of the Eternal City, may all this vast concourse, glorified, immortal, clad in
the royal regalia of the King, sceptered and crowned, appear before the presence '
of His glory, with exceeding joy. Amen.

The following Ode, adapted to the air of " America," was then
sung by the Masonic choir, with accompaniment by the band:Hall, Masonry divine!
Glory of ages shine
While time shall last !
Where' er thy vot'ries are,
Let Love and Peace be there,
Let thy good works compare
With ages past.
Great mission thine belowThis pilgrimage of woe
Thine 'tis to cheer.
With open heart and hand,
Thy sons in every land,
At Charity'11 demand,
Are ever near.
As, since the Day of Light.
Blazing with lustre bright,
Thy star hath shone;
So may its brightness send
Joy, gladness, without end,
Till Eternity attend
And Time be gone. •·
