The Hon. HoRACE DAVIS, Vice-President and acting President of
the "GARFmLD Monument Association of the Pacific Coast," then
addressed the Grand Master and the listening public as follows :Most Worshipful Grand Mast,er of Masons and Fellow Oitizens :We are here to·day to lay the corner-stone of a monument consecrated to the
memory of a great and good man, whose life was spent in the service of his country,
and whom that country had crowned with the highest honors in its gift.
Wherever in human history the people have had a voice, they have raised such
tributes as this to the dead whose lives have been sanctified by self·sacriftce and
devotion to their country. Such monnments are an honor not alone to those whose
uames they bear, but to human nature ·itself, They are a standing testimony to its
reverence for unselfishness and devotion. And in this spirit we raise this statue of
President GARFIELD, here, in this plaoe of public resort, to testify to our respect for
his exalted position, onr gratitude for his eminent example, and our love for his
memory.
I am glad that we are enabled to inaugurate this memorial edifice with these
"olemn ceremonies, on an occasion when so many of his countrymen, from every
part of the land, could be here to do honor to his memory.
To yon, Masons and Knights Templar, I say I am glad that you are here to add
solemnity to this occasion, for he was an honor to your order, true and faithful to its
principles.
And yoa, soldiers, who shared with him the perils of the battlefield, it is right
that you should be here to drop your tears to the memory of your great comr&de.
Ye,;, every man now present bas an interest as an American citizen ln this solemn
oere,nony, for the bronze image, the base for which we lay to-day, is but a type, an
emb l~ 1u of that more lasting Image, planted in the alfoctlons of his countrymen.
The monument we are buflding here Is a voluntary tribute of the respect and
love of the people. The fand for its erection was raised by the wllling olferlngs of
hi ~ countrymen. It contains no appropriation from the public funds. It represents
no sect, no party, but is a spontaneoud outponring of gifts from the people, repre·
sentiog many thousands of mourners--not only the liberal gifts from men of means,
but the still more precious tributes of multitudes, who gave all that they could spare
from their necessities. Prom every part of this Western coast our appeal was
answered, and the name of every giver will be inscribed on un imperishable roll,
to be preserved in our Hall of Records.
It is a common custom that the foundations of publ!c structures be consecrated
by Masoni~ ceremonies. In accordance with this usage we have Invited the Grand
Lodge of Masons of the State of Callfornia to lay this corner-stone during the week
of this solemn Conclave. It seems especially appropriate, as he in whose honor
it is laid was himself a Mason of high rank and a Knight Templar. The Grand
Lodge has accepted the responsibility, and it Is now my duty to Invest it with the
authority.
Most Worshipful Grand Master: In the name of the GAJtFilllLD Monument Association of the Pacific Coast, I ask you to lay the corner-stone of this monument
which we shall raise to the memory of JAMES ABRAM GARFIELD, twentieth President
of the Unitbd States. And to this end we tender you this instrument, one of the
emblems of your order. May ~he work you shall do with it to-day stand to the end
of time.

At the conclusion of his address, Mr. DAVIS, as indicated therein,
presented to the Grand Master a beautiful silver trowel, mounted with
gold, which had been prepared for the occasion and which bore an
inscription proper for its commemoration.

Spe.cial Communication of the

[Aug. 24,

The Grand Master, the M.-. W.-. CLAY WBBSTER TAYLOR, responded
to the address as follows :- ·
Mr. President, Brethren, and Fellow Cilizens:The Frateroity of Free and Accepted MnRons have, from beyond a period long
since lost io the remote mists of antiquity, been accustomed to lay the corner-Rtone4
of important public edifices, when invited so to do, with the solemn and impressive
ceremonial observances of the Craft.
The grand temples, cathedrah, castles, and monuments of ancient history were
designed and erected by Masons, who were both operative and speculative; and
to-day, as representatives of the ancient builders, and as speculative Masons, we
make use of the same implements that are used in prosecuting the material labors of
operative Masonry,' for the purpose of symbolically illnstrating certain great moral J
truths and of metaphorically inculcating the God-given principles of our fraternity.
The gavel, the sq11are, the level, the plumb, and the trowel have each their symbolic
te•chings, and to the Free and Accepted Mason their significance requires no
elucidation.
We have assembled here to·-day in this beautiful park of the Golden Gate-where,
by untiring zeal, industry, and per•everance, the Rterile sand dunes of the desert
have been literally made to bloom and blossom aR the rose-citizens from every
portion of this grand republic, Masons from every country and from every clime, •tH·
rounded by the waving plumes and gleaming swords of a grand army of magnani·
moue and valiant Knights Templar, who have performed a long and weary pilgrimage
hither, and to-day join with us in the great and glorious undertaking of laying the cor·
ner-stone of this monument to be erected and dedicated to the late chief magistrate aod
ruler of a mighty nation-a Mason who wore with equal honor the lambskin apron of
the Master and the gleaming sword of the Knight Templar-a citizen, who, springing
from among the lowliest of the people, b1• his own unaided efforts, his indomitable
energy and perseverance, rose to rank with the most exalted of bis time.
When the news flashed acro•s the continent that our brother, JAMES ABRAM GAB·
FIELD, President of the United States, wa~ stricken down by the hand of an assassin,' 1
our hearts stood still with horror at the atrocity of the crime. From the humblest
firesides to the most imposing sanctuaries of our land, forvent prayers ascended to
the Throne of Grace, that his life might be spared, under Providence, to continue to
fill the exaltAd position which he oceupied; but the dread messenger came, ~nd
lik,e a valiant Knight he calmly and resignedly obeyed the summons.
Stricken down, not in the morning of active life, nor in the sere and yellow Tear
of ripened age, but at the meridian height of his power and usefulness, his spirit'
winged its flight to the unknown world, and the angels from on high looked down
upon the spectacle of a nation in mourning. No partisan feeling qualified the genuine and heartfelt grief for his loss, but the nation monrned as one man, and from
kings, Q.ueens, princes, and potentates throughout civilization came messages of sym·
pathy and condolence for a stricken people.
On the eastern slope of the continent, whose banks are bathed by the briny
waters of the broad and stormy Atlantic, near the scenes of bis earthly career, he
rests mid the distinguished dead of the republic, with its heroes an~ statesmen; and,
as we are wont to commemorate the memory of the knightly martys of tl.te olden
time, whose deeds of prowess and valor provoked the admiration of. the world, so
should we commemorate the memory of this noble Knight who fell with his armor
on; and it is eminently fit and proper that here, on the western slope, whose golden
sands are washed by the mighty but calm and peaceful Pacific, we should erect an '
enduring monument to his name and memory, which, like theirs and like the great
deeds of American history of which be was a part, will live until the evening stars
shell fade away.

Thus we honor the memory of JAMES ABRAM GARFIELD. He sleeps in his native
du1t. His voice will be beard no more in the councils of the nation, and his sword will
nover again be drawn in its defense. The snows of winter will cast their bleak mantle
around his tomb. The earliest buds of spring will unfold their beauties over bis last
ro1tlng place, and the acacia-typical of life beyond the grave-will gsrland it,
while the summer winds will sing over it their soft requiem.
His name will be recorded on brass and bronze, and chiseled in marble and granlle; but when brass and bronze, marble and granite, shall have corroded and dislntearated, and when this corner-stone, to be well and truly laid to-day, shall, with the
monument which will surmount It, have crumbled into dust and be scattered to the
ruur winds of heaven, then, as season follows season, so will the memory of our
departed brother ever spring fresh and green in the hearts of the American people.

MOST WORSHIPFUL GRAND MASTER AND BRllTHREN, MR. PRESIDENT AND MKMBEB8
OF THE GABFlJlf,D MONUllll<NT ASSOCIATION, AND FELLOW·CITIZENS':Jt is often said that the age of great oratory, of great poetry, of great dramatic
works, is over. In a certain sense the assertion is true. The world of fact, with its
ever-developing possibilities, has taken the place of the world of the imagination. The
human mind, trained and educated by the very process of acquisition, is no longer
compelled to evoke, from ita own mystic depths, the thought that stirs, the image..,
that tbrilfs, the dark phantoms that tear, the lmman heart. We live, neverthe~e-.
in a period of terse and inspiring eloquence. Nature, with its innumerable forms of
grace and beauty, addresses hourly an illuminated and enfranchised intelligence~
Law, with its myriad voices, tells ns of order and of applied jnstice that exclude the
arid theory of chance. True science, often confounded with the mere assumption•
and formulas of mental egotism, spreads from pole to pole exact and useful know!·
edge. Discriminating history gathers up the record& of the past and warns and iastructs us by its lessons. The acts, the ideas, the words, of men are heralded through
all the zones. And while, in the wondrous increase of organized communities, indi·
vidnal importance is being steadily diminished, unrestricted intercourse is blending
humanity into a net-work of relations which transcend governments and territorial
divisions, and, in the midst of strife and apparent confusion, are solving the most
difficult problems that have been transmitted to us throngh the statesmen and philos·
op hers of six thou~and years. It is not surprising that, in such a complex aggregate
of realities, in which the miracle of the Creation is perpetuated and expanded, the
genius of fiction, the productions even of the loftiest intellects of all time are
eclipsed. ' Civilization at once epitomizes and magnifies the grandest conceptio~s of
the poets. The daily achievements of man upon land and sea, the diversified industries in which he is employed, the advance of liberty through all the grooves of trade
and commerce-multiplying the comforts and elevating the general level of popula·
tions-constitnte a ceaseless oration which excels the measured rhetoric of DEMOB·
THENES and of PERICLES. And every man who is not a drone and an incubus, one of
the supernumeraries of society, is himself an actor, from the cradle to the grave,•in
a perfect drama which depends upon no legend for Its origin, which wlll end only
when the consummation of humanity shall be accomplished, whose Author and whose
Finisher is God.
This glittering pageant, which is born not all of joy nor all of sorrow, and in
which the diversities and even the antagonisms of every part of the Union are
grouped and harmonized, is full of an intense significance which History wiU appre·
bend and describe, and which it Is my duty to the extent of my ability to interpret.
In the presence of this vast multitude, the oldest of human institutions and the new·
est phase of civilization have met together, and Freemasonry, type of the severe and
of the e.ntiqne, hes exercised e. normal function by co-operating with civil society in
a simple e.ct, designed to mark a great calamity and a great triumph. The calamity
was the death by violence of a man who had been elected President of the United
States, and who was in himself an illustration of the excellence of our national insti·
tutions; -the triumph is that of constitutional freedom and order In a Continental
Republic.
We are assembled here, not under the invocation of a barren science that would
emasculate the world of all that is not visible or susceptible of explanation through
an arrogant human intelligence, but in the name of God, the Supreme Architect of
the Universe, the Creator of Heaven and Earth, the Source and Origin of the forces
e.nd laws that have developed and shaped both men and nations, to place on the ex·
treme western verge of the American continent the foundation of a durable memorial to human progress e.s illustrated by American institutions and by the American
people. A stone, accepted by the builders, though formally dedicated to the mem·

ARTICLE Ill.
OF !TB POWERS AND AUTHORITY,
SECTION 1. The Grand Lodge is tbe Supreme Masonic Power and Authority in
this State, possessing all the attributes of sovereignty and government-legisllitlve,
exec utive, and judicial- limited only by a •trict adherence to the Ancient Landmarks
of the Order, and by the provisions of its own Constitution and Regulations.
SEc. 2. Hs legislative powerR extend to every ca•e of legislation not expressly
delegated by itself to the Lodgas; and the Constitutions and Regulations, which it
has an inalienahle right to adopt and promulgate at itR own r,onvenience, and to alter,
amend, or repeal at its own pleasure, under tl1e limitations therein imposed, are final
and binding upon all Lodges and Masons within its jurisdiction, until so altered,
amended, or repealed.
SEO. 3. Its executive powers include the granting of dispensations and charters
to establish and perpetuate Lodges within this State, and in other territory where
no Grand Lodge exists ; the revocation or suspension thereof; the issuing of special
dispensations for all purposes permitted by any of the provisions of this Constitution;
and the exercise, generally, of all such authority as may be necessary to cury its
own legislation into complete eftect.
SEc. 4. Its judicial powers are of two kinds :1st. Original-Including the decision of all controversies between any of the
Lodges, or between one of them and a member or members of another; and the
enforcement of discipline npon its own members and upon the Lodges under its
jurisdiction : and
2d. Appellate- Embracing the revision of a.II matters of controversy or discipline,
proper for Masonic investigation , which may have arisen in any of ~he Lodges, and
over which it has not retained original jnrisdictien.

PART III.

Of the Subordinate Lodge,s.
ARTICLE I.
OF THE ORGANIZATION OF A LODGE.
SBOTION 1. A Lodge can only be formed by authority of a dispensation from the
Grand Master, or of a charter from the Grand Lodge; and no charter shall be granted
to any Lodge until it shall have worked a time under dispensation, and shall have
exhibited to the Grand Lodge satisfactory evidence of Its Masonic capability.
SEc. 2. Upon th11 p etition of twelve or more Master Masons being presented to
the Grand Master, in the form prescribed in Art. III, Part VII, he may grant them a
dispensation to open and bold a Lodge at the place therein tci be named, with power
to make Masons and receive members by affiliation : and he shall therein appoint the
Master and Wardens of the new Lodge. But in no caeo shall such dispensation be
issued unless the petition be accompanied by a recommendation from the ne11l'est
or mo~t convenient chartered Lodge, (if from a town or city where more than one
Lodge exists, then from a majority of such Lodges,) setting forth, in the form pre·
scribed In Art. III, Part VII, that the petitioners are all Master Masons in good
standing, that the establishment of the new Lodge is of manifest propriety and will
conduce to the good of the Order, and that a safe and suitable Lodge room has been
provided therefor; nor unless the petition shall also he accompanied by a certificate
of withdrawal of each petitioner from the Lodge of which he was 111.st a m41mber,
and by a certificate from a Master, whom the Grand Master is satisfied Is well skilled
in the Oraft, in the form prescribed in Art. III, Part VII, declaring that the Master
and Wardens proposed in such petition are fully competent properly to confer the
three degrees of Masonry and to deliver entire the lectures thereunto appertaining.

REGUL.4.TION.-By a regulation of the Grand Lodge is meant any resolution, edict,
law, or ordinance of any kind whatever, other than the Constitution, which it may
adopt.
SuBPRNSroN.-The suspension· of a Lodge is an arrest of its charter and a tempo·
rary .prohibition to assemble or work as a legal Lodge, until ·again authorized so to
do by competent authority; and the act suspends all its member~ except those especially exempted from its eft'ect.
The suspension of the Master of a Lodge is a temporary deprifation of his office,
and prohibits all recognition of him in that capacity until he be restored by compe·
tent authority.
The suspension of a Mason is a temporary deprivation of all his rights and privi·
leges as such, and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding a.ny Ma~onic intercourse with him until he sh.all be legally restored in the manner herein before prescribed.
EXPur.sroN.-The expulsion of a Mason is the highest penalty known to the Masonic law. It is an absolute deprivation .of all the rights and privileges of the Order,
and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic Intercourse with him
forever, unless he be restored by the Grand Lodge.
NOT!F!CATION.-A notification, or notice, is a ca.II issued by the Secretary, by
order of the Lodge or Moster, or by other competent authority as herein before provided, to attend for some specific purpose at the time aod place therein indicated, or
to perform some specific duty therein set forth; and it is the doty of every Mason to
comply with its direction if he can, without great inconvenience, do so. It shllll be
either written or printed, and shall, when practicable, be personally served upon the
brother to be notified by a Tyler or some other Mason properly deputed for the pur·
pose . If this cannot conveniently be done, it shall be left at the residence or usual
place of business of such brother, or, if such residence or place of business is distant
or unknown, it may be placed In the Post-office, addressed to him at his last known
place ofresidence; and this shall be deemed due and sufficient service.
SUHMONS.-A summons is an Imperative order, issued by the Master of a Lodge
and attested by its Secretary, or ·b y other ·c ompetent authority as hereinbefore provided; tO ·appear at such time and place as may there.in be designated. The obll·
gatlon to obey it is absolute and the penalty for disobedience shall be expulsl<;>n,
unless it shall be shown that such disobedience was unavoidable or was occasioned
by some pressing necessity.
STATllD MEKTING.-'fhe stated meeting of a Lodge is the one only meeting in
each lunar month at which business may be done, with the exceptions specified in
Sec. 2, Art. II, Part III. It shall be designated as snch in the by laws of each lodge,
and no adjourned or oalled meeting shall ever be considered as a part of such stated
meeting.

PAST GBAND OFFICEB.-This title applies only to one of the six elective Grand

PAST MABTER.-Tbis title applies only to one who bas been regularly elected or

VAOANOY.-Vaca.ncies in office, either in a Lodge or in the Grand Lodge, may

JmusnrCTION.-The jurisdiction of the Grnnd Lodge includes all Lodges and

without this State, acting under its authority.
The jurisdiction of a Lodge includes all its own members, wherever residing, and
all Masons residing nearer to its place of meeting than to that of any other Lodge
within this State, except in towns or cities where more than one Lodge exists, in
which case each ·of such Lodges has separate jurisdiction over its own members, and
concurrent jurisdiction over all Masons, not members of one of such Lodges, who
reside in such town or city, or nearer thereto than to any other place where a Lodge
exists.

regularly received it. (1855, 1859.)

forbidden, while that body shall continue its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of
the jurisdictional right~ of the Grand Lodge of New York. (1855', 1859.)

excess o.v er the current p1f:pendltures of .a t least one thouRand dolla,r•; which excess
shl\ll each year be set aside, aR an accumulating fund, to be known as the'' Reserve
Fund.'' which shall be kept and Increased for purposes of emergency, and shall only
be drawn upon therefor. It Rhall be the duty of the Grand Treasurer to judiciously
invest all moneys Ret aside for such fund, and all moneys accruing from the interest
on such inveRtmentR, Rod to report the exat't condition thereof to the Grand Lodge
on the first day of each Annual Communication; and for !ts safe keeping and proper
disbnriiement be i<hall be responRlble on his official bond. (18.>6, 185~, 1869, 1879.)
No i~~ge un4er this jurisdictioµ sball be allowed to transact buein~·ss, other
than the conferring of degrees, with a less number than seven members preaeqt,
(1859.)

5 •. Tiie Gr1md Secretary is authorized to charge the sum of one dollar, for the
uRe of. tile Grand Lodge, for each copy of its printed proceedings for the current
vel!.r, other than the four copieA to be sent. to each subordinate Lodge, and those
required for transmi•sion abroad, for future binding, and for the use of the Grl!.nd
Lodge at its next succeeding Annual Communication. (1869.)

6•. All llla•oM, heretofore stric~enfrom the rolls of. Lodges within this jurisdic·
tion for non-payment of does, who have n,ot been reinstated, ar~ ,hereby declared to
be snspended, RR provided in Sec. 11. Art. III, Part rn. of the Coo8titntion. (1859.)

denominated "The Represent11.tive ~and ; " and it shall be the duty of the several
Lodges to pay the said sum at the time 1tnd in the manner directed in the Constitution
for the payment of their ann.ual dues. (lll61, 1865, 1873.)
8. At the close of each Annual Communication, a committee, to be known as the
"Committee on Pay of Members,'' and to consist of five, shall be appointed by the
Grand Master, whose duty it sball be to ascertain, during the year succeeding, the
exact codt of transportation for one penon from the location of each Lodge in the
State to the place of .meeting of the Grand Lodge and back again; and, at the following Annual Communication, to report such cost of transportation as th11 sum due
to the officers or representative in attendance from each Lodge, whiah sum shall be
p11.id by the Grand Treasurer, such report beiag his voucher therefor. But no payment "hall be allowed for the officers or representative of any Lodge, the dues of
which •hall not have been paid in full. (1861, 1873, 1879.)
9. The appointed Grand Officers and the chairmen of standing committees shall
receive payment for their necessary expenditures for transportation to and from each
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge, in the same manner as ordered for the
oll!cers or representatives of Lodges; bot no Grand Officer, chairman, er officer or
reprpsentative of a Lodge, shall receive such payment in more than one of those
capacities, nor shall he receive it unles" he shall have been in attendance at such
Communication from the first to the 111.st day there Of, inclusive, unless excused by the
Grand Lodge. (1861, 1863, 1873.)
10. The work and lectures presented by the committee appointed for their examination and revision, are approved, adopted, and made obligatory upon all Lodges
within this jurisdiction ; and any Lodge which shall have had opportunity to obtain
instruction therein, and shall neglect or refuse to learn and use the same, shall, upon
.representation of that fact to the Grand Master, be liable to the arrest of its charter,
if, in his discretion, he shall think it proper. (1864, 1865.)
11. The person who desires to be made a Mason must be a man; no woman nor
eunuch; free born, being neither a slave nor the son of a bond woman; a believer in
God and a future existence; of moral cond11ct ; oapable of reading and writing ; not
deformed or dismembered, but hale and sound in his physical conformation, having
his right limbs as a man ought to have; and able to conform literally to what ~he
several d.egrees respectively require of him. (1864.)
12. No Lodge under this jurisdiction, located beyond the limits of this State, shall
receive any allowance for the expenses of a representative to this Grand Lodge;
nor shall any Auch Lodge be chargeable with dues on account of the Representative
Fund. (1867.)
13. All Masonic intercourse between this Grand Lodge and the Grand Orient of
France is hereby suspended, and the Lodges and Masons of this jurisdiction are
forbidden to recognize or hold communication with any brother who hails from or
acknowledges allegiance to the Grand Orient of France, so long as that b0dy continues its unlawful and reprehensible invasion of the jurisdictional rights of the
Grand Lodge of Louisiana. (1869.)
14. Each Lodge within the jurisdiction of this Grand LodJe, so far as it is able
so to do, shall see that the needy of its own membership and neighborhood are not
made a burden to others. (1871.)
15. The Grand Master shall appoint for each district an officer, to be called
·Inspector, who shall be a resident of the district for which he is appointed, and whoee
duty it shall be to visit e~ch Lodge in his district whenever desired by any Lodge, or
whenever he may deem it necessary for the faithful performance of his duties; to
inspect the work, and, if necessary, cc>rrect the same in accordance with the work as

16. No Master of a Lodge shall be installed until he shall have produced to the

17. No dispensation shall hereafter be granted to any Lodge which shall have
adopted the name of a living perRon. (1878.) ·
18. Whenever an appeal sh~ll be taken from the judgment of a subordinate
Lodge upon the report of trial-commissioners, any and all additional evidence, which
either the accuser or accused shall desire to have heard on the appeal, shall be taken
and reduced to writing within sixty days from the day on which the announcement
of the result of the tifal shall be made by the Master to the Lodge, and all arguments
and representations which it is desired to have considered on the appeal shall also be
reduced to wi·lting; and no additional evidence, arguments, or representations shall
be considered on the ap11eal unless the same shall be reduced to writing and transmitted to the Grand Secretary at least sixty days before the commencement of the
next Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge. (1874.)
19. The Lodge conducting the ceremonies at a funeral will or,cnpy the post of
honor, and will assign such positions to other societies that may join in the procession or ceremonies as the Qircumstances of the case may seem to render proper.
The members of a Lodge may join in the proces<ion, as citizens, when the ceremonies are conducted by other organizations, but the Lodge can only appear on
such occasions when the ceremonies are under its direction. (1877.)
20. The election of Grand Officers shall be the first business of the Grand Lodge
on the day fixed therefor by the Constitution, and until the election shall have been
concluded no other business shall be considered. (1879.)
21. All r,odges in thh jurisdiction are forbidden to resort to any means of per.
petuating testimony in cases of trial other than those provided for by our Consti·
tution and Regulations. (1880.)
22. Whenever the Secretary of a Lodge fails to forward to the Grand Secretary
a certificate of the election and installation of its officers, within a period of twenty
days after such election and install11.tion, the amount which would otherwise be
allowed to the representative of such Lodge shall be withheld. (1880, 1881.)
23. No Lodge in this jurisdiction sh!l.11 receive an application for affiliation until
the applicant shall have proved, to the satisf11.ction of the Master of such Lodge,
that he is a Master Mason. (1880.)
24, Every transoript of a trial-record, when prepared by the Secretary of any
Lodge in this jurisdiction, shall, before its transmission to the Grand
Secretary, be submitted to the Master of the Lodge, who shall carefully examine
the same and see that, it complies with the "Form of Records of Trials and Transcripts thereof," heretofore adopted by this Grand Lodge; that it is fairly and legibly
written, with sufficient spaces between papers and testimony; and that it otherwise

Which report was concurred in, and the brethren therein named
were admitted to seats.
The JJI. •• W. ·.WILLIAM HAYES ScoTT, Past Grand Master of Masons
in Illinois, was introduced by Past Grand Master LEONIDAS E PRATT,
and invited to a seat in the East.
The Grand Master announced that, at the request of Brothers
MICHAEL J. KEA.TING and GEORGE HINDS, he had exchanged their
respective places on the standing committees to which they had been
appointed at the last Annual Communication.
The Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge, as follows:-

1

BRllTHREN OF THE GRAND LODGB :The Grand Lodge of California begins its thirty.fifth Annual Communication at a
most auspicious time and under the most favorable surroundings. Our Great He·
public is prosperous beyond historic example, and at peace with all the world. The
Golden State is blessed to an unusual degree with health, prosperity and happiness,
Her snn·lit fields teem with a wealth of harvest rarely vouchsafed to the most fa·
vored lands; her workshops resound with the cheerful clang of rewarded labor;
her productions float upon every sea ; and her commodities are a striking feature in
the markets of every land. Moral training and intellectual development have kept
pace with material growth in the grand march of human progress. Those qualities
which tend to make a people wiser, better, and happier, are being assiduously
cultivated ; and, under a wise and judicious system of public instruction, her sons
and daughters are growing into practical and useful cit.izenshlp, ready and fully
qualified to dischar~e, with honor to themselves and credit to the State, every
public and private duty, and to adorn homes of content and happiness. In this
grand advance it is pleasing to note that Masonry is marching side by side with
progressive humanity, that thoughtful, earnest men are everywhere enlisting beneath
its banners, and that the expansive force of virtue and morality is steadily pushing its
standard into every land where principles that elevate and virtues that ennoble
warm and delight the human heart. Not only has this moral and intellectual advance

1884.] .

Grand Lodge of Oalifornia.

557

brought great accessions to its membership from good and true men, attra.cted by its
pure principles and sublime teachings, but it has infused new energy and vigor into
the Order itself.
From personal examination and observation, as well as from. official and private
reports, it is cheering to be able to chronicle the fact that, throughout this Grand
Jurisdiction, Masonic teachings are better observed, charity is growing warmer,
brotherly regard more fervent, and the Fraternity steadily advancing in Masonic
knowledge and improving in social intercourse. Of course, individual instances are
not wanting where this pleasant view is not sustained, but, happily, such instances
are not sufficiently numerous ~o affect the rule.
During the past year the immediate care and protection of the Omnipotent Grand
Architect has been especially manifested to the Fraternity. No past or present
Grand Officer has been summoned to the "undiscovered bourn,'' and the Craft
throughout the jurisdiction has been singularly favored with the blessings of health
and happiness. Yet our sky of life has not been entirely clear. Dark and gloomy
shadows have, now and then, floated across its placid face.
On the eighth day of November, 1883, died at Eureka, in the county of Humboldt,
our beloved brother, JOHN ANDBEW WATSON, a respected and useful Past Master
of Humboldt Lodge, No. 79, and, at the time, Inspector of the First Masonic District
of the State. We mourn his loss, and our grief is rendered doubly distressing by the
dreadful manner of his death-he having, by mistake, taken carbolic acid for a nee es·
sary and harmless remedy. A good man and true, he has passed to immortality,
sincerely mourned by all who knew him.
For· the purpose of &equiring accurate information as to the condition 11.lld
requirements of the several Lodges in the jurisdiction, I have made such visits to
them as time and business duties would permit.
On the fifth day of November last, I paid an official visit toSanta Barbara Lodge,
No. 192, and Magnolia Lodge, No. 242, at Banta Barbara. The Lodges met together
in pursuance of notice, and a large attendance filled their beautiful and spacious
hall. Pleasant and profitable discnHsion was had upon interesting Masonic subjects.
The books of both Lodges, as well as their financial affairs, were carefully inspected,
and for the most part found correct. A pleasant entertainment succeeded official
duties.
'
On the thirtieth day of November, I visited officiii.lly at Ban Bernardino a joint
meeting of Phwnix Lodge, No. 178, Pomona Lodge, No. 246, and Evergreen Lodge,
No. 259. Phrenix Lodge had but a few hours' notice, yet a large portion of her mem·

A great and unprecedented flood occurre<J in the Ohio River and its tributarie1
in January and February last, culminating about the middle or the latter month.
The banks of that great river for h.andreds of miles presented the most distressing
scenes of desolation-hundreds, nay, thousands of people being driven by the turbid
waters naked, cold, and hungry into the darkness and gloom of cheerless winter
night, to battle unproter:ted against the chilling hlasts of a pitiless storm, while their
homes, their stock, their all, were swept away by the remorseless waters. Through·
out that grand and fertile valley the most appalling scenes of destitution and suffer·
ing marked the track of the destroying flood. The cry of distress quickly touched
the Masonic heart. Noble Masons of the oity of Cincinnati hurriedly organized a
Masonic Flood Relief Committee and issued an earnest appeal to the fraternity at large
for immediate aid. This appeal came to me by telegraph, thanks to the watchflll
care of our Grand Secretary, at a time when, by reason of extraordinary rains in
southern California, communication by rail as well as upon the pulilic highways was
almost wholly suspend~d.and it was therefore impracticable to call the Grand Lodge
togeth6r, In fact, the necessity for immediate relief was so pressil!g that the delay
incident to convening the Grand Lodge, even under the most favorable circumstances, would have deprived this jurisdiction of the satisfaction and pleasure of
contributing to the relief of that afflicted and needy people. Under these circum·
stances I unhesitatingly assumed the responsibility of transmitting a small contribu·
tion, and accordingly, on the thirteenth day of February last, directed the Grand Sec·
retary to telegraph in the name of this Grand Lodge, the sum of one thousand dollara
to the Masonic Flood Relief Committee at Cincinnati, in the full assurance that the
generous heart of a California brotherhood would commend and approve the act.
That committee promptly acknowledired the receipt of the donation, and, after
the completion of their noble work, returned to this Grand Lodge the sum of four
hundred and fifty dollars, being thus much in excess of their needs, together with a
carefully prepared statement of their receipts and disbursements. It Is evident from
this report that the committee managed the funds C!Jnflded to their care In a mo~t
admirable and satisfactory manner; and I entertain no doubt that their prompt and
well directed labors brought sunshine and joy to many a sorrowing home. The
most gratifying feature of this report is the promptitude with which contributions
were forward ed from all parts of the country. The committee say: "Cincinnati
Masons contributed $1,630,-telegrams and letters came thick and fast, each bearing
messages of charity and good will. Far oft' California sent a thousand dollars by
telegraph, and asked, in her usual whole-souled manner, if moi·e was needed. From
every part of the country Masonic bodies were being heard from until the relief fund
amounted to a total, In money alone, of nearly $14,000." It is a source of pleasure,
in this connection, to record the fact that the Bank of California fnrnished t he ex·
change and the Western Union Telegraph Company sent our teJ.egrams, free of
charge-acts of liberality demanding special recognition.
A great number of questions have been propounded upon Masonic Jaw and usage,
and rulings asked upon the fac~s stated. From the mass the following are selected
for your consideration :1. Can a Past Master, in the absence of the Master and both Wardens, open a
Lodge and transact its regular business?
No. In the absence of the Master and Wardens a Lodge cannot be opened even
for the burial of a brother·; but either of those officers, being present and presiding,
may call to his aid a Past Master, or, for that ma1ter, any other well informed Mason, to confer degrees or transact business.
•
2. Five commissioners appeared at a trial for which seven had been elected, and,
after hearing the case and deliberating thereon, two voted guilty-three, not guilty.
The Master declared the result a finding of not guilty, and ordered a record to that

1884.]

Grand Lodge of California.

565

eft'ect. Did th~ Master err? If he did, what steps should be taken in the further
prosecntion of the matter? Can the same commissioners again try the case?
Grave error was committed. Where a commission consists of seven members,
ft'VB, or even four, may try the case, but a majority of the whole nv.mher elected
must concur in the judgment; a majority of those present is not sufficient. For the
further prosecution of the charges new commissioners should be elected. No person
who acted as a commissioner on the first, is competent to sit as a commissioner on
the second trial.
3. Is It the duty of a Lodge to give Masonic burial to a Mason who resides per·
manently in this jurisdiction, but retains membership and pays dues to a Lodi:e in
another State? If yes, who is to pay for it?
It is the duty of a Lodge to give Masonic burial to every Mason in good standing,
within its jurisdiction, when requested so to do. Ordinarily, the mere force of Ma·
sonic comity and a sense of right and justice will secure prompt payment of auoh
bills by the f,odge to which the decedent belongs. When these fail, I know of no
way of compelling payment.
·
.
·4, Has a Master the right to exclude from his Lodge a member who is intoxi·
cated?
Be has, although the right of a Mason in irood standing to attend the meetings of
his Lodge is a very sacred right. and should only be denied in plain cases; but this
right pre-supposes that he conducts himself with due order and propriety. No l!xed
rule of ac'tion can safely be laid down. The Master must judge of each case as it
arises, and he should exercise a sound discretion, to the end that the mem hers be
not annoyed nor scandal brought upon the Lodge.
5. In a case where the Grand Lodge had reversed a judgment and ordered a new
trial, the charges were subsequently dismissed by a vote of the Lodge. I directed
the Master to disregard such action and proceed with a re-trial in accordance with
the order of the Grand Lodge, precisely as though ·no such diamiBBal had been
attempted.
6. I was asked to issue a dispensation authorizing a Lodge io confer the three
degrees of Masonry upon the same candidate at one meeting.
Refused ; there being nothing in the Constitution authorizing the issue of a dis·
pensation tor such a purpose.
7. Would it be proper for a Lodge in California to receive and act upon an application for affiliation from a Master Mason who resides In another State ?
It would not. While there may be no direct provision of our law that in terms
prohibits it, it wonld be an invasion of the rights of a sister Jurisdiction and might
produce . irritation, and possible conflict. It involves the same principle exercised
by our Grand Lodge in denying to persons residing in thls State the right to petition
for and receive the degrees in another Jurisdiction.
8. Can a Master take the charter of his Lodge to a place within its jurisdiotlon,
other than that named. in the charter, and open 'the Lodge for the purpose of con·
ducting a funeral 7
No. It is his duty to open the Lodge at the proper place, before preoeeding to
that proposed for the funeral service.
9. Where objections were made to conferring the second or third degrees upon a
candidate, and the Lodge refused to sustain them, and the same brother again made
substantially the same objections, can the Lodge entertain them a second time!
No doubt a Lodge may entertain and paBB upon the same objections as often as
it sees proper; but it onght not to permit itself to be trifled with in that manner.
The Master should not allow the same objections to reach the Lodge & second time.
10. Can an Entered Apprentice Mason receive Masonic burial?
He cannot,

566

ProceedingB of the

[Oct. 14,

11. Where charges have been preferred against a member for speaking disre•
spectfully of the Order and accusing a brother of cheating him, and before trial
apologizes and promises reformation, and all parties being satisfied and desirin11: to
stop proceedings; can the Master dismiss the charges, or must they be tried?
Where charges do not involve gross immorality.or criminal conduct, and the
parties are satisfied, or where charges are frlvolons, the Master can and ought to
dismiss them.
12. A case bas occurred where, upon a motion to grant a recommendatory cer·
tificate, three voted in favor and one voted against, while a number did not respond.
The presiding officer declared it carried, but the Secretary refused to issue the cer·
tiflcate, upon the ground that a majority of those present did not vote in favor. I
held that, while every member ought to vote, there was no law absolntely requiring
them to do so; and that. members who, in silence, allow a matter to pass mast be
presumed to assent to it. But that in no view of the case conld the Secretary be
permit~ed to call in question the ruling of the presiding officer.
· 13. On a case presented I ruled that, where from some private pique or personal
dislike, one brother refuses to speak to another, or even remains away from the
Lodge in consequence of the other's presence, It was not in itself such an offense
as would sustain charges; and that the proper remedy is friendly admonition, leaving
all the rest to time and cool reflection.
14. A Lodge grants permission to an Entered Apprentice to apply to another
Lodge for th; second and third degrees, and sends thirty-five dollars, balance for
degrees not conferred, to the Lodge in which he proposes to apply : I am asked,
among other que&tions, the following-Shonld the ballot be unfavorable, to whom
does the thirty-five dollars belong?
I answered :-It should be returned to the candidate.
15. My attention has been called to the clause In our blank petitions for degrees
which reads, "that he has resided in the State · of California for more than one year,
&c.," with the suggestion that it seemed inapplicable to Hawaiian Lodge No. 21.
I replied that it should be construed, Jurisdiction of California, and they could
if they desired, insert-Kingdom of the Hawaiian Islands, in the Jurisdiction of
California.
16. Where two Lodges bad consolidated, one being at the time Indebted to a
third Lodge for funeral expenses advanced, I was asked: Is the consolidated Lodge
responsible for the debt?
I answered, Yes.
17. In Sec. 2, Art. III, Part III, of the Constitution, it is provided that a dispensation for a new Lodge shall 11ot issue, unless, among other things, the petition "be
accompanied by a certificate from a Master, whom the Grand Master i~ satisfied is
well skilled in the craft, in the form prescribed In Art. III, Part VII, declaring that
the Master and Wardens prbposed are fully competent, &c." I suggest that this
section should be amended to read, "from the Inspector of the district," instead of
"a Master.'' The Inspector Is generally best qualified, and it is directly within the
line of his duty.
Some of these rulings are mere copies from former decisions of the Grand Lodge,
and are here repeated merely for the purpose of placing them in a position more
easy of access. It is a source of satisfaction to be able to report that in every case
my rulings have been cheerfully acquiesced lo, and in some instances have had the
effect to produce peace and harmony where discord and confusion seemed imminent.
When I first entered upon the duties of this office, the questions propounded
were so numerous and the time required to examine the Oonstituilon, Regulations,
aud reports for the purpose of determining the Jaw was so great, that, taking the
work of Past Master RoBINBON as a nucleus, I commenced the preparation of a digest,

The correspondence of this office during the year has been very heavy, but fortunately a considerable portion has been of such a character that little more was
req_ uired than simple reference to particula1· sections of the Constitution and Regulations. In this connection I take pleasure in acknowledging my indebtedness to that
living digest of Masonic law and usa.ge, the V:·. l:V>. Grand Secretary, whose valuable
information and personal assistance has at all times and upon all occasions been
inost cheerfully accorded, and bas served to make the duties of the Grand MaHter
comparatively light and pleasant.
The year of my stewardship is drawing to a close, and here and now I desire in
the most earnest and heartfelt manner to thank you all for the honor conferred, and
to express my deep sense of gratitude for the cordial and prompt assistance, the
uniform kindness aud fraternal regard with which I havA been every.w here received
and welcomed; and especially do I desire publicly to th1mk that thorough master of
our Masonic ritual, the Grand Lecturer, and generally, all the officers of the
Grand Lodge, for the friendly confidence and never varying kindness and brotherly
advice which, in their respective departments, they have cheerfully and generously
accorded me.
The great authority with which a generous brotherhood has entrusted me bas, to
the best of my skill and ability, been wielded in an earnest effort to promote the true
interests of the Craft; and the measure of my reward will be complete if, by indnatry
and diligence, I have succeeded in some small degree in supplying the want of that
transcendent geniuR which enabled my illustrious predecesser~ to lay broad and
deep the foundations of Masonry in this jurisdiction, and to erect thereon the symmetrical and beautiful superstructure which so justly excites our pride and secures
to California a place in the front rank of Grand Jurisdictions.
With the · earnest prayer thM Heaven's richest blessings may ever rest upon the
noble work of our beloved Order, that a deeper reverence for and a more perfect
practice of its sacred tenets may mark the history of a glorious future, that all hearts
may be drawn more closely together by the tender ties of brotherly love and affection,
and that our present labors may be marked by harmony and forbearance and wisely
directed for the general good of the Craft, I now invite your attention to the business
of this Annual Communication.
JONATHAN DOAN BINES,

In February last there appea.red in the newspapers, from the Masonic Flood Com·
mittee of Cincinnati, a statement regarding the great fiood in the Ohio river and an
appeal to the Masonic Fraternity for assistance to the sufferers therefrom. Iofor·
mation thereof was immediately telegraphed to the Grand Master with the Inquiry
whether one thousand dollars, or more, should be sent, which was at once responded
to by a direction to send the thouea·nd, with apromise of more should It be required.
That amount was· sent the same day by telegraphic transfer and was in due season
acknowledged, with the information that no more would probably be required. At
a later period a commnnlcation, dated on the twentieth day of May last, was received
from Bro. W. B. MELISH, Secretary of the Masonic Flood Committee, stating that the
labors of that committee had been concluded, that more money had been received
than was found to be necessary, and that it had been directed that the eurplosforty-11.ve per cent.-be returned to the several donors. A check for four hundred
and fifty dollars accompanied the communication, which amonnt, Iese one dollar for
collection from a Cincinnati bank, will be found among the receipts in the ftnancial

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report to the Grand
Lodge, as follows:To the M.·. W. •, <lrand J,odge of Oalifornia :In accordance with a regulation of our Grand Lodge I herewith present my
annual report of the working oondltlon of the various Lodges in this jurisdiction, as
ascertained by penonal visitation and by correspondence, and by the reports of the
Iuspeo\ot1 of the several Districts.
ln company with the Grand Master, I have visited offiolally the Lodges at Salinas,
Stockton, Santa Oruz, Santa Rosa, Visalia., Tulare, :Merced, Somerevllle, and Ba.n Joie,
a.tall which places we were cordially received, and, In most of which, the work was
exemplified in a satisfactory manner. The officers or these J,odges are fairly pro·
ficient in the work, and manifest a strong desire to correct any discrepancies or
departure from the authorized ritual. The general condition of the Lodges of the
jurisdiction ls, on the whole, eminently satlefaotory. Although many of them have
done little or no work, there is apparenily a ·more general desire on the pa.rt of the
officers to perfect themselves iu the lectures and ceremonial observances of the eeT.
ere.I degrees than h~retofore, and fewer complaints are made of weak and splritleBS
Lodges. The lnapeotore, too, have more generally fulfilled their duties, especially
in the matter cf reporting the condition of the Lodges In their several Districts; and
thus I am enabled to approach more nearly the consummation of my desire- the
preaentatlon of a fnller report than I have ever been able to do In the paat.
I have received reports from the Inspectors of all the Districts save two, viz.: the
Second and Tw11nty·thlrd. I should be highly gratlfted could I for onoe submit to
the Grand Lodge complete reports from all the Districts, and I can see no good reason
why this should not be done at eaoh Annual. Communication~ From the reportll re·
ceived I present the following abstract for the information of the Grand Lodge:Inspector BYRON DJl.MING, of the First Dlstrlot, reports that he has visited each of
the five Lodges therein, and finds them in good condition and the officers prollclent
in the work. He thinks that that is better done this year than ever before, and that

Inspector JAMES W. ANDERSON, of the Twenty-fourth District, submits 11 very
able and elaborate report of the condition of the seventeen Lodges assigned to his
care--sixteen of which are located in the City and County of San Francisco, and one
in the county of Marin. Bro. ANDERSON, in the discharge of his duties, visite.d twelve
of these Lodges, leaving five unvisited. Of these five, three work in l11nguage1
unfamiliar to the Inspector, and, of course, he could form no idea of the correctness
of their work. Of the remaining two, one had no work during the year, and the other
was under the immediate inspection of the Grand Lecturer. The books and accounts
of all,'however, were thoroughly examin~d. and the Secretaries are generally com·
mended for the neatness and correctness of their records and other books. In commenting upon the work of the Lodges in this district, the views expressed by Bro.
ANDERSON are so thoronghly in accord with my own, and his suggestions are so
pertinent and opportune, that I Bhall not hesitate to embody a portion of them in,
this report. He says :"The L~dges display a commendable zeal in the spirit of the work, and, as they
have acquired it, they acquit themselves in a very creditable manner. But, in the
lefter thereof I find them greatly at variance with each other and with the work as
taught by the Grand Lecturer. Indeed I find 11 much greater lack of uniformity in
the several Lodges visited than I had supposei to exist, and this lack of uniformity
is found both in the phraseology and in the manner of conferring the degrees. This
difference is attributed to severe.I causes, among which I may enumerate the following:" lst. Little, if any, attention has heretofore been given by the Masters to acquiring a knowledge of any part of the secret work, or of the ·manna! work, except
that immediately appertaining to the Master's station. The term 'Master' does not
simply imply one who controls or governs, bnt has the broader signification of
teacher-one whose duty it is to give good and wholesome instrnctioi.i in all things
whereby the Craft may be better enabled to erect a more beautiful and symmetrical
moral and Me.•onic edifice. No one is fitted to occupy the Master's chair who has
not, by study and experience, prepared himself to render the work of any station or
place in the Lodge. Knowing that one cannot teach that which he has not thoroughly
learned, and believing this partial preparation of the Masters of Lodges to be the
most prolific source of variation in the work, I have signified to all expectant Masters my intention to require a correct knowledge of', at least; the secret work entire
in all the degrees before granting the requisite certificate of proficiency.
"2d. Heretofore the Masters and other officers have usually acquired the secret
work of the degrees from their predecessors, or from some one reputeti as knowing
it. These parties, having themselves acquired the work in incorrect form, have thus
perpetuated the errors which have gradually crept into it. The Masters, at least,
should apply to the Grand Lecturer, or to the Inspectors of their Districts,•for such
aid as would enable them to perfect themselves in t~e work.

1884.J

Grand Lodge of California.

583

" 3d. The officers fail to give to their duties that degree of study requisite to fit
them for 11 proper rendition of the work. Too many consider themselves accom
pllshed when they have memorized the mere phraseology, while the meaning and
1entiment are sealed from their notice. The officer who hopes to sll'.cceed in any
position must study as well the character as the language appropriate to such position. Especially is this the case in the third degree. I find few in onr Lodge~ who
have done more than merely prepare themselves to articulate so many words.
"4th. The officers of the Lodges seldom, if ever, meet for rehearsal in the conferring of degrees and for consul tati on as to the best methods for discharging the
duties of their respective positions. The Masters should oall their officers together
for frequent consultation and exercise, and should see that no one be permitted to
remain ignorant of the duties of his station or place.
"5th. Inspectors make their positions too often mere sinecures, or, at least, too
of'ten consider their whole duty accomplished when they have visited the Lodges of
their respective dietricts and cursorily examined the books thereof. Too often do·
they feel that they are subjecting themselves to adverse criticism if they attempt to
correct any errors into which the Lodges may have fallen. This delicacy, or fear of
giving offense. deters them from exerting that strictness in the discharge of their
duties which alone can result in benefit to the Lodges under their supervision. Especially does this seem to me to be the case in granting certificates of qualification
to Masters elect, else how can it be th~t we find so many Masters so poorly qualified
for the duties of their station?
"6th. There is no accounting for tastes! What is pleasing to one is displeasing
to another. One Master must have his Deacons take position in one way, another in
another. One insists on ' compasses,' another on ' compass' as the correct appellation of a prominent working tool. One is 11 stickler for• great and good,' another
for 'good and great.' Some Senior Deacons; in the second degree, and some Mas·
lers, in the first and third, will persist in introducing extraneous matter, because,
as they say. these portions are so beautiful and impressive; but obviously, as I think,
for the same reason that impelled the Scribes and Pharisees to make broad their
phylacteries. If ever 11 desirable uniformity is attained, it will be when the officers
and members of Lodges inform themselves with reference to that which is the
adopted work, and then unanimously say 'agreed.'"
Bro. ANDERSON has been a faithful and conscientious Inspector, and, in order the
more fully to carry out his ideas of uniformity in the work, he has established a
school of instruction which meets on the second and fourth Fridays of each month,
and which has proved 11 perfect success in more respects than one. California Lodge,
No. 1, under his supervision, has attained such proficiency that it will be requested
to confer the thiril degree in the presence of the Grand Lodge, on the evening of the
third day of its present Communication. It gives me much pleasure to bear testimony to his zeal and fidelity in the discharge of his duties.

The undersigned regrets to be obliged to announce to the Grand Lodge the death
of one of our oldest and most zealous and faithful Inspectors, Bro. JoHN A. WATSON,
of the First District. Bro. WATSON was a member of Humboldt Lodge, No, 79, and
was enthusiastic in all tha~ pertained to Masonry. He was greatly respected and
beloved in the neighborhood in which he lived, and leaves a large circle of friend'
to mourn his loss. He was peculiarly fitted to teach the work of Masonry, as he had
a singularly retentive memory and the faculty, which so few possess, of imparting to
others the knowledge which he had himself acquired. "The will of God ia accomplished." "Life's fitful fever over, he sleeps well."

ALABAMA.
The sixty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Alabama was held
in the city of Montgomery, commencing on the third day or December. 1888,-U.
R.·. W.·. JOHN HOLLIS BANKH:&AD, Deputy Grand Master, presiding in the absence
the Grand Master, and the R.·. W.·. DANIEL S.&YB"E being Grand Secretary. One
hundred and eighty-eight subordinate Lodges were represented.
The M.·. W.-. Grand Master, Bro. R. W. COBB, was neither present nor had he sen\
an Address; one, however, came before the proceedings were in print. It is ver7
concise. He bad granted, during the year;flfteen dispensations for various purposet,
six being to continue work in Lodges th1't had forfeited their charters. He had no
rulings or decisions to report, for it was a somewhat remarkable fact that aU quer
tions on Masonic law and asage that bad been submitted to him, were fully answered
in the Book of Edicts as published in 1882-a quiet but just rebuke to those Masten
and brethren who will oot even try to inform themselves as to the written law, and
areyetforever pestering the Grand Master with needless questions. On one.snbjectth'
head of the Grand Master is eminently level. He had been asked for a d1spensatiot
to confer two degrees on a candidate th" same evening, in the direct face of a prohibition or the Grand Lodge. Some brothers, wiser than Solomon, insisted that the Grand
Master was not bound by the edicts of the Grand Lodge, bat was a supreme law to
himself; and that, therefore, he could do what the constitution expressly inhibit.eel.
The Grand Master could not see it in that light. "I know, 11 he sayR, "of no reason
why constitutional limitations are not equally as binding upon the Grand Master as
upon any Master Mason. If he can disregard one constitutional pro~ision h~ may a.a
well disregard every other, and thus render the entire organic laws 1nop.era:•v: at his
will and pleasure. In fact, if he should see proper to do so, he could revolut1omze ~he
entire system of Masonic Jurisprudence as adopted by the Grand Lodge, and which
the Masters of snbordinate Lodges must enforce." Sticklers for the extra and uncontrolle? prerogatives of the Grand Master should answer this reasoning if they ~l>D.
The Grand Master regretted his inability to be present at the Annual Commul11ca.tion, but the importance of the interests confided to him demanded his presence
elsewhere.
·
.
All the Lodges whose charters bad ·been forfeited, but which had been workmg
under dispensation and had now paid dues and made returns, were reinstated. We
suppose that this refers to the six mentioned by the Grand Master. So It appea~a
that the allopatbic dose of medicine administered last year worked effectually ID
some cases.
The Committee on Correspondence submitted an able special report on the ap·
plication for recognition of the "Independent Symbolic Grand Lodgu of Spain," at
Seville. For want of the fullest information as to the actual facts In the case, the
committee recommended a postponement of action, and it was so ordered.
We note the action of the Grand Lodge on one case of appeal, because it shows.
what high gronnd is taken on the subject 1n that jurisdlcti.on. A brother was !n•
definitely suspended by bis Lodge on a general charge of immoral and ti~m~~
conduct. The specifications were three: 1. That he bad "been engaged m manufacturing spirituous liquors." 2. That he bad further been engaged tn "selli11~ tba
same at wholesale and retail at bis grocery; " and 3. That he had "sold such liquor
on S'Uflda1s"-all which was alleged to be "in violation of his· duty as a Mason,
and to the scandal and disgraee of the Masonic Fraternity.'' The Lodge, by nearly
an unanimous vote, found him guilty on all the specifications, and sentenced him to
an indefinite suspension. The committee of the Grand Lodge reported in favor of
sustaining the verdict, and the Grand Lodge concurred. We give the report of the
committee without· comment; it speaks for itself:-

or

Grand Lodge of OaU/arnia.

1884.J

591

~·rom the evidence in this case your committee is satisfied that HENDERSON Is
proven to have done what ie laid to his charire in the foregoing specifloations ; and
further, it is apparent that he chooses to pursue a course of conduct which is extremely detrimental to the interests of Masonry and the well-being of society in that
community. We do not discuss the right of an individual to traffic in liquor under
the laws of the United States, because such a discussion is not pertinent to the pres·
ent Instance, but we do call attention to the fact that prohibition obtainB In the
ooanty of Calhoun, in accordance with the laws of Alabama. In the opinion of your
committee it were better for Oross Plains Lodge that the dust of years should settle
undisturbed upon its vacant chairs than that it sb.ould keep, in its family of brothers,
a man whose course is so subversive of good morals, peace, and prosperity.
Preliminary steps were take~ looking to the establishment of a " Masonic Home
and College,'' at no distant day.
The evedastlng subjeot of maims and defects came op, and in the form presented
was thns disposed of by the Committee on Jnrisprudence and the Grand Lodge:To the question-" Is a person who has lost his second, third and fourth fingers
of the left hand, eligible to receive the first three degrees of Masonry?"
Yonr committee would answer," yss, notwithstanding the apparent stringency of
the old regulations. It is now almost, if not quite, universally held that, if 11 person
uan perform the ritual, be is eligible to receive the degrees in Masonry."
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence is again from the pen of Bro.
PALMER JoB PILL.A.NB, P. G. M., and is an excellent, well written document of one
hundred and seventeen pages. The opening paragraph called forth our deepest
wympathies, which we beg leave to express to ·our affiicted brother. We know how
hard it is to think and write when the heart is burdened with domestic sorrow:-

We have labored in the preparation of the following report under ~rlevons affilctlon, and, if It comes not up to your expectations, we Invoke your charity, for .daring
all the time we were traveling hand in banJ with the great destroyer, and wlien we
had emerged from the dark valley of the shadow of death, our eyes were dimmedwe uould not see-and our bead and brain sore, we could not think. Slowly, for
months, we watched and waited the gradual, yet rapid, decay of both the mental
and physical powers of her who bad, for more than thirty-eight years, been our solace
and our pleasure. And now, brethren, when yon shall have read this report, think
of the writer as of the past, 11nd be charitable.
Brother PILLANB has a very genial and somewhat extended notice of the California proceedings of 1882. He thinks oar system of Inspection Districts, with its requirement of proficiency on the part of a Master elect, before installation, an excellent one-far snperior to that in vogue In his jurisdiction. He copies at length the
report of our Committee on Jnrisprndence relat.lve to the Grand Lodge of New
South Wales, and approves it, albeit his own Grand Lodge had given in its recognition of that Body, which he thinks was hasty and injudicious. We thank our
brother for his kind and fraternal reference to our own report and to us individually.
There are two hundred and eighty Lodge.a in this jnrisdiction, with a membership
of seven thousand eight hundred and seventy-five. The M.-. W.·. JOHN BOLLIS
BANKHEAD was elected Grand Master, and the R.·. W.·. DANIEL SAYRB was re-elected
Grand Secretary.
ARIZONA.
Again we greet our youngest sister on the sooth and east. The second Annnal
Communication of the Grand Lodge of Arizona was held in the City of Tucson,
commencing OD the thirteenth day of Nov.e mber, 1883,-the M.·. w.·. JOHN TABER
ALs.&P, Grand Master, presiding,' and the R.-. W. -. GEORGE J.uras RoBll:RUGE being
Grand l:!ecretary. Four Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, in his Address, congratulates the fraternity that the year jnst
past bad been one of prosperity throughout the jnrisdic.tion. 'l'he mines·had poured
forth their wealth, and great had been the increase of flocks and herds. Masonlcally,
no discord or contention had existed among the brethren, or it so, it had not come
to bis knowledge. Thirty-six Grand Lodges bad already extended the hand of recognition and fellowship. The fear entertained by some that the Grand Lodge organi·

4

tl92

toct. 14,

zation was premature, and that the financial burden of sustaining it would he too
great for the few brethren to bear, had been dispelled by actual experience,.
There was no indebtedness, bnt a surplus of $370 in the treasnry. To the efficient
Grand Secretary much of this result was doe. No new Lodge had been organize4'
during the year. There were, as he believed, scores of unaffiliated :Masone In the
jurisdiction, which was " a standing reproach and shame to the Order.'' He recommended tho abolition of the fee for affiliation, and the Grand Lodire so ordered.
The Grand Secretary submitted a brief but interesting report. The number of
Masons in the jurisdiction bad increased from three hundred and five to three hon·
dred and fifty-five, a net increase of fifty. Only one member bad been suspended
for non-payment of dues. Well done, youtllful Arizona.
The Grand Lodge adopted a report of a committee on establishing a " Widows'
_ and Orphans' Fund." Each Master Mason is to pay fifty cenle per annum for ench
fund, all to be disposed of by a Board of Trustees consisting of the Grand Master,
Deputy Grand Master, and Grand Secretary. No moneys are to be expended nntil
five annual payments have been made to the fond.
The salary of the Grand Secretary for the year was fixed at one hundred dollars.
We hope that the Grand Secretary will not act npon the hypothesis of the traditional
Indian: "Poor pay, poor preach!" A very readable oration by the W.o, Bro.
JAMES A. ZABRISKIE: is published in the proceedings,
Our Arizona brethren have done well to commence their Masonic life with a
Report on Correspondence. The first report, by Bro. MORRIS GoLDWATEll, is
comparatively brief, covering only forty pages of the proceedings, but it le well
written and will probably be improved upon in hie future etforte. He makes
an unnecessary apology for what he deems its shortcomings, by saying that It was
compo~ed during odd hours stolen from bueineBB pursuit&, and that he. is "more
accustomed to handle weights and measures than pen and eoieeors." We are quite
sore that if he does the former as well as the latter, he mnst be successful as a boei·
neee man, as we have no doubt he is. He is very liberal and complimentary in hie
notice of California for 1882. Of Bro. ANDEBSON's oration he says: "It has seldom
been our fortune to read a more instructive or entertaining address. Those who had
the pleasure to listen to its delivery certainly enjoyed an intellectual treat.'' We
thank our brother for hie flattering notice of our own report, but the following le an
enigma to us :We looked in vain for the farewell sent by Aitlan Lodge, No. 177, to her Mother
Lodge, but there is no notice taken of it. Nor le there any mention made of the
correspondence had between Aztlan Lodge and the M.-. W.'. Grand Master of' Call·
fornia relative to the statue of Aztlan Lodge , should she refuse to join the Grand
Lodire of Arizona. We are inclined to think that, if the letters were published, the
Grand Secretary of Indian Territory wonld have omitted that part of hie notice which
we have put in italics.

Looking to the report fl'om the Indian Territory, we find the term" bulldoze "
need in this connection. We say this le an enigma to us. It le the first we !1ave
heard of any letters or correspondence on the subject. Doubtless what our brother
refers to is among the archives of the Grand Secretary's office. But, as our duty was
and Is to notice the proceedings of other Grand Bodies, rather than of our own, we
do not see that our Grand Secretary was called upon to furnish us the written corree·

sending it. We are glad to learn that all resulted in harmony and good feeling, and
that all the Lodges in Arizona are working In peace and brotherly love.

The Grand Master, In his Address, alluded to the wonderful progress made In
Dakota in the le.st few years. This was Illustrated in the city where they were
assembled:Five short years before it was uninhabited ; the winter winds swept across the
prairies without adding to the dis<:omfort of a single settler; the wonderful and almost
incomparable fertility of the soil, as well as the beauty of the verdure under e. summer sky, were nnapprecie.ted and unseen by those who have since made it their
home. The railroad and iron horse appeared as swift and unexpected as a vision, but
fortunately with more stable qualities; towns and cities, with their hundreds and
thou~ands of !nhabitanbi, at once sprang into being; and this vast and fertile region
Is bemg rapidly subjected to the needs and reqairements ot civillzed life.
The progress of Masonry had been almost as rapid and unaxpeoted. The Grand
Master sometimes feared that they were proceeding too rapidly. Eighteen new
Lodges had been constituted during the previous year, and twelve dispensations had
been issued for the current term. Thus far all had prospered and succeeded equal
to the expectations of the most sanguine. Several other applloatlooe were submi'Lted to the Grand Lodge.
The Grand Lodge was in h11rmony with all other Grand Bodies. Fair progress
had been me.de in the promulgation of the adopted work, bot much remained to be
done, and the Grand Master recommended schools of instruction in various parts of
the jurisdiction. Severe.I corner-stones had been laid by the Grand Lodge, particularly those of the University of North Dakota at Grand Forks, and of the Normal
School at Bpearftsh.

The Address of the Grand Master is well written, and makes pleasant reading,

The Grand Master ha.a words of hearty commendation of the work of Escambia.
Lodge in Pensacola daring the ravages of yellow fever in that pla.oe. His appeal for
help to other Lodges in the jorisdiotion met with a liberal response, the sum of
$1295 28 having been contributed. Circulars were also sent to neighboring Grand
Lodge jurisdictions, which brought to the relief of the sufferers the further sum of
$<l,263 23. "Emergencies such as these," remarks 'the Grand Master," touch the
great heart of Masonry and draw us very near to each other. In the presence of a
great sorrow, the principle of our common brotherhood starts into fresh life and
becomes a reality." Be mentions one incident connected with the epidemic, which
we copy here, knowing that a.II good Masons will be glad to read it for themselves:1 will mention here one incident whiob will make a deep impression upon the
heart of every Mason. A poor family, consisting of father, mother, and fonr youn.1
children, were among the sick. The father, a stranger, we.a 11 Mason from MichigaD.
'fhey were faithfully ca.red for, bot the parents both died, leaving their four little
ones, aged from four to ten ;rears, orphans, They were ca.red for until the epidemic
was passed and th~ qu11ra.ntme raised, and then, provided with g.ll that they required,
they were started for their distant home in Michigan. The oldest boy was furnished
with railroad tiokets and with an open letter from Escambia Lodge, stating who the
little travelers were, and commending, them to the care of all good men and Masol)ll,
They met with kindness and help from one end of' the journey to the other, and were
safely delivered to their friends. At many points they were not allowed to pay
anything for their meals, and money was colfected among their fellow passenger&
ror their benefit. Brethren, to bring thi• incident home to your hearts, lot each one
of us suppose for a moment that tho~e helpless children had been his own. ls It not
a privilege to belong to a brotherhood under whose protecting arm children of
tender years may travel from one end of this broad land to tho other, seoare of
meeting friends and protectors at every step ?
We answer, yes, and venture the prediction that no member of Escambia Lodge
will ever be permitted to saffe_r within the jarlsdlotion of the Lodge In Michigan to
which the father of those little ones belonged.

The Grand Master feelingly and reluctantly alluded to the case of JOHN F. Bua·
RILL, formerly and for eight years the honored Grand Secretary, but who for defalcation in the use of Grand Lodge funds, was deposed from office some two or more
years ago. As the record of criminal proceedings in his case appears in the volnme
before us, we will state brie6.y the salient points thereof, An examination by a
committee of the Grand Lodge satisfied that body that the brother had been criminal and .not merely unfortunate in his action. They therefore procured an indictment
against him. BURBILL, having fled to Minnesota, was brought back on a ~equisition
and placed on trial at ,Springfield. He was ably defended, though mainly on mere
technical grounds. But the proof was too direct and convincing, and be was found
guilty and sentenced to five years' imprisonment in the State Penitentiary. A sad
case, indeed.. As the Grand ·Master says:JoHN F. BUBRU.L filled positions of honor and tr ast In our Fra.ternity, audit would
have been a pleasure to the members of the Grand Lodge if he could have explained
his defalcation consistent with his innocence. But they believed him to be guilt>::•
and it would have been inconsistent with our teachings of honest;v and integrity 1f,
through sympathy, he had been permitted to go without prosecution.
The moral of all this is in that pithy saying of Holy Writ, "Let him that th,inketh
he standeth, take heed lest he fall."
Great damage having resulted in some parts of the jurisdiction from the overflow

sulferers belonging to the Fraternity. The response was liberal, amounting to a contribution of $4,354 88.

The Committee on Masonic Jurisprudence reported adversely upon one of the
by-laws of a subordinate Lodge, which provided that "the Junior Deacon should
be appointed by the Senior Warden, and the Stewards by the Junior Warden.'' In
their opinion the Master is the only appointing power, In the case of all non-elective
officers, and should always exercise his prerogative. They admit that precedent is
ag1e.inst them, but that, they urge, should not override principle. If such a principle
be involved ia this, then our own jurisdiction is at fault, for with us the Senior
Warden" may" appoint the Junior Deacon. We turn the case over to Bro. BELCHER.

Bro. GURNEY agrees with Bro. BELCHER and our Grand Lodge In their action, or
rather non-action, in the case of the Grand Lodge of New South Wales. He Insists
that that body must comprise a majority of the regular Lodges within its proposed
jurisdiction, or it has no right to claim exclusive territorial jurisdiction; and , if not,
cannot or should not be recognized as a sovereign Grand Lodge by other bodies.
" This," be says, "ls the well-established '.American d,octrine,' from which there
cannot be a departure except at the expense of the harmony of the Masonic world."
He takes issue, however, with Bro. BELCBJ:B in his reports on the" status of non-aft!!.
iates," anu also upon what he designates as "the Masonic right of a Grand ~dge
to dictate the charities of its constituents, in form or measure." Here, again, we
decline t~ interfere in this battle between giants, not being even an armor-bearer
on either side.
Our thanks are due for his kindly notice of our own report, and we only wish we
deserved one-half of the compliments paid us. We would like to quote mo~e liberally
from this excellent paper, but must not exceed our allotted limits.
