INDIANA.
The sixty-fifth "Stated Meeting" of the Grand Lodge of Indiana. was held in the
city of Indianapolis, commencing on the twenty-seventh day of May, 1884,-the
M.·. w... BBUCR CARR, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. w... WILLI.A~ H.
SHYTBlll being Grand Secretary. Four hundred and fifty-seven Lodges were repre·
se'nted.
Thie being the biennial session, (no Communication having been held in 1883,) the
Address of the Grand Master covers a period of two years. Nine Lodges bad been
constituted, dispensations issued for four others, and the charters of thirteen had
been annulled. The He.Us of eleven Lodges bad been dedicated with appropriate
ceremonies.
Complaints bad been made to the Grand Master that, in several Instances, the
M1111ters of certain subordinate Lodges •bad persisted in conferring degrees, not·
withstanding the objections of members. In some cases ignorance of the laws of
Masonry was pleaded, and the otfending officer let oft' with a reprimand. In other
cases be was removed from office, as be deserved to be.
We note one of the decisions of the Grand Master, because, so far as we know, it
was the first time that such a question bad arisen. A petitioner for the degrees, in
all respects physically a perfect man, had from early childhood worn a truss, and
·t we.a so necessary to his well-being that without It he could not stand erect. The
Grand Master decided that "it was such an essential part of the individual that it
could not Interfere with his proper initiation."
No Grand Communication having been held 1ast year, and other causes helping
in the same direction, the Grand Lodge debt had been reduced to the amount of
ts2,900. If the Grand Lodge would authorize another adjournment for two years,
the Grand Master was sure they would be free from debt by that time. And we may
here remark that such an adjournment was agreed upon, aud so there will be no
Grand Communication in 1885.
Due notice is taken of the death of Paet Grand Master THOMAS R. AUBTIKrat the
ripe age of seventy-four years. He was e.n Englishman by birth and a graduate of
Oxford. He came to .America in 1833, was first a physician and subsequently an
Episcopal clergyman. "The last years of bis life were full of sutfering, caused by
ill health, yet through all he was the same genial, true hearted Christian.''
The Grand Master, referring to the calamities of l!ood which bad visited the
southern portion of the jurisdiction, pays a deserved tribute to the charities of t~e
Fraternity, who so nobly responded to his appeal. A total ot $7,212 24 was dis·
pensed tb1·ougb the Masonic Committees of Relief.

It appears from the report of the Committee on Grievances and Appeals that in
Indiana, as well as elsewhere, the brethren occasionally make use of the Lodge to
collect their business debts. One brother, who unfortunately could not pay what
be owed, was tried and expelled. Thia is what the committee say of the case, and
our readers can judge for themselves on whioh side the true spirit of Masonry was
exhibited:-

There seems to be a hardship in this case. The accused, if unfortunate in hia
personal atfalr~ , onght not to be turned out of Masonry on that account. Masonry
1s. ~ot 11 collectmg agency. The courts are open, and the pla!Je to advance or assert
civil remedies can be found elsewhere than in a Masonic Lodge. Masonry does not
;equire one Mason ~o !end his na.me as enrety on a note for another. He may do so
1f be chooses, but it 1s not a crime In Masonry to become so poor in this world'&
goods that be can not, at any given time, pay all of his debts. It is the duty of a
Mason to pay his debts, but It is not just to expel a Mason because misfortune overtakes him at some period of his life. Tb.ere is nothing in the evidence to show that
the a.ccused acted in bad faith. The committee recommend that the action of the
Lodge be reversed and the case dismissed. (Which wae concurred In.)
Ia another case, where an old Mason was accused of " cheating," "to., because
be was compelled to make an assignment on account of the failure of a bank In
which his funds were placecl, and yet was tried and disciplined by his Lodge, the
committee thus rebuke its action-a rebuke sharp enough, we should think, to pierce
through the bide of a rhinoceros:In this case the proof shows that the accused bad a distressinir failure of crops
and hie negotiations for a foreign loan were broken oft' by the failure of said bank'
and bis creditors crowded upon him, and be, being an old man, was oompelled t~
succumb. It was the wrong thing to do, under the circumstances, to harness him
up before the Lodge and drive him out never to return. He made his promises in
good faith, and If circumstances afterward combined against him, and made com.
pliance ,impossi!>le, he committed no M11eonio crime. Brother STEPHENS ought t o
have been acqmtted under the proof as shown by this record. It being suggested
that the accused has departed this life, the committee recommend that the cause
ab~te, and that a copy of this opinion be certified down to Unity Lodge and spread
on its minutes.
In another oase, where a Md.Son bad deliberately Imposed upon his Lodge by
proposing for membership bis son, knowing at the time that be was not of lawful
age, the Lodge expelled him, and tho committee and Grand Lodge concurred In
approving or its action.

INDIAN TERRITORY.
The ninth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of the Indian Territory
was held in the town of Fort Gibson, commencing on the sixth day of November,
1883,-the M.·. W. ·. HARVEY LINDSKY, Grand Master, presiding, and the B.•, W.•.
JoSBPH S. MURROW being Grand Secretary. Fourteen Lodges were represented.
The Grand Master, In his Address, congratulated the Fraternity nn the general
ha.rmony and prosperity that had prevailed. One Lodge, however, was in marked
contrast thereto, and needed a thorough overhauling. In another Lodge the Master
had been guilty of gross irregularities, and was on trial therefor. "The Lodge,"
says the Grand Master," was in fearful confusion." While under charges, and hence
in quasi suspension, the Master bad gone on and made Masons almost by wholesale.
The Grand Master informed these that they had been illegally ma1e, and required
them to come to him, as the Grand Medicine Doctor, and he healed. The Grand
Lodge expelled this unworthy Master and Mason, J. D. HENRY by name. Dispen·
sations bad been granted for two new Lodges.
We find this Item in the proceedings: "On motion, this evening, qfter supper,
and to-morrow evening, same time, were set apart as the times for the exemplification of the three degr~es before the Grand Lodge." This reminds us of the religion~
meeting notices we were accustomed to bear in our boyish days in the "land of
steady habits." The officiating minister would always say that they would "commence at early candle !i,ght," and for aught we know the custom is still kept up.'
About as definite time that as" after supper."
The Grand Secretary reported that he had purchased a set of Grand Lodge Jewels
for seventy-five dollars. He remarked that he might have gone up to five hundred
dollars, but the finances would not permit. Ile wants, too, some additional furniture
in the Grand S.e cretary's office, all there, except a stove, being his iudi vidual proper.ty,
and he needed the use of it elsewhere. Is our brother about to take a helpmeet and
set up housekeeping?
He su11gests to thP- Secretaries of subordinate Lodges to write out the names ol
members in full. "The mere initials of a man's name is too indefinite. For instance,
who can tell whether the Jin the name J. S1111TJI stands for JOB, JAOOB, JosEPH,
JEBOSAPHAT, or possibly John!'' Well put! The SMITHS, and especially John,
will "please take notice and govern themselves accordingly.''

an address, (the custom, we believe, in this jurisdiction.) and from it we copy a. few
sentences~.-

Although Masonry is not a substitute for nor a form of religion, yet it is a
handmaid to that Divine institution, from whence comes all our earthly and eternal
happiness. And to this end I have always held, from the night I was placed in the
north-east corner of the Lodge as a just and upright Mason, that the Worshipful Master should be a man of God. Can we not call to mind Masters who have presided
in the Ee.st, and have heard them instruct the candidate as to the name of the

The Grand Lodge had one disagreeable subject presented for its action, but it was
met and disposed of in a truly Masonic spirit, although it required the. application of
the surgeon's knife to sever a dead and useless limb from the liviog body. This was
the trial or Past Grand Master J. R. HARTSOOK, who a year or two ago was charged
with unmasonic conduct, in the embezzlement of funds and other frauds practiced on
his Lodge and brethren. Charges, with a host of specification~, were made against
him, and the Grand Lodge, at its previous Communioatiou, directed the Grand Master
to proceed to the subordinate Lodge trying the brother, sod preside at the trial.
This he did. All the charges and specifications were abundantly proven, and so the
Lodge voted by a decided majority on each. But the local I.aw of Iowa requiring a
majority of two·thirds to convict, and that vote oot having been obtained on any ooe
of the chargM, he was declared oot guilty. This the Grand Master considered as
little less thao a moral outrage, aod reported the whole ml\tter to the Grand Lodge,
with the reoommeodation that it assume original jurisdiction of the case and try the
brother de novo. The Committee on Appeals reported in favor of such action, and
after due trial the offender was declared guilty and expelled.
It wa.s resolved to make the new library building fire-proof, and to meet that and

The Grand Master congratulated thc fraternity upon the eminently satisfactory
relations with all sister Grand Jw·isdictions. Close fraternal relations had been
effected with the Grand Lodges of Arizona and Peru. Of the latter we have the
following pleasing information :4I need not refrain from pronouncing my conviction that this establishment of
Masonic-diplomatic relations between Peru and Louisiana is a matter of the utmo~t
significance. Symbolic Masonry in South America has been in a somewhat chaotic
state. The Grand Lodge of Peru, independent, untrammeled, and properly organized upon the system of tbe North American Grand Lodges, stands before the M!'-·
sonic world upon a footing equal to our own. She deserves our hearty support in
the effort she is making to firmly establish the American system in South Ameri~a.
In the midst of the distractions of internecine and foreign war, she has, with dehb·
eration and fortitude, reformed and consolidated the Masonic elements within her
territory.
What the Grand Master also says of Masonry and its progress in the Republic of

in the review of the proceedings of Foreign Grand Bodies.

"Jackass Guieb,'• " Shirt-Tail Callon," "Whisky Diggings," "Hangtowo," "Humbug,'' etc., as specimens. But it was reserved to the miners in a certain camp in
B - - county to "out-Herod HEROD," by the adoption of a name that smacked
strongly of a certain fire and brimstone locality spoken of In Holy Writ. And
rumor has it that the people were about as hard as the name. In course of time
one of the miners died, and a deputation was sent to procure the services of Father
PETER, of Marysville, at the funeral. The good padre went, and so touched the
people with his eloquent appeals, tbat..they asked him to establish a church forthwith. Now the worthy father loved a joke as well as some of the profanes, and so,
while promising his individual eft'ort>", he quietly suggested a slight change in the
name of the camp. "For," said he, "if I should write to my Bishop and tell him that
I had started Christ Uhurch in HeUtown, he might object to the le.st part of the
name ! " The miners saw the point and promised an amendment, but we believe the
old appellation still sticks to the locality.

Our first ins~al)ment of the proceedings of the Grand Lodge of' Massachusetts contains the account of several Special and one Q~arterly Communications.
The first Special Communication was held in Charlestown on the eleventh day of
Sept.ember, 1883, and was called for the purpose of participating in the one hundretb
anniversary of King Solomon's Lodge, in that ancient town. The M.·. W.·. SAMUEL
CROCKER LAWl\ENOE, Grand Master, presided, and the B.·. W.·. SERENO D. NICKERSON
was Grand Secretary.
This Lodge has a history which well justified this commemoration. From the
record before us we learn that it was i11stituted September 11th, 1783,-JosIAH
BARTLETT, M. D., being the first Master; tfie charter bearing the name of the patriot
JOHN 'WARREN, a brother of the distinguished General and Mason who fell at Bunker
Hill. Dr. BARTLETT was a citizen of no mean renown. He entered the medical department of the American army in April, 1771i, being then only sixteen years old. He
served therein until 1780, when he resigned bis commission, but served for two years
thereafter as a surgeon on board of a ship of war. The remainder of his life be spent
In Charlestown, and rose to the highest rank in his profel!8ion. When he became a
Mason is not known, but he was appointed Master of the new Lodge in 1783. In the
Grand Lodge he served fonr years as Senior Gritnd Wdrden, one year as Deputy
Grand Master, and three years as Grand Mester, the last being In 1810., He died in
1820, at the age of sixty years. He was an earnest; devoted Mason as well as physician, the productions of his pen in both capacities taking the first rank in the literature of the day.
.
An elaborate orstion was delivered on this occasion by the Deputy Grand
Master, the B .·. W.·. EDWIN WRIGHT. We can cull only an item or two touching
upon the history of this ancient but always flourishing Lodge. It was constituted
with eight members, who set to work, immediately npon the establishment of peace,
to found an institution whereby, to use the language of their petition, " we hope to
erect a fabric planned in Wisdom, supported by Strength, and adorned with Masonic
Beauty.'' We .give the names of these eight; possibly some of our brethren may
recognize some that are familiar: JosIA.H BA.11.TI,ETT, BENJAMIN FROTHINGHAM, ELIPH·
A.LET NEWELL, EDWARD GooDwIN, DAVID GoonwlN, JosEPH CORDIS, CALEB SwAN,
and WILLIAM CALDER. Brief biographies of these brothers are given. One of the
subsequent Masters was OLIVER HOLDEN, the composer of the tune " Coronation,"
which has been sung by untold millions, and is as new and as fresh now as when its
composer was wont to start it in his Lodge with the old fashioned "pitch-pipe "-for
organs were then unknown among our Puritan fathers. One enthusiastic admirer
of this grand old tone Is qnite sure that it will survive the destruction of this earth,
and be sung by the heavenly choirs world withont end. We learn from the orator
that this Lodge bas always beeri noted for its banquets "of innocent festivity," and
for its works of charity to its members and their widows and orphans. It has lleld
one thousand and one communications, bad forty-four Masters, initiated eight bnndred
and twenty-five, and bas at present a membership of one hundred andelghty-two.

NEBRASKA.
The twenty-sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Nebrask'a was
held in Beatrice, commencing on the nineteenth day of June, 1883,-the M.·. W.·.
EDWIN F. WARREN, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.·. W.·. WILLIAM R. BOWEN
being Grand Secretary, Sixty.two Lodges were represented.
Prior to the proceedings of this Annual Communication, we have those of a
"Quarterly Cent~nniul" Communication, held In Omaha on the twenty.third day of
September, 1882,-that being the twenty-fifth (or silver wedding) anniversary of the
organization of the Grand Lodge. As the banquet on this occasion, held at the
"Omaha Driving Park," was literally a fel\st of fat and good things, we propose to
give our readers a taste thereof, if it be only a few crumbs gathered from the overloaded tables. Among the guests were nine Past Grand Masters of the jurisdiction;
the Grand Master of Iowa, M.·. W.·. GEORGE B. VAN SA.UN; Past Grand Masters of
Iowa and Kansas, M.·. W.·. Bros. THEODORE S. PARVIN and JOHN H. BBowN; and our
worthy predecessor in the Grand Chaplain's chair, Bro. 0, C. WHEELER, of California. After the wants of the inner man had been fully supplied, then followed
" the feast of reason and the flow of soul." Grand Master WARREN delivered 11n appropriate and eloquent address of welcome. We give 11n extract to •how the
changes wrought during this quarter of a century:What was our situation then (in 1857)? Three weak Lodges, with 11 membership
in 1858 of one hundred and seven; now a roster that embraces ninety chartered
Lodges, with fourteen others under dispensation, and a membership of over foor
thousand. Then they met in a small hamlet situated upon the west bank of the
treacherous and muddy Missouri, upon the extreme confines or civilization, upon
what was then believed to be, and so marked in our geographies, the Great
American Desert, where tempestuous winds and shifting sands presented a scene of
desolate sterility. How great the change! What was then a village of a few hun·
dred inhabitants is now a compactly built, prosperous, energetic, elegant city of fifty
thousand souls, presenting in her manufactures, railroads, churches, schools, and
public works evidences of 11 solid and substantial prosperity. And what was once
so dreaded as the desert is dotted with thriving villages and cities, surrounded by
fertile fields of yellow grain or serried ranks of corn.

The Addre'S of the Grand Master Is very brief. He was happy to say that intemperance among Masons did not -prevail to any great extent in the jurisdiction, and
be hoped thBt the time would soon come when intemperance e.nd gambling would
be unknown among the Craft. To all which we respond "Amen" and would add,
profanity to the list. '
The Grand Master desired much that uniformity of work might be attained in the
jurisdiction. But few of the Lodges used the same work. The remedy, he thought,
would be to create the office or Grand J,ecturer, but the present state of tbeir,llnances
would not admit or that. He left all, therefore, to the careful consideration or the
Grand Lodge. He had oo legislation to suggest: The Constitution and Regulations
were ample for t he government or the Craft for many .vears to come, and be did not
believe in "tinkering with laws unless there existed a great necessity."
'!.'he Report of the Grand Secretary is equally brief, but abounds in figures . He
hat! received and forwarded two hundred and thirty dolle.rs for the relief of suffel'ers
by floods in the valley of the Ohio, being the contributions trom four Lodges.
The Grand Representatives from seventeen sister Grand Lodges were formally
presented and received with the Grand Honors. The Representative from Ce.lifornla
was not present.

ally; and, 2d, thllt the salary of.the Grand Secretary be fixed at six hundred dollars.

is also very complimentary to the report of Bro. ABELL, the oration of Bro. HIGHTON,

each .

We should judge from the report of the Committee on Trials and Appeals that
some of the Lodges in New Hampshire, as well as elsewhere, need 11 schoolmaster
to teach them the alphabet of Masonic proceedings in the trial of brethren. One
brother, whom we will call JOHN Dos, was tried for unmasonic conduct in that," in'
conversation with 11 profane, he threatened to blackball any man that certain members might recommend." The LodgA found him guilty, and then the Master put
this queer question to the Lodge : " Shall JOHN DoE be expelled from all the
rights and benefits and membership of - - - Lodge, No. 67?" Of course the
Lodge voted in the affirmative, but the form of the question was so palpably in
violation of the requirements of the Constitution that the committee recommended
a reversal of the sentence, and that the Lodge should try again. Then Bro. JoHN
DoE turned upon Bro. RIOBARD Rom, and had him tried for "endeavoring to ascertain
the manner in which 11 brother voted on the application of 11 candidate." All being
proved as charged, the committee recommended a reprimand, and it was so ordered.
Then Bro. JoaN DoE pitched into another brother of the same Lodge, but for what is
not stated. His appeal was dismissed. We think that the arrest of the charter of
that Lodge for a little while would be 11 wholesome medicine.
The "Orphans' Home" had been incorporated, and would be ready soon for
active service in its line of duty and benevolence.
The Report of the Committee on Correspondence is again from the pen of Bro.
ALBERT S. WAIT, who has filled the chair so often and done so well that he may be
considered as one of the veterans of the corps. We often ll.iffer widely from the
brother in his arguments and conclusions, as do others of the reportorial scribes, but
Bro. W. never flinches from the contest. He is gentlemanly, but positive, and the
antagonist who expects an easy victory will find himself mistaken. Sometimes,
however, we almost think he comes within the scope of that line of Hudibras (was
it not?) : " A man convinced against his will,'' etc.
The present Report occupies one hundred and eighty pages, and is ably written,
California for 1883 is honored with a four page notice, and we are afraid he will think
that ours in return is "short commons·" Indeed. He cordially approves of the decisions of our Grand Master, and, in reference to that where the Grand Master ordered
a ballot to be had at the next stated meeting, when the Master of 11 Lodge had
declared a candidate re,Jected at the first ballot, wherein only one black ball had
appeared-which decision waa antagonized by the Committee on Jurisprudence·
and reversed by the Grand Lodge-Bro. WAIT still sides with our Grand Master and
has these comments upon the final action :It was undoubtedly wrong in the Master to declare the can~idaterejected; it was
his clear duty, without declaring the result, immediately to order a second ballot.
He did not do this, and by his act.ion a wrong was done both to the candidate and
the Lodge. The rights of both were by it disregarded and sacrificed. On the view
of the committee there is no power anywhere to right such 11 wrong. It seems to us
that the case might have been regarded as one not contemplated by the by-Jaw, and
that the prerogative of the Grand Master extends to the correction of such an error.
The ver7 object, or at least, one of the objects of this prerogative, is to supply the
place o legislation where it fails in any case to anticipate 11 possible wrong, and to
provide specially for itR correction. This seems to have been the view of the Grand
Master, and Wtlre it in New Hampshire, we should in 11 similar case hope he would
do as .did our Most Worshipful brother of California.
With a neat and deserved compliment to Bro. ANDBR~ON for his Report on Corre·
spondence, Bro. WAIT passes on to haul other Grand Bodies over the coals when
they deserve it.

last sleep. The fact ls, "homes," or "colleges," or "retreats," or by whatever
name they may be known, eavor so much of the "poor-house,.' that no widow or
orphan of a Mason, If they have I\ spl\rk of we;manhood or manhood left will for a
moment entertain the Idea ol' becoming an "Inmate.'' Better, cheaper, .iiore satisfacto~y every. way, for each Lodge to look after and provide for the Indigent of its
own Jurlsdict1on.

OREGON.

The thirty-third Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Oregon was held
in the city of Portland, commencing on the eleventh day of Jone, 1883,-tb.e M.•, W.·.
JOSEPH N. DOLPH, Grand Master, presiding, and the R.'. W.•, FBELON J, BABOOOK
being Grand Secretary. Sixty-eight J,odges were represented.
The Address of the Grand Master is very long, occupying twenty-four of the
pages before us, is well written, and Is almost entirely devoted to the business of
the jurisdiction, He speaks first of the wonderful prosperity that has visited the
State. He says:An unprecedented tide of immigration Is setting toward our State. All the transportation lines leading to our borders are crowded with enterprising and Intelligent
people from nearly every portion of the civilized world, seeking l1omes In our fertile
valleys. Every branch of Industry in the State is being stlmala.ted by the Influx of
new energy and capital. l!iew ~nterprlses are being undertaken. Labor is in demand and commands remunerative wages. Contentment prevalla. SohoolB and
educa.tlonal Institutions are being multiplied. In short, we appear as a State to have
fairly entered upon such a career of development and prosperity as has scarcely been
witnessed In any other portion of the Union.
Right glad are we to hear such good news of our sister State, On the Pacific
Slope there should be no local jealousies. The prosperity of one State or Territory
enures to the benefit of a.II. Oregon has Indeed a bright future before her, and we
a.re pleased to know that talent and true worth are appreciated by our" web·foot"
brethren, for they have elevated the writer of that glowing eulogy to a seat In th~
United States Senate, where we venture to predict that he will be no more a cipher
than he was when presiding over the Intelligent Craft of our l!lster joriadiotion,
He had granted dlpensatlons for three 11ew Lodges. We find a large number of
his decisions reported In full, all based on good Masonic law, but all, or nearly all, of
local Interest only.
The Grand Master at some length urges the colleotlon and compilation of a Masonic history of the jurisdiction, and also an adoption of some syPtem of uniform
work. .At present, he says, o1oarcely any two Lodges have the same ~rk, and In
some cases the " bright Maaons" of the same Lodge will dift'er in their views and work.
He thinks such dift'erences very deleterious to young Masons. It was measurably so
in this jurisdiction until 186,, when a uniform system of work was adopted and ma.de
o!Jliga.tory upon the J,odges, no matter what the "bright Masons " thought of It. Our
Oregon brethren are moving in the same direction, and, not to be too modest, we
venture to say that they might " go farther and fa.re worse'' than to adopt the California. work.

"The tide of immigration had fully set in, and the east, west, north, and south
were pouring in their hundreds and thousands to make their homes in Oregon." He
was sanguine that in a few years their young State would assume a position of
importance in the civil and Masonic world second to none.
The Grand Master bad made as many visitations to the subordinate Lodges as hie
business arrangements would permit. The Deputy Grand Master and the Grand
Wardens had also done the same. But, considering the large extent of' territory and
the isolated position of many of the Lodges in the jurisdiction , he was fully convinl'ecl
that the Grand Master should not be a business man. "Masonry, we are taught,''
he says, "is not intended to conflict with one's necessary bueinese, which should on
no account be neglected. I am therefore of the opinion that a Grand Master should
be a well informed brother, of practical leisure, who can devote a large amount of
time and attention to the interests of the Craft, and not be hampered by cases of an
official or personal character." Very good in theory, perhaps, but not practical, we
apprehend. The best man should be chosen, regardless of his particular avocation.
Dispensations had been granted for three new Lodges. Among hie official decisions was one that ~ Lodge had no right to draw funds from its treasury "to pay
the expenses of celebrating ST. JOHN'S Day.'' He says:If the renting of a hall, the expense of music and a ~rand ball, can by any stretch
of the imagination be considered as " purely Masonic ' or charitable, then possibly
it could be considered proper to appropriate Lodge funds to meet such expenses.
The Gran 1l Master thought not, and the Grand Lodge concurl"ed. So the dancers
must "pay the fiddler" in Oregon.
In answer to an appeal In behalf of the sufferers by the Ohio fioode, the sum of
$1,500 had been forwarded to the Grand Secretary of Ohio. Of this sum $950 bad
been returned as not used, and was then in bank, subject to the order of the Grand
Lodge.
· The Grand Secretary could report, as Bro. ABELL bas done for very many years,
that all the Lodges had made returns. There must be something in the invigorating
effect of the Pacific breezes that makes our Lod~e officers so prompt, or our Grand
Secretaries so determined that subordinate officers shall do their duty.
The Committee on Uniformity of Work reported that they were relldy to report
by the conferring of the three degrees. They did so in the Enterel! Apprentioe
degree, and their work was generally discussed. When they offered to confer the
Fellow Craft, the Grand Lodge, instead of giving permission, coolly discharged the
committee. We ask for more light. Why this "marching up the hill and then
marching down again?"

which the f,odge finally acted." It appears that two brothers disagreed about a
claim amounting to one dollar and seventy.five cents. Ill·feeling was engendered,
when the Lodge appointed a committee to arbitrate between the brethren and reconcile their differences. One consented to leave his case with the committee, but
the other refused ; whereupon the committee reported a resolution that he be suspended for contempt of the committee,..and the Lodge so voted. Neither of the parties ever made a charge against the other. The action was reversed and the
brother reinstated. We wonder much what will be hauled next into the legislative
or criminal claws of a Lodge? Texas, in former times, used to present some funDy
transaotlons, but that Lodge in Pennsylvania can " take the cake" this time.

The Committee of Fifteen, to whom had been referred the subject of a Home for
aged and Indigent Masons, submitted an elaborate report thereon, giving their cordial a.nd full approbation to the project, but coming to the conclusion that it should
be the work of subordinate Lodges or individual Masons. They therefore reported
n resolution that It was not expedient for the Grand Lodge to take further action on
the subject, which resolution was adopted by the Grand Lodge.

and we wish them all prosperity until their debt Is wiped out.

But we find far more to praise than to cavil at in this excellent report. We quote
with great pleasure a few lines from the exordium :Since the first stones were taken to erect an altar at which God was to be worHhipped, the Freemason never failed in all the ages to bow before the " Great
Lights" of the Fraternity, both to invoke and adore. Faith in·Freemasonry is a liv·
ing spirit. God in Freemasonry i• the eternal, ever existing, ever recognized, abiding, prevailing source of our trust in time and our hope of immortality. Without
God, Freemason.ry is not even a name. From the beginning, thus it ever has been
in our ancient and honorable Fraternity.
True it is that troubles have existed 111 our Craft, that unharmony has raised its
voice, and contention has sought to separate the brethren. These profl\ne •plrits
were driven out of our Temple, as aforetime money changers and those who sold
doves were expelled, so soon as their real purpose was ascertained. 'rheir existence
i• now among our traditions. The failures of their efforfB are among the great
glories which ennoble our inheritance. From the rising of the sun to the going
down of tho same, to-day there is only peace and harmony within our borders.
And here Is something for Bro. BLANCHARD and bis horde of" Anti-Secret Society" followers to read and digest1There are in ~his our day Individuals who have, as they think, received some
"revelation," and, in the darkness of the cloud out of which they pretend it has
come, they decry our Craft, It Is only "in vincible ignorance" that assumes the
role of a perverted, misconceived iconoclasm. It is as harmless as it is amusing. It
is the outcome of many modern teachings, in which Ignorance and mediocrity strive
for supremacy. To exist, they must" agitate," else they would not be. It ls the
noisy rivulet that proclaims its shallowness. When truth becomes aggreBBfve to dispel error, its characteristics are moderation, persnaslon, and argument. Against
these there Is no law. If declamation, outcry, denunciation, Ignorance, false witness are the marked and only agencies used in any contest, it is the arsenal of
error that furnishes the weapons, and be who runs may read it.
Bro. VAUX reviews the prooeedings of llfty-fonr Grand Lodges, inclnding those of
California for 1882 and 1883. In his review for 1882, he speaks In high terms of the
Address of the Grand Master, characterizing it as " a very creditable paper, painstaking, anxious, earnest and conservative." Our brother bas so much to say of our
own report of that year, and says it so genially, even while wielding the scourge,
that we feel like surrendering unconditionally, and crying " Peccavi ! " But even
then, like Gurr.Eo, our stubbornness revives and we feel like again and always as·
serting, that "the world does move.'! We thank our brother heartily for hie words
of personal commendation, and, to show bow impartial we are, we will qnote what he
says in re public installations. We have had our ny and now yield the fioor 1 Bro. BILL'S report is a monument of patient, intelliKent, exhaustive researoh
into the reports of tho GTand Lodge• nuder his review. His style is bright, attraoti ve and cultured. If he would only devote hie time to a digest of the laws and decisions of the State of California, he would rank among the ablest of legal reporters
and digester• of the oountry. We have been verymuoh ainused, and so bas Brotb~r

members of the Craft know both, foreign jurisdictions have no intllr~dt In them, and
as to the out•ide world it is none of its busineBB. If Bro. BILL doubts the propriety

try Lodges" subserve the true interests of the Craft. We eho11ld have been better

Several amendments were adopted to the Grand Lodge 'constitution, soma of

though, as a matter of fact, no one ha.s been elected who had not been a Master of a

Another amendment is certainly curious, and we fail to see any good reason for

of parrots in a Lodge, but we do not see how it would add either to the moral qualitl.·
cation or usefulness of a Master Mason. The Grand Master reported that he had
dispensed wit.h the rule in three several cases which had arisen between the SemiAnnual a.nd Annual CommunicationR. We think that it will be a short-lived proposition.

TEXAS.
The forty-eighth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Texas was held
in the city of Houston, commencing on the eleventh day of December, 1883,-the
R.·. W.'. WILLIAM H. NICHOLS, Deputy Grand Master, presiding in the absence of
the Grand Master, and the R: ..W.·. GEORGE H.BRINGHURSTbeingGrand Secretary.
One hundred and sixty-three Lodl!es were represented. ·
The M. ·• W:, Grand Master, Bro. CllABLEB STEWART, who, being 11 Representative
in the United States Congress, had been obliged to leave for W llBhington before the
meetinj of the Grand Lodge, had left his Annual Address with the M:. W:. MAR·
cu~ F. MOTT, Past Grand Master, who p~ted the same to the Grand Lodge.
It is a very able document. and of unusual length, occupying not less than thirty pages
o~ the proceedings•. It proved one thing, that the Grand Master had been 11 very active and hard workmg officer. He regretted his absence, but important duty called
him elsewhere.
The Grand Master returned thanks to the Giver of all Good for the bleBBings
vouchsafed the people of the State during the year, In these blessings Freemasonry
had shared, not so much in the increase of Lodges as in the inculcation and practice
of the noble tenets of the Craft. He had granted dispensations for the formation of
seven new Lodges. He had, for good and sufficient reasons in each case, permitted
e~even Lodges to change their location. In only two cases had he granted dispensa·
t1011~ to co~fer degrees upon candidates who had not served in the preceding degrees the
required time, One was that of 11 seaman whose ship was about to sail on 11 long
voyage, a.nd the other that of a soldier of the U. S. Army about to be ordered to 11
distant portion of the country. A custom, which had prevailed in this and some other
Southern jurisdictions, of performing the Masonic Burial Service over the graves of
brethren long after their interment, had been forbidden by 11 resolution of the Grand
Lodge, passed at the last Communication. The Grand Master apologized for having
permitted this on one occasion-he not having then soen or been aware of the edict.
But subsequently ho had refused 1111 like application&, and instead thereof recommended that the Lodges concenied hold " memorial 1ervioes." Dispensations had
been issued for the laying of corner stones on seven different occasions.
The Grand Master stated that, on most of the questions submitted to him, it had
only been necessary to refer the applicants to former rulings. But in fifteen other
cases, new point& were presented, and he gives his decisions thereon, hoping that the
same may meet with approval. One related to physical maims, and he decided that
the loss of an eye, or of the second or middle finger, were physical defects that disqualified an applicant. He. had also decided that "Masons who belonged to Lodges
working undbr the sanction of the Grand Lodge (sic) of France or undllr 11 regular
constituted Lodge working in the Ancient Rite of Herodfilll of 'Scotland oth~rwise
known as the Scottish Rite, may be permitted to affiliate in our Lod~s P" This
may be all right, but were we appointed. 11 committee to examine an applicant, we
should be at 11 loss where to begin or end, or what to do. We think the Massachusetts plan the best-send all such to the Masonic doctors to be " healed.''
In one case, where the Master and Senior Warden elect of a Lodge had both
refused to be installed, the Grand Master ordered that the Junior Warden should be

670

Proceedi,ngs of th.e

[Oct. 14,

installed as such, and then act as the Master during the year. In reporting three
cases of discipline which had been administered by him, he mentions one case where
he had suspended a Master for being drunk and " generally a drunken toper."
Served him right, surely, and if he had suspended the Masons who would elect
such a man, that would have been right also. In another case, be did do justice to a recreant Lodge. Two of its members had engaged in a cutting affray in
the public streets, and yet the Lodge refused, on various pretexts, 1.o take any action
in the matter, though positively ordered to do so by the District Deputy Grand
Master. After this conduct bad continued for more than three months, and it was
evident that the members of the Lodge were determined to do nothing, the Grand
Master arrested the charter of the Lodge. Upon the showing to the Grand Lodge
that the action, or non-action, of the Lodge was owing to certain circumstances
beyond its control, the charter was restored. Th11re is nothing better, sometimes1
than heroic measures to bring members and Lodges to their sober senses.
Another case was so peculiar in itself that we copy what thti Grand Master says
of it without comment :On the 10th of April last, Hubbard City Lodge, No. 530, issued a circular to the
various Ledges in this State, stating that said Lodge, together with Aquilla Lodge,
No. 196, had employed lawyers to prosecute a man who bad attempted to ravish a
MasterMa,son'sdaughter and had killed her father, and requested the Lodges to help
them pay the expenses of the prosecution. When my attention was called to this circular, I at once addressed a letter to the W.·.M.·. of each one of the named Lodges and
informed them that, in my opinion, the issuance of such circulars was unmasonic,
and requested that they desist from making such appeals to thefr sister Lodges. I
know that the members of Hubbard City and Aquilla Ledges were prompted by
their better feelings to issue this circular, conceiving it to be their duty to have
properly punished the perpetrator of this unparalleled outrage. In matters of this
kind we cannot be too cireumspect. In m:y judl;illlent we should not, as a Fraternity,
army oul'!lelves in a body for the vindication ot an individual wrong, no matter how
great that wrong may be, and we cannot be too careful in our action in regard to
matters which do not effect us so much as Masons, as they concern us ·as citizens of
a commonwealth. If Masons can in this manner be permitted to make themselves
felt in the prosecution of crime before the judicial tribunab of the State, it is difficult to see where it will end. Such action can only bring injury to the Craft.
Besides my own conception of this matt.er, I felt that, under the precedent established
by this Grand Body, I was right in requiring these Lodges to desist from asking
other Lodges to aid them in prosecuting the case. As far back as 1853, a case somewhat analogous came before this Grand Body. Washington Lodge, No. 18, publicly
offered a reward for the murderer of a member of said Lodge, and this was condemned by this Grand Lodge as an act contrary to Masonic usage. Evidently this
Grand Body thought that it was improper for Masons, as such, to attempt to take
the place of the constituted authorities of the country.
Past Grand Master P. W. GRAY, who, in his life time, had collected one of the
most valuable Masonic and general libraries in the State, by his will bequeathed the
same to the Grand Lodge, to be held in trust for historical purposes. His widow
had, in pursuance of this bequest, passed the same over to the Grand Master, and
he ho.d accepted the trust. The Grand Lodge approved of and endorsed· his action.
The Gmnd Master gives a synopsis of the reports made to him by the District
Deputies of the thirty-four districts, and then, with a few general remarks, closes
his long and able address.
But no sooner au. we done with the Grand Mast.er, than the R. ·. W:. Deputy steps
upon the platform and speaks his little piece. His address of eight pages fairly bristles
with poetic quotations. In the prose portion he gives a graphic account of laying
the comer-stone of the New Masonic Temple in Galveston. What made this service
especially interesting was the fact that, twenty-six years before, his father had "per•
formed a similar service on the same hallowed ground."

The Grand Mast.er speaks a timely and earnest word in favor of the Reports of

We pass all of ou1· share ov~r to Bro. DIEHL, for he deserves it all:It is a law of this Grand Lodge that its proceedings shall be read in open Lodge.
In these, and more especially in the Correspondence Report, plenty of matter will
be found which will furnish abundant material for profitable conversation and
debate. It is always replete with informaiion on most all Masonic subjects, including the biographies of men who have been eminent in our Institution. It is a perfe<$
store-house of gathered and garnered knowledge of Masonic history, jurisprudence, .
and usage, as well as of the current questions of the day.
It has come to be an acknowedged fact that the Report& on Correspondence,
written, as they usually are, by the beat mentally equipped men in their respective
jurisdictions, and published with the proceedings of nearly every Grand Lodge in
the country, have bad a greater influence than any other one thing in advancing the
Masonic art in America.
There is not a page of the report of our own committee but what contains matter
of interest to every member of the Craft. Bro. DIEHL, our chairman, ranks among
the beat of Masonic reviewers. His work is performed with such admirable skill
and judgment that you will not find it "d17 reading." You will here find copied,
in wbole or in part, the o~iniona of sister junsdictiona regarding our position towards
the " Powers that be" m this Territory-opinions, with which every one here
should make himself perfectly familiar. During my visits to Denver and San
Francisco, last summer, I enjoyed an excellent opportunity, by asrociatinlf with the
best informed Mason;; from all sections of the country, of learning something of the
standing of this Grand Lodge amon~ its sister Grand Lodges; and I am pleased to
inform you, and know that you will be pleased to learn, if you did not know it
before, that although an infant in years, it is not in the rear, but in the advance
guard of American Grand Lodf!01!· I am thoroughly convinced that this eminence,
over which we have a right to mdulge in a little self-glorification among ourselves1
is mainly due to the Reports on Correspondence; and I am just as thoroughly convinced that they are more read and better appreciated in other j uri8dictions than in
our own. Every brother should avail himself of this ready means of obtaining
Masonic knowledge.
I recommend to the Masters of the Lodges that they obey in its letter and spirit
the following order of the Grand Lodge: "It shall be the duty of each Master to
have these proceedings read in_ o~n Lodge, that no brother can plead ignorance of
the transactions of the Grand J.,octge."
Although there had been.but a alight increase in membership during the year,
yet the Grand Master could report the Lodgee as in a prosperous condition. The
inner door of every Lodge-room had been well guarded. Here is a word-picture of
what a Master and Lodge should be, which it would be well for every Mason to
"read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest:"The Master of a Lodge should be a studious and thoughtful man, and above all
a man fruitful in resourcee. Should the energy and zeal of the members of his
Lodge begin to slacken, and their attendance become more and more i"eluctant and
infrequent, he should be able to devise some scheme, to put into operation some pl:in,
by which he may win them back to their allegiance. The Lodge-room should be
made, next to home, the moat delightful and attractive place on earth-a pleasant
retreat from the cares and dividing influences of every-day, active, "t>uaineBB life.
Every Mason should regard bis Lodge as a perennial fountain to which he may
come at all times, and have his own moral courage, and hi~ confidence in hie fellow
men, increased and strengthened. Does business annoy him or financial disaster
threat.en, he here learns that no man should be regarded for bis worldly wealth or
honor. Is he discouraged and disheartened by the repeated instances of ·dishonesty

VERMONT.
The ninety-first Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Vennont was
held in the city of Burlington, commencing on the thirteenth day of June, 1883,the M:. w.-. Luoros C. BUTLER, Grand Master, presiding, and the R:. W.-.
WILLLIAM H . RooT being Grand Secretary. Eighty-.iight Lodges were represented,.
The Grand Master opened his Address with some remarks upon the Elubject. of
perpetual jurisdiction, which had caused some difficulties between Lodges on the h~e
of Vermont and Massachusetts. Though deciding against his own Lodge, and Ill
favor of Massachusetts, in conformity with the strict letter of the law, the Grand
Master is of the opinion that such a strict construction is unjust, an<j. that there
should be some limit during a man's life-time to the claim of a Lodge in another part
of the country' over him, even if he had once been 'rejected,-and perhaps for no
good cause. We think so too, and that the word "perpetual" should sometimu
have a "Picwickian" construction I
The Grand Master does not believe that a suspended Mason should be required
to pay dues " during his !!uspen.sion." While thus s':'8P6~ded, he. ar~ues, " he is
Masonically dead, and must remain so till the hiatus m his M~mc life shall 1'.8
bridged over, not filled up by the resurrecting process of reetomtion. _Do Masomc
justice and equity require the Masonically dead brother to be. taxed while he cann~
be represented p I think not." And so do we, if the BUBpenslOn was for unmasomc
conduct.
.
The Grand Master gives a humorous account of a serious invasion of his jurisdiction in July, 1882, by a party of over one thousand people fro-:n ?anada, "Masons and their wives, sweethearts, and children," to hold a grand p1cmc on the shores
of Lake Champlain. Everything passed of in fine style, and the Grand Master
thinks that the oftener such invasions are made the better.
An invitation was extended to the Grand Lodge, and accepted, to re-lay the
comer stone of the new building of the University of Vermont . A statue of
Lafayette in the University Park was unveiled at the same tiJ11,e. The first co~ner­
stone of the University building was la.id fifty-.iight years ago by the Marquis de
Lafayette himself.
The former Grand Secretary, Bro. HENRY CLARK, was to be tried before the
Grand Lodge on the first evening of the Communication, ~or: an alleged misappi:o~
priation of the funds of the Grand Lodge while in office. We suppose that the trial
was had, but we find no further notice of it or of the result.
The sum of two hundred dollars was appropriated for the benefit of Past Grand
Secretary JOHN B. HOLLENBECK, a very aged and infirm veteran Mason.
.
After the election and installation of Grand Officers, a gold wMch and cham was
presented to Past Grand Master BUTLER, Appropriate speeches were made on both,
sides. In his reply of thanks the Past Grand Master stated that there was then•,
but one brother in the Grand Lodge who was a member when he first entered
it thirty-one years ago.

VIRGINIA.
. !he one hundred and sixth Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Virgm1a was held in the City of Richmond, commencing on the tenth day of December,
1883,- the M.-. w... REUBEN MURRELL PAGE, Grand Master, presiding, and the
R.·. w.-.WILLIAM BRYAN IBAAOB being Grand Secretary. One hundred and twentyeight Lodges were represented.
The G~nd Master, in his Addmss, said he was happy to be able to say that the
Craft was m a sound and healthy condition in the jurisdiction, and that there were
harmonious relations with all other Grand Bodies. He announced, with feelings of
sorrow, the somewhat sudden death of the Grand Treasurer, W:. Bro. OSOAR M.
MARSHALL, who ''.was a most efficient officer ; as a Mason, he was loved and
esteemed ; a.nd as a man, he had endeared himself to a host of friends by his warm
heart and manly nature."
The Grand M1~ster reporti:d one somewhat anomalous caso of discipline. A
brother charged with a Masomc offense confessed. his guilt before tho investigatin
committee. Whereupon, without balloting on the question of guilt or innocenoog
the L~ge P~~~ to vote on the question of puniahment, and there not being ~
two-thirds maJonty m favor of any of those provided for, the accuaed was declared
ac~ttitted.. The Grand Master set a~l this e,side and required the Lodge to comply
strictly with the law, and pass defimtely on both guilt and punishment which wae
done on the second trial. The Grand Master maintains that, no matte; how much
the accused may confess his guilt, it is still the duty of the Lodge to ballot on the
question of guilt or innocence. This may be good law, in the stricteet sense of the
word, but it strikes us as an entirely wmecessary proceeding.
In reference to maims and defects, the Grand Master seems to be more liberal
than some of his cotempora?es. He decided that it was "lawful for a Lodge to
advance an Entered Apprentice who, before initiation, had lost the middle finger• of
the_l~ft hand from the knuckle joint;" and also that a Lodge" could act upon the
pet1t1on of a man who had lost the thumb of his left hand, or one who had lost one
finger and the thumb of his left hand." The world dce8 move I
Mississippi does not stand alone on the question of the dignity of a Grand
Master-notably him of Pe1msylvania. Finding the fact to be that there were
~o rep~tatives to or from the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, the Grand Mastor
instruc:OO the ?-rand Secretary to communicate with the Grand Secretary of Pennsylvania relative to t he mutual appointment of such representatives. The reply
was a refusal unless the request came directly from him as Grand Master. Believing
the Grand Secretary to be the executive officer of the Grand Master, our Virginia
Grand Master fell back upon his own dignity, and directed the Grand Secretary to
close the correspondence and withdraw the request I
Dispensations had been granted for the formation of six new Lodges. The Grand
Master closes his very able Address with a neat and deserved oompliment to the
Correspondence Report, submitted by Bro. WILLIAM F. DRINKARD.

WAS GEORGE WASHINGTON MASTER OF A LODGE?
RIOHMOND, VIRGINIA, 5TH SEPTEMllER, 1883.
GENERAL A. T. PIERSON, St. Paul, .Minnesota:
DEAR BROTHER PIERSON :-Your proceedings for 1883 are at hand, for which
accept thanks. I note your report on Vir~ia for 1881. My letter to you of September, 1882, was not intended for publication, but simply to remove any" lingerin&
doubt" resting on your mind on the question, "Was Washington a Master of a
Lodge?" I will endeavor to satisfy you, and this letter is for such use as you may
think proper to make of it. Let me premise by saying that he was initiated in Fred,:.
erwksburg Lodge, No. 4, in November, 1752, Passed in March, 1753, and Raised
in August, 1753, and bis name appears, for the last time on the reoords of that Lodge,
as among the attendants in September, 1753.
Alexandria Lodge, No. 39, at Alexandria, Virginia, was chartered by the Grand
· Lodge of Pennsylvania on the 3d February, 1783, and it continued to work under
that Grand Jurisdiction until March, 1788, when it surrendered its charter and
" decided that it would be more convenient for it to work under the authority of the
Grand Lodge of Virginia," " " " therefore," having resolved to make application to the Grand Lodge of :Virginia for a charter, 'recommended the following persons for appointment by tht Grand Lodge-GEORGE WASHINGTON, Esq., for Master,"
&c. " " " General WASHINGTON having given consent to the use of his name,
the application to the Grand Lodp;e was accompanied by the following letter, dated
October 25, 1787, prepared by Cofone! CHARLES SIMS and ROllERT MoCREA, Esq.,"
" " " " It is also the earnest desire of the members of this Lodge, that our
Brother, GEORGE WASHINGTON, should be named in the charter as Master of the
Lodge, &c." The prayer of the petitioners was granl;ed, and a charter was issued
to Alexandria Lodge, No. 22, by " EDMUND RANDOLPH, Governor of Virginia and
Grand llCaster," on 28th April, 1788, " " " "by, and with the consent of the
G~d Lodge of Virginia, do hereby constitute and appoint our illustrious and wellbeloved Brother GEORGE WASHINGTON, Esq.• late General and Commander-in·Chiet
of the forces of the United States of America, and our worthy brethren, " " "
together with all such other brethren, ,t,c.," and at the annual election of officers on
the 20th December, 1788, WASHINGTON was re-elected Worshipful Master for the
year commencing with St. John's Day, (27th December, 1788.) It would coneume
too much of your time to trace from year to :year the evidences, as strong as Holy
Writ, of WASHINGTON'S interest in and affection for our Institution to the day of
his death; ·but it is eminently appropriate to the occasion to refer to the part devolving upon, and performed by him in laying the comer-stone of the Capitol building',
at Washington, in September, 1793.

So much for the recorded evidences during the lifetime of our distinguished
Brother. Let us now tum to evidences furnished by his contemporaries subsequently
to his death. He died on Saturday, 14th December, 1799, and was buried with
Masonic houors, on the Wednesday followin~. In October, 1799, Alexandria Lodge
No. 22, petitioned the Grand Lodge of Virginia to change its name to Alexandrid
Washington Lodge, which petition was granted and "Alexandria Wiiahingt-On
Lodge, No, :.!2 " was, and is to-day, a Lodge of vigorous manhood.
. In 1810 the question of forming a Grand Lodge for the District of Columbia was
ag1~ted, and No. 22 was invited to unite in the movement. This invitatiion was
declined, and several reasons were assigned therefor-the "third" of which reads as
follows· "that the Grand Lodge of Virginia, having granted a charter to this Lodge
at the special solicitation of our illustrious and ever to be revered Brother, Gene111l
GEORGE WASHINGTON, our first Master, have no doubt, should this Lodge with~raw t"!iemselves from their ju1isdiction, that the Grand Lodge of Virginia would
immediately demand a surrender of that charter so much valued by every member
of this ~ge.'' Again: on the ~c~sion of the visit of General LA FAYETTE to this
country 1~ 1825, be was the recipient of courtesies extended by Lodge No. 22, in
Alexandria. Iu the address of we~come by th.e Worshipful Master, and delivered in
the P.resence of many contemporaries of Wasbingtou. we find the following very expressive language: " " "It affords me in~xpreesible pleasure to be the organ of my
brethren here assembled, to welcome you into the bosom of this Lodge, in which
your highly valued f~end, the belov~ F!'ther of our country, was wont to preside
ove·r our labors and inculcate the principles of our Order-Friendship, morality
brotherly love and charity." "While it is our boast that we have had him to rul;
over us, we also esteem oureelves particularll happy in having you for our patron.
When Masonry has such supporters, its principles will be maintained; ita cause must
f!ou~is~:" e.nd LA FA!ETTE, in_ ~is respouse, says : " " " "It is particularly
gratifying to my feelings to vmt a Lodge over which our lamented, illustrious
Brother w ASHINGTON presided.''
With this I rest my case. I think, dear Brother P., I have established the fact
that WASHINGTON was the Master of a Lodge, and that he presided over it; that he
always had an exalted opinion of the Institution; and that that opinion (combined
with a warm affection) he retained to the last.
I am, truly and fraternally yours,
WM. B. lSAAOS.

A resolution of a nature so grave, affecting the very essence of the Institution,
as might naturally be expected produced the most profound astonishmeut. How
could the Supreme Council of Peru suspend sentences of perpetual expulsion when
its own General Regulation, article twenty, section fifteen, prohibited it? How
could it pretend that the Lodges, faithful until then to the Supreme Council in spite
of its despotic rule, would consent to submit to a.n obedience to perpetually expelled
:Masons, forgetting the antecedents o! those brothers, and, what is more, their own
sense of dignity and decorum? On the other hand, supposing that the Supreme
Council of Peru could relinquish the government of the blue degrees, it had not,
nor has it, the right to transfer that government to another body, even if that body
hns a legal existence.
It is here proper to Ray thl\t this so-called Grand Orient reached the melaooholy
end which was the proper and logical result of its spurious ori11in, on the night of
the nineteenth of December last. Its dise.ppearance from the Masonic scene, with
the siugalar circumstances or its origin, the unusual form in which it existed, and the
immediate consequences produced by its demise, are so notable that we may point to
that event as the best evidence of the regularity of the proceedings of the Lodges
which have proclaimed their liberty and independence. On the memorable night of
the nineteenth of December, the only Lodge-Order and Liberty, No. 1-working
under the jurisdiction of the Grand Orient, de clared itself under the presidency of
the newly elected Grand Commander, and, in i;>resence of the Supreme Council,
also decl11.red that it withdrew from the Grand Orient, whose org11.nization and edicts
it did not recognize. And the Grand Commander invested and installed in their respective places, the Worshipful Master and officers of the Lodge Order and Liberty, No.
1. who were unanimously elected at the same session. The Grand Commander and
the Supreme Council, then, have been the first to sanction by this one act the extinction of the Grand Orient and the regularity of the proceedings of the Lodges.
These things recalled the resolution of December sixth, and exhibited the inj ustic'e of
the Supreme Council in sustaining the Grand Orient; and one of the LodgesVi1-tue a'lld Union, No. 3-presented a vroject for the establishment of a Grand
Lodge, according to the An cient York Rite, as the best method of avoiding future
dissensions, giving to the Lodges their own government.
To this just and reasonable demand the Supreme Conncil replied by two resolutions: the first, dated December 8th, to the effect that" by decree of ihe sixth of
that month it ha.d relinquished, unanimously and absolutely, the government of the
first three degrees;" and the other, dated on the .twenty-first of the same month, de·
claring that "It is illegal to e•tablish a Grand Lodge of the Ancient and Accepted
Scottish Rite : " from which we infer that it iii legal to establish one of any other
Rite.

For the items following, relative to the progress and work of Freemasonry in
other countries outside of the United States and British America, we are indebted
to our brethren of the corps in Louisiana, Florida., Maine, and New York:ll!EXIOO.

This country has been so long and sadly a priest-ridden commonwealth, in the
worst meaning of that term, where every opprobrium has been hurled against
Masons and Masonry, that we take special pleasure in noticing the progress of
Masonry t herein. Men there begin to think for themselves, and that is all that
Masonry asks. She is the bulwark of freedom against both civil and ecclesiastical
despotism. We quote the summary by Bro. DRUMMOND, of Maine, of the article
by the Brother from Louisiana, who, being himself of Spanish descent, must be
competent to speak of his brethren of the same race :The Supreme Council of the Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite, 33', for the
United States of Mexico, a body in affiliation with the Supreme Councils of the
Northern and Southern Jurisdictions of that Rite in the United States, recently
abandoned all control over the Symbolic Lodges in Mexico, leaving .t hem free to
manage their own affairs. 'f he L odges of the Federal District have taken the
opportunity, and in convention the majority of the legal Lodges of the District have
organized a Grand Lodge, adopting, as their ad interim constit ution and by-laws,
those of our Grand Lodge. The application before ue will be followed by others
from the different States of Mexico, and the question before the Grand Lodge of
Louisiana is simIJly this : Shall we assist the foundation of Ancient Craft Masonry in Mexico, by recognizing and exchanging representatives with the Grand
Lo~e of the Federal District? A thorough examination of the Proceedings of our
Mexican brethren, on file in the office of the Urand Secretary, will afford oppor·
tunity to satisfy every doubt as to the position of this new Grand Lodge. It is
not extravagant to believe that your action in response to this application ma~
result in extending the benefits of our institution at least to the limits of the cont1·
nent.
We have received the Proceedings of that convention. F ourteen Lodges in the
city of Mexico participated in it. During the session, members of an alleged suspended Lodge at Tenango appeared in t he Temple, and were admitted to the hall,
but were not allowed to participate in t he proceedings ; and thereupon a discussion
arose which finally took such a violent form, on the part of the new-comers, that
the presiding officer declared the session adjourned to a future day, and the representatives of the fourteen Lodges left the Temple. At an appointed time they met
and completed the organization of the Grand Lodge.
At a subsequent session, applications were received from Lodges in the different
States to become constituents of the Grand L odge, as there WllB no Grand Lodge
in their respective States ; and, upon consideration, their applications were
granted, and they were entered upon the roll of the Grand Lodge. It is understood that the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Louisiana, with the neeessary
changes, was adopted.

From Mother circular we learn that twelve Lodges in the "Federal District "
two in the State of Mexico, and five in the State of Hidalgo, had given in th~ir
adhesion to and been accepted as constituents by the new Grand Lodge.
We learn, however, that the alleged suspended Masons, whom we nave already
mentioned, and others associated with them, formed another Grand Lodge.
If this be so, the recognition of this movement will be delayed; In any eventi
one very important step has been taken. The Supreme Council has renounced al
control over or interference with the Lodges and Symbolic Masonry for the purpose of allowing the formation of Grand Lodges according to the ~ystem of. the
York Rite. TheJlan contemplates the organization of a Grand Lodge in every
one of the Unite Mexican States. We think this will ultimately be effected.
There will be delay growing out of a want of harmony. We have already alluded to
one schism. The Grand Lodge of Colon and Cuba has chartered three Lodges in Vera
Cruz, and they have formed a Grand Lodge. That is another disturbing element,
as we find that it claims to be a Grand Lodge for the whole of Mexico! We at
first supposed it was a Grand Lodge for the State of Vera Cruz, and were disposed
to consider its claims favorably; but its claims to be the Independent Grand Lodge
of Mexico are so absurd that 1t scarcely deserves a passing notice.
Some of the Lodges publish a magazine as an organ of the Lodge. We have
not been able to examine all that have been received; but we have gone far enough
to learn that the condition of Masonry in the Mexican Republic is badly "mixed."
We hope, howeveri now that the Grand Lodge system has been adopted, that
gradually order wil come out of chaos.
PERU.
We have received the Proceedings of this Grand Lodge, and it is a handsome
and ably-edited book. This jurisdiction is, perhaps, the best-governed of the
various foreign Grand Bodies with which we are in correspondence. I do that
Grand Lodge but simple justice when I say it might be justly called a "Model
Grand Lodge." The enthusiasm of its constituents, the perfect harmon;v which
prevails among the Craft under the most trying circumstances, the perfect10n they
have reached in so short a time in the routine of business, the sound masonic
teachings they disseminate throughout their jurisdiction, the correct rulings and
decisions of their distinguished Grand Master-all these entitle our Peruvian
Sister to the front rank among older Grand Lodges. ·I am pleased to see that
Grand Master ARENAS, of Peru, has made a most happy appointment of Grand
Representative, in the person of R. W. Deputy Grand Master D. R. GRAHAM, a
most fitting representative of as enlightened and distinguished a body of Masons as
ever congregated in any Lodge. I regret to state that, in a communication dated October 20th, 1883, R. M. Bro. EGO-AGUIRRE, Grand Secretary of this Grand Lodge,
notifies all the Grand Lodges with whom Peru is in correspondencel of the invasion
of its territory by the "Grande Oriente Italiano" (Italian Grana Orient), which
has constituted a Lodge in the city of Lima, under the name of "Stella d'Italia."
I think the proceedings on the part of the Italian Grand Orient should be denounced
in severe terms by every Grand Lodge on this hemisphere, and I would respectfully recommend that the matter be referred to the Committee on Law and Jurisprudence for consideration.
ENGLAND.
We have the pamphlets containing notices of the several Communications held
during the year 1883.
The matter of principal interest appears to be the reconstruction of the Temple,
pretty thoroughly destroyed by fire about a year ago. Extended discussion appears
to have been had, and a great variety of opinions demonstrated-so much so, indeed, that up to this writing the how and when of the reconstruction is still an
open question. .We think the English brethren wise in not moving with undue
haste.
During the year there has been ii very thorough revision of the Book of Constitutions, in which there seems to us to be enough law to govern a kingdom. The
American Grand Lodges may congratulate themselves upon the infinitely simpler
codes prevalent on this side of the ocean.
The Prince of Wales is still Grand Master; Col. SHADWEJ,L H. CLERKE, Grand
Secretary; and the old Mother appears to be moving along in stately dignity and
great harmony.

AND BRllTBBEN OF TBE GRAN!l LODGE:-

Again we are assembled to review the work of a year and to take oounaei together
for the future, a future which I hope will he as happy, prosperous, and harmonious
as has been our Immediate past.
The Impulse In the mind of a yonng Mason, and 1 am one of the youngelt among
you, on an oooasion like this, when he is imbued with that zeal and admiratl_on of a
great and noble association which Is natural to the novitiate, is to speak of its first
organization, of its history, and to point out with pride the various mile-stones which
mark its progress in the past. But this is not my purpose to.day. A survey of the
past is for the student, and au analysis of the causes which gave rise to and have
fostered Masonry is for the philosopher. The present and the immediate future is of.
most Interest to us who now bear the heat and burden of the day, and upon whom
Is devolved the duty of tr11.nsmitting to the next generation our Order, Improved,
solidified, and bet ter for our having been Its proteotors and promoters.
I would not by any means be understood as shutting out the past, nor Is its study
without profit to ail; but in these stirring times in all departments of soienoe, labor,
and association, it is not for Masons to dwell among the dead, hut-standing as thoy
do upon a platform of but one plank, and that Humanity, and endorsing the principles
of that faith which seeks Its object until found, of that hope which burns fiver
brightly within the human breast, and of that oharity which oovers the whole earth,
extends beyond its conftnes and across tli.e ·dark river into that unknown country
from whose bonrne no traveler returns,-to carefully consider the present
and wisely deterinine the future. As we are endowed with knowledge by the Supreme
Grand Master, and opportunities are afforded us for the ennobling of our race and
of bettering our own condition, in that proportion are our respousiblllties the greater.
Onr talents were not given us to hide, or to let rust in idleness, ~ut to be increased
and added to.
Perhaps more than ever before In its history Masonry 111 threatened with innova·
tions • and whether it r an and will withstand them is about to become a very serious
question with us. This is an age of innovation, an age of free-thought and disregard
for the past and its precedents, and, in our own Order, ntany are lending themselves
to the encouragement ot' schemes and societies which t end to lessen, by the natural
process of familiarity, the respect in which some of our best founded tene.is are n_ow
held. It is true that the horizon seems clear to the eye and no dark cloud 1s loommg

Around oar altar poverty and riches, comparative ignorance and shining intelligence

Such ~s the fore~ .o.f Hsoc1at1on; and as our Order, in its effects upon the present

. Good morals are not only taught, but their practice ls demanded; and thus the

Man being so naturally social in his nature , lt would have a very beneficial effect
upon our Order if its members would· altend more regularly the meetings of their

the altars of our hearts. There are too many who utterly neglect attending their
own or any Lodge. It is not unusual to hear a 111.as~n remark," I have not a ttended
a Lodge for years." Is it sti-ange that such a one becomes indifferent to its obligations, forgets its forms, and neglects its teaohlngs-that be should run after strange
11ods, and too often disgrace the Order? Certainly, it Is not; but it is the natural result of those natural laws which regulate man's condhct ; and this result would be, in
a great degree, avoided by more frequent association with Masonry and its tee.chings ;
for by this a beneficial effect accrues directly to the brother himself, and indirectly
be assists every other brother by the eneouragem11nt t hus given him. No man ls so
insignificant in any particular but that he exerts an influence in the world for good
or f'or evil, which influence reacts upon himself. Bear this in mind and let the good
have the preference,
" Present example gets within our gaard,
And acts with double force by few repelled.
As bees mix nectar drawn from fragrant fiowers,
So men from friendship, wisdom and delight."
I
Masonry does not seek to make' proselyte&, but it demands the active co-operation
of all its members and is continually striving, silently but eifeotively, to arouse
and keep alive faith in the present and in the future ; such faith as makes glad the
heart of man and illumlnates his path way, elevates humanity in the principles of
morality, Increases domestic and personal happiness, and makes life worth the living
and the rewards promised In the future of value.
"Faith speaks aloud, distinct, even adders hear;
Faith builds a bridge across the Gulf of Death,
To break the shock, kind nature naunot shun,
And lands thought swaetly on the farther shore."
Again, the progress and welfare of our Order are t o be greatly enhanced by the
exeroise of prudence in t he administration of its affairs. Personal prudence is the
duty of every man, and by lt3 exercise he attains .success; by lts disregard be meets
with failure. The disregard of this virtue by an individual in bis own affairs brings
immediate punishment, and bis attention Is oontlnnally directed to the preser vation
of his mental and physical health by the suffering which follows the infraction of
nature's laws; b11t this ls not necessarily so In, organizations or societies of men.
The consequences being more remote, the results of Imprudence are more Iikelv to
be overlooked and carelessness indulged In. I sometimes question the propriety of
having so many Lodges-many of them being so weak that it is practically impossible
to exemplify in their purity the tenets of Freemasonry. I do not mean to discredit
the zealous eiforts of those worthy brethren who have organized and maintain small
Lodges , but in brotherly kindness say unto them-have you not, in too many instances,
undertaken too much ; has not your zeal overstepped y~ur prudenoe, and fire you not
staggering under a load greater than yon can bear ; and, in yonr efforts to maintain
your position, are yon not continually doing imprudent things? Again, in the
matte'r of mem bersblp, there is a growing tendency to a rivalry among Lodges, such
as leads to the admission of many who are deficient In some of the qualifications
requisite in a Mason. Too little inquiry is made into t he character of the candidate,
and often regret follows bis admission because the exercise of prudence did not precede it. Great numbers are not requisite, but good material is-such material as will
act as leaven, and, by its acts, its example, its daily walk, tend to leaven the whole
world. In reading, I have often been pleasantly affected by the example.oftbe vii·

such an one as the poet describes" A true' good man there was there of religion,

The influence of such a man is not beotLuse of his learning, but by reason of his
.sympathy, his example, his faith in the good, and his frowning upon the evil about
him; arid such is the influence the Lodge should exert. To do this there must be an
aggregate of men, each of whom is an example of himself; for remember that the
charitable sympathy of a Lodge is continually exercised in the sight of God and
man, as well as in that secret, unostentatioas manner which stamps the gift as com·
ing from brothers who freely give for the love of giving.
The Lodge is atfected in the eyes of the world by the action of any one of ita
number, and the criticism of the scotfer is poured upon the whole body for the fault
of one of its members. Bear this in mind and exercise the utmost care in the first
admission of any man within our sacred portals. Weigh him in the balance as well
as it is given us to know how, and see that he is uot wanting, so far as our under·
standing allows ns to judge; be nctuated by the desire, not uf swelling our numbers,
but of gathering together the good and true; thus we shall continne to merit and
receive the admiration and respect of the world at large, increase our field of uaefulness and influence, and last, but not least, have the approval of our own consciences.
It is net permitted to anything to be perfect, but the degree of perfection which may
be attained is unlimited except by the existence of life itself.
Prudence, therefore, is the rock upon which the existence f\nd progress of
Masonry largely depends, and by its exercise the history of the past may be verified
and the· promises t>f the future become realities, while the happiness of the present
is Indefinitely increased.
Again, the inftuence of our Order is at times impaired by the false charity and
sympathy which too frequently permits an unworthy member to retain his position
as such. Of course it is an unpleasant duty to perform-the trying and punishing of a
backsliding Mason-but life bas many unple&Bant duties and they are not to be
sbnnned, but must be performed or evil results must follow. All society has to purge
itself of those who disregard the.Ir obligations, and the necessity for so doing is but
the effect of their own misconduct. He who becomes a Mason has every incentive
to be an honest man, and thus reap all the honors and happiness allotted to mortals
upon earth and which follow a life well spent. Upon the threshold of Masonry he
ls met with the assurance, and guaranteed, that brotherly Jove is no idle phrase, but
that it greets him in truth and 8incerity, and will relieve bis necessities as well as
encourage and aasist him in prosperity. The virtues of temperanoe and fortitude and
prud.ence and jnstice he is counseled to praotioe, not as a compliment to Masonry,
not as meaningless advice, but because they are essential to his welfarEl In tLis world
and indispensable to his happiness in the next. Within the Lodge he Is constantly
taught to do unto others as he would have them do unto him. He has become a member of an Order which has withstood the mutations of time and endured persecution
for the sake of right and justice; whjch has seen governments and States totter and
tumble, and rulers of r enown lose their powers ; which has fostered and preserved
true religion when attacked by bigotry and superstition; and which has been held
together by virtue of the trust and confidence of man in man, and by its observance
of our fundamental tenets taken from the inexorable laws of the Deity· (the nonobservance of which would produce political, moral and religious chaos); and which
is therefore justly entitled to receive his respect, yea, his veneration. Such is the
