Again, the ritual is slighted oftentimes in our Lodges to the detriment of the
Order. A knowledge of our forms and ceremonies, and the ability of our officers to
observe an,d go through them without halting and btumbling, is necessary to obtain
and maintain for them the respect which is their due. Mankind like to be engaged
in, and connected with something mysterious; there is a fascination connected with
secresy, with signs and emblems, and a certain ptjde exists in the brenst of every
man who knows something that the world at large is ignorant of; but a careless,
iudifferent, halting performance of the ceremonies, and an uncertain manner in giving
and interpreting signs and emblems destroys this fasoination, removes the glamour of
the mysterlons, and puts the whole matter too much ·within the realities of life to be
eft'ective; therefore the 'good of our Order rtquires that everything be conducted
with confidence and knowledge, and that no Mason should accept an office unless able
and wi!ling to perform its duties in the manner and with the knowledge and spirit
expected of him, and which Masonry has the right to de~and he shall us_e. and
exhibit. Our burial service is most impressive, perfectly simple and exq01s1tely
beautifnl and vet bow often is it wofnlly emasculated, mutilated, and rendered in a
manner ~ainfnl to Masons and unintelligible to friends I All matters of this kind can
be e&Blly remedied by attention and application, and, while their neglect may not
aft'ect the substance of our belief and Interest, yet it does insensibly but materially
aft'ect our feelings and jnstifiable enthusiasm. Masonry is rapidly swelling its membership throughout the United States at the present time. Let us therefore be more than
ever careful that in the excitement of the moment, we do not weaken Its esseutialsand
their due obser~ance; but on the contrary Jet us be more vigilant in preserving the
beauties of Its order and simplicity, for in the observance of details is to be found
the trne index of the quality of our work, the interest and sincerity of our·convictlone.
Thus have I endeavored, in accordance with our Constitution, to speak of matters
pertaining to the welfare of the .Oraft. With a heart full of love and admiration for

To the M.·. w;·. Grand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee have considered the reports of the Boards of Relief of San Fran•

The Board of Relief of San Francisco still has increased calls for charity, and its
funds are now nearly exhausted. To enable it to carry on its good work it will, in
the opinion of your committee, be necessary that the Grand Lodge increase the
appropriation or last year at least one thousand dollars. They therefore offer the
following resolution for adoption:Resolved, That the sum of four thousand seven hundred dollars be appropriated
from the General Fund, to be distributed as follows:To the Board of Relief of the city of San Francisco, ............ $4,000
To the Board of' Relief of the city of Oakland,.................. 400
To the Board of Relief of the city of Los Angeles, ........ , . , . , , • 300
The report of the Board of Relief of Sacramento does not state the full amount of
funds on ha:nd at the beginning of the year. It commences with a reference to a
"sinking fund." If a Board of Relief has a reserve fund, why does it ask for an appro·
priation from this Grand Lodge, without first acquainting it with the amount held in
reserve and giving that body the opportunity to judge in regard to its needs? Being
unable to solve this question, your committee offer the following resolution and
recommend its adoption:Resolved, That the request of the Board of Relief of the city of Sacramento for
a donation from the funds of this Grand Lodge be and is hereby denied.

the sum of one thousand dollars of the funds of this Grand Lodge for the relief of
our suffering brethren at and in the neighborhood of Oincinnati, be and is hereby
approved.

Your.committee, to whom was referred that portion of the Report of the Grand
·Secretary relative to the neglect of the Secretaries of certain Lodges, viz.:
San Joaquin,
No. 19, Howard,
No. 96, Granite,
No. 222,
Los Angeles,
" 42, Hermann,
" 127, Lompoc,
" 262,
Saint Mark's,
" 85, King David's,
" 209, Olive Branch,
" 269,
to transmit certificates of the election and installation of their officers within the
period prescribed by law, have had the same under consideration. The General
Regulation, No. 22, of this Grand Lodge is as follows:Whenever the Secretary of a Lodge fails to forward to the Grand Secretary a
certificate of the election and installation of lts'officers, within a Jferiod of twenty
days after such election and installation, the amount which would otherwise be
allowed to the representative of such Lodge shall be withheld.
It is the opinion of your committee that a strict enforcement of this regulation
will accomplish the object for which it was intended and so much desired by this
Grand Lodge. The above cases all come within the scope of this regulation. Your
committee have received no evidence of inability to comply ther.ewith, or of any extenuating circumstances in excuse for the neglect, except in the case of Lompoc
Lodge, No. 262, the representative of which states that it was owing to circumstances
entirely beyond its control, viz.: that fioods and wash-outs prevented the mails-from
crossing the stream!! in its vicinity during the time prescribed to perform this duty.
In view of this representation yonr committee offer the following resolution for
adoption:Resolved, That Lompoc Lodge, No. 262, be and is hereby exempt from the action
of General Regulation, No. 22, at the present Commnnic~tion of this Grand Lodge.
Your committee have also had under consideration that portion of the Report of
the Grand Secretary relative to Columbia Lodge, No. 28, which reads as follows:Columbia Lodge, No. 28, elected a Past Master as Master. .A note from the Secretary, dated December 27, 1883, states "that the Master elect was not installed,
his certificate not having been received in time set for our installation." In the
annual report of the Secretary, the brother referred to is returned as Master of the
Lodge, but no evidence of his installation, as snch, has been received.
Bro. HENRY C. CALHOUN, the Master elect, informs your committee that he was
duly installed by the retiring Master at the stated meeting next succeeding his election. General Regulation, No. 16, makes it the duty of the installing officer to report
such fact to the Grand Secretary, which duty, in this case, has apparently been neglected. Your committee hope that merely calling the attention of that officer to the
above will be sufficient to prevent a repetition of the error. ·

Grand Secretary, that officer furnishes sufficient reasons, and no action, therefore,
appears to be reqnired.

Bro. JOSEPH C. WARD, from the special committee upon the Report
of the Grand Lecturer, presented the following report:To the M.·. W. •. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom was referred the .Annual R~port of the Grand Lecturer,
have examined that paper and find it, as usual, replete with valuable information
and suggestions, which we commend to the careful consideration of the fraternity,
an.d particularly to the Inspectors of the several Districts and the Masters of Lodges.
Your committee take pleasure in calling attention to the fact that the reports
from the various Masonic Districts are more complete than in any former year; yet
it is a matter for regret that, notwithstanding what has been said from year to year
on .this subject, each .Annual Communication shows some Inspectors to be derelict in
their duty towards this Grand Lodge. This neglect deserves coustant censure, for

Bro. WILLIAM O. BELOHEB, from the Oommittee on Jurisprudence,
presented the following report :To the M.·. W." Grand Lodge of Ctilifornia :Bro. CHARLES E STONE, Master of Yuba Lodge, No, 39, proposes to amend Sec.
1, Art. I, Part II, of the Constitution, by adding a new paragraph, or subdivision, to
be numbered 9th, and to change the numbers of the subdivisions now numbered 9th
and 10th, to 10th and lltb, respectively. The paragraph proposed to be interpolated is as follows :9th. Upon the request ofa Master, to whom charges ofnnmasonic conduct against
a Mason have been presented, to transfer the trial of the accused from the Lodge
having jurisdiction by Teason of his membership or residence, to some ot)ler Lodge
to be named in his order, whenever, for the convenience of witnesses or other good
cause, such transfer is, in bis judgment, necessary or expedient; and to direct, in
case of such transfer, that the charges and the order of transfer be transmitted to

1884.]

Grand Lodg~ of California.

721

the Master of the L~dge to which such transfer shall be made; and that such

!Ifaster, upon the receipt thereof, shall proceed in the manner and form provided
m Art. IV, Part VI.

The purpose of this amendment is to provide that, when it is either necessary or
expedient, in t.he opinion of the Master to whom charges have been presented against
a m~mber of his Lodge or a Mason residing within its jurisdiction, the trial should be
had m some other Lodge, he may report to the Grand Master the circumstances
which render a change of the place of trial necessary or expedient, and request a
transfer; and that the Grand Master shall have the authority to direct that the case
be transferred to, and the trial be had in, some other Lodge.
The power to direct such change of the place of trial should be vested In some
officer of the Grand Lodge, and to none can it be so safely entrusted as tot.he Grand
Master. Your committee therefore recommend the adopt.ion of the amendment.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM C. BllLCHllR,}
N. GBBENE CURTIS,
LEONIDAS E PRATT,
Oommittell.

A ~lack B.ook, in some form, is certainly to be recognized as a necessity, and your

[Oct. 17,

The plan proposed by Bro. AARON wonld leave the record incomplete. It is true
that suspension for non-payment of dues may be only temporary, bnt then it also
may be perpetual. Whatever the time of its continuance, its effect, so long as it
lasts, is the same as suspension for any other cause-exclusion from all participation
in the aftairs of Masonry; and it would seem to be quite as important that we
should be advised of the present standing of one who had been suspended for that
cause as for any other. There can be no doubt that the record ought to be complete,
and that it ought to be written up promptly, on receipt of the Grand Secretary's
reports, In order to make it so. ·
The file of circulars proposed by Br(). REm would, In a short time, become practically useless as a means or ready reference, unless the Secretary should make and
keep up a complete index .thereof, which would cost as much labor as the Black
Book now does; and the file, even with such index, would be less convenient than the
present book.
Youi: committee can see no reason for adopting either of these propo sed amendments, unless It be to relieve the Secretary of a Lodge from a portion of the duties
now required to be performed by him. '.l'hat not being deemed a sufficient one, it
is reoommended that neither or the proposed amendments be adopted.

granted, and find that they conform to the requirements of the Constitution ; and

discretion. They therefore recommend that his action in the premises be approved.

Relative to the membership of Brother BENJAMIN W. SHEPHERD in Binoerity
Lodge, No.132:In 1878 Sincerity Lodge suspended Bro. SHEPHERD for non·pnyment of dues. An
appeal was taken to the Grand Lodge, and in 1879 the matter of his appeal was
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, and with it a memorial from him and
a letter .written by Bro. GEORGE W. BOYDEN, then Master of the Lodge, addressed to
the Masonic Board of Relief of San Francisco, in which the facts were fully detailed.
After an examination of the memorial and the letter, the committee reported, and
the Grand Lodge decided, that the suspension was without authority of law and void,
and that Bro. SHEPHERD was a life-member of the Lodgu in good standing, and most
be so returned by the Lodge.
In 1880 Bro. SoYDBN, being ·still Master, filed a statement with the Grand Secretary, In which, In elfect, he related that he had been misled in his former statement
by what he had beard and supposed to be trne,and asked the Grand Lodge to rescind
its former order. That request was refused,
Th.e Lodge now presents a memorial purporting to state the facts, giving copies
from its records, so far as they pertain to the matter In hand, and asking that a
rehearing be granted. Your committee have carefully examined this memorial
and find that the facts therein stated correspond very oloeely with the facts as
stated by Bro. BoYDEN in his letter to the Masonio Board of Relief, before mentioned, and show that· there was a contract and agreement, at the time of the
removal of t.he Lodge from Rich Bar to Taylorsville, that the members of the Lodge
at Rich Bar should, as a consideration for the removal, become In effect, if not
in words, life-members of the Lodge when removed-that is, that th•y should be
thenceforth exempt from dues.
It is evident from this memorial that such was the understanding of the members
of the Loage at Taylorsvllle, as well as of those at Rich Bar, although no formal action
was taken by the Lodge in the matter of changing its by-laws In such form as to
declare them life-members, or that they should be thenceforward exempt from the
payment of dues.
In their report in 1879, your committee thoaght, and still think, that the Lodge
was bound by tills contract, and that its action In 187~, in suspending Bro. SnBPHBBD
for non-payment of dues, was wholly unauthorized, and that it was the duty of the
Lodge to rescind itf action In respect to him.
It.appears from this memorial, as well as from the letter of Bro. BOYDEN, that
several of the members, who had formerly resided at Rich Bar, subsequently requested
the Lodge to again place their names upon the roll of paying members, and that
they were so placed, their does op to the time being remitted; bot that Bro. SHBP·
nERJJ never made such req nest.
The memorial further shows and states, as a reason for the action of the Lodge in
1878, that Bro. SHEPHERD had, prior to that time and prior to the removal of the
Lodge from Rioh Bar, been guilty of divers immoral and unmasonic acts for which
he poaslbly might, at the time, have been dealt with by his Lodge, but of which 00
notice had been taken. This, in our judgment, is no reason why the Lodge should
have suspended him at the time it did, and for the cause that wa" assigned for such
suspension. If there had been any reason why he should have been tried and suspended for unmasonio conduct, the law prescribed the course to b.e pursued. That
course the Lodge did not follow, and, if in this regard there was any fault, it was the
fault of the Lodge in allowing one of its members to maintain his membership under
sacb circumstances.
Your committee see no reason no.w for modifying in any respeot the order that

year; and they recommend that the reqnest for a rehearing in tJi.is matter ~e denied.

Bro. LEONIDAS E PRATT, from the same committee, presented the

To the M.·. W. •. Grand Lodge of California:·Onr1 Vesper Lodge, No. 8,, asks special permission to confer the second and third
degrees of Masonry upon Bro. JOHN HILLHOUSE, an Entered Apprentice of that
Lodge; and the facts upon which this somewhat novel and unnsual reqnest is based
are as follows:Bro. HILLHOUSE was elected to receive the three degrees in that Lodge, and, in
due time, the degree of Entered Apprentice was regularly conferred upon him. Soon
after this event, the hall, charter, and property generally of the Lodge were destroyed by fire, and the Lodge was compelled to, or at least it did, suspend work for
a period of several months. During this period the brother, while in the pnrsuit ofhis
usual avocation, lost a portion of his right hand, whereby he became "disabled
from conforming literally to what the several degrees respeotively require of him."
When the Lodge resumed work, the brother, in his then maimed condition,
reqnested that he be passed and raised. The I;odge, with a wholesome recollection
of onr hitherto rigid enforcement of the Eleventh Oeneral Regulation, which pre·
scribes the qualifications of candidates, donhted Its right to comply with his reqnest,
and now appeals to the Grand Lodge for instruction.
Your committee make the following snggestlons as furnishing, in their judgment,
a rational basis for the conclusion at which they have arrived:First-The Eleventh General Regulation, as they interpret it, does not by its
terms, nor in its spirit, preclude the brother's advancement. That Regulation, by
its own expression, applies only" to the person who desires to be made a Mason."
Bro. HILLHOUSE is not such a person 1 for he has already been made a Mason in the
true sense of that expresPlon. His status is mate;rially changed from that of a mere
profane, and we are bound to recognize the fact that, as an Entered Apprentice, he has
claims upon ns and certain, perhaps not very definite, yet still substantial, Masonic
rights which he did not before enjoy. It being tbus seen that the Regulation in .
itself presents no barrier to his advancement, the only remaining question is :-What
should be done with him upon the broad and general principles of Masonic right,
jnstice, and charity?
Second-It is apparently no fault of the brother that he did not receive the second
and third degrees before his misfortune befel him. If the work of the Lodge had
not been interrupted by disaster, he would probably have had no occasion to be here
now asking our favor or indnlgence.
Third-If w.e should now refuse to complete his Masonic education, we would
seem to be unjnst. We shall have gathered tribute from him without having given
him any equivalent therefor; for all will concede that the degree of Entered Appren·
tice alone can be of no possible benefit to him; but, on the contrary, that fact being
known and not explained, might possibly suggest a presumption that something wrong
in his character had barred his progress. Would it be just to leave him in that position for no fault of his own? The li!f4t which hi' has already received would thus be

1884.J

725

Grand Lodge of California.

made a source of disquiet to him, as it would but strengthen and stimulate the desire
which he had before he entered upon the ground floor of the Temple.
Fourth-By no possibility can we be harmed by now finishing the work. If he
should be unable to prove himself among strangers, by reason of his loss, he alone
will be the sufferer thereby. He will simply be in the same condition as the Mason
who might meet with a like misfortune, after having been passed and raised. We
should never dream of expelling the latter. Why should we inhibit the advancement. of the former?
Your committee think that it would be little less than cruel to add to the brother's
present misfortune' by withdrawing from him all Masonic consideration. Let him be
advanced then, unless there be some more cogent reasons why he should not be.
All which is respectfully submitted by
WILLIAM C. BBLOHBB,
N. GBEENB CUl\TIS,
LEONIDAS E PRATT,
CLAY W. TAYLOR,

Brp. ALVAH R. CONKLIN, from the Committee on Grievances, presented the following report :To the M. ·• W. •• <kand Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred the appeal of Cmi.NllLIUS VEBMASON, who
was expelled by Welcome Lodge, No. 255, on the seventh day of June, 1884, for unmasonic conduct, report that they have fully and patiently investigated the same,
and considered the evidence adduced before the commission and incorporated in thetrial-record in that case ; and find therefrom that the entire transaction between the
accuser and the accu8ed was of a purely business character-there being no evidence
to show that there was any moral turpitude, of any degree whatsoever, which should
have rendered the accused amenable to any of the penalties of the Masonic law.
Your committee are of the opinion that this Grand Lodge was not instituted for the
purpose of affording a channel through which transactions of every·day life in trade
and co"mmerce should be adjudicated-there being plentiful redress for such griev·
ances, if.any there be, in the courts of the country. They therefore offer the.follow•
ing resolution and recommend its adoption :R11solved, That the findings of the commiBBioners, and the subseqnent action of
Welcome Lodge, No. 256, in expelling Bro. CoBNELIUB V11RMASON, be reversed and
set aside, and that he be and is ~ereby restored to all his rights and privileges as a
member of that Lodge.
-All which is respectfully submitted by

Bro. ALVAH R. CONKLIN, from the same' committee, presented the
following report :.,To the M. ·• W.•• Grand. Lodge of Oalifornia :Your committee, to whom was referred the petition for restoration to all the
rights and privileges of Masonry of CHABLES HowABD GoBDON, of which he was
deprived by the findings of a commission convened by Woodbridge Lodge, No, 131,
on the sixteenth day of January, 1875, upon a charge of unmasonic conduct in
" accusing Bro. JAMBS P. FoLGllR. of participating in burning property at Mokelumne
Station," have given the proceedings of the trial-commisSion in that case a thorough
examination, and the facts introduced in evidence, as therein set forth, their earnest,
candid, and impartial consideration; and find as follows:That, from the testimony of one witness, the accused had made the declaration
"that they had burnt him out," and when asked who he meant by " they," replied,
" JIM FOLGER and others : "
That, to another witness, the accused had made the same declaration, and
that, upon the trial in a civil court, upon a criminal charge against one SMITH,
the accused had said, while under oath, "that he had stated that FOLGEB (among
others) had burnt hie butcher shop, and that he (the accuoer) believed it. That he
(the accuser) had been before the Grand Jury with the matter, but failed to get evi·
dence to sustain the charge, and that he had circulated the same report after being
before t}'e Grand Jury : "

1884.]

Grand Lodge of Oalifornw.

733

That, between the last witness and the accused some enmity existed, owing to
newspaper articles published, which accused had written:
That the evidence of the last witness is contradicted by a presumed credible witness holding an official position, and the former witneBB referred to is corroborated
by the testimony of one of the jurors.
This Is the substance of the evidence introduced before the Trial-Commission.
The record also exhibits the fact that, before any examination was had of the charges,
the accused, while denying them, expressed his willi.agness, for the sake of· harmony,
to tender to Bro. JAMES P. FOLGER an apology for any act, word, or deed of his
which he (FOLGBB) might consider injurious to him as a Mason or derogatory to him
as a man ; provided, tha.t Bro. F-OLGllR would also 11.pologize to him (the accused) for
the opprobious language used by him (FoLGBR) towards him (GORDON) in the pres·
ence of the Lodge.
In 1873 the case came before the Grand Lodge upon an appeal, and, on account
of some informality, was reversed and remanded to the Lodge for a new trial. .After
such re-trial, in 1874, it again came to the Grand Lodge upon an app~al, and was
again reversed and remanded. It was again tried in 1875, and, at the Annual Com·
munieation of the Grand Lodge for that year, the appeal was dismissed only for the
reason that sufficient notice of such appeal had not been given.
In 1876 a petition for a re-hearing of the case was presented to the Grand Lodge,
and the Committee on Grievances reported "that they regret that they are unable to
recommend a re-hearing of the case, owing _to a failure of the accused to give the
proper notice ; '' which report was concurred in.
In 1877 the accused applied to the Grand Lodge for restoration. The Committee
on Grievances fully set forth the case in their report, recommending the granting or
the petition ; which report the Grand Lodge refused to adopt.
In 1878 the accused again asked for restoration, and a majority of the committee
reported that, "though still holding to the opinion expreBBed by the previous com·
mittee in regard to the injustice of his (the accused's) expu]jiion, yet, after taking
the advice of prominent Masons, and in view of the continuous and bit&r opposition
to his restoration, it was for the best interest or Masonry that the prayer of the
petitioner should not be granted;'' which report was concurred in.
In 1879 he again applied for restoration, and there was a report from the Com·
mittee on Grievances, of which, as before, Bro. WM. T. RllYNOLDB was Chairman,
confeBBing that the previous report was erroneoUll, declaring that a gross injustice
had been done to the petitioner, and recommending that he be restored. A minority
and adverse report was made,urging the rejection or the petition upon the ground
that the expelling Lodge objected to the accused being restored; which last named
report was concurred in by the Grand Lodge.
In 1888 he again petitioned the Grand Lodge to be restored. The Committee on
Grievances recommended thjlt the petition be granted, but the Grand Lodge indefi·
niteJy postponed the consideration of the report.
.
And now again, brethren, is this matter before you for your determination. More
than a decade of years has passed by since this case had its birth, and it is still
accompanied by its previously attending oircumstances-persistency upon the part
of the petitioner in the assertion of the wrong which he thinks has been done to him
by Woodbridge Lodge, No. 131, and the almost traditionary feeling on behalf of that
Lodge in opposition to his restoration.
Your committee realize the fact that the opposition of the local Lodge to granting
this prayer, or any of a similar nature, has heretofore received; and, possibly, is
entilled to receive great weight and consideration ; but, while this may be true, it
should not be permitted to override our sense of justice, or infiuence ns to such an
extent as would stifie even the pleadings of mercy. They cannot convince themEelves that, under the evidence, the petitioner was guilty of such a Masonic offense

734

Proceblings of the

[Oct. 18,

as justified the decision of the commission. But should that decision have been
deemed to be right io the mind of this Grand Lodge, has it no ear for pity, and will
not the voice of charity and mercy towards a possibly erring brother find a willing
listener io a body whose cardinal principles involve those virtues?
One of the brethren, who is opposing this petition, remarked to your committee
that the time might come when Woodbridge Lodge would oooseot to this restoration.
But when? The petitioner has been followed with a heavy ha.od, aod the hatred aod
animosity evinced toward him seem to have been left as an inheritance; aod time,
which usually consigns all things to .oblivion, appears In this case to have forgotten
its customary habit. If the report of your committee be adopted, it will not restore
the petitioner to membership io Woodbridge Lodge, but only to the general rights
and privileges of Masonry. "Vengeance is mine," saith the Lord, aod this prerogative has oot yet been delegated to our body or to Masonry. "To err is human, to
forgive divine." "The quality of mercy is not strained." It blesses him who gives
as well as him who receives.
Eleven long years has the petitioner suffered and been weighed down under the
oppression of (as a former committee expressed it,) "a gross injustice." Is
this oot sufficient? The wrong appears to have been caused by a business rivalry,
aod found expression in the warmth and excitement of self-interest or Imagined
injury. In the spirit of those promptings which should, aod will, and do dominate
our better nature, with charity towards all, aod with the sincere belief that they
propose to do right and rectify that which they are convinced has been wrong, your
committee offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:.Resoloed, That the petition of CHA.BLBB HowARD GoBDON to be restored to all
the rights aod privileges of Masonry be aod is hereby granted.
All which Is respectfully submitted by
ALVAH R. CONKLIN, }

Bro. WILLIAM C. BELCHER, from the Committee on .Jurisprudence,
presented the following reports : To the M.-.

w.-. Grand. Lodge of Oalif'ornia : -

The Grand Lecturer reported last year that a Lodge•in the Twenty-third District
(Brooklyn, No. 225,) had received a petition for affiliation which was not accompanied by a dimit from the Lodge of which the petitioner had last been a member,
nor by any written statement lo explanation of its absence; and had, upon a favorable report of a committee of reference, balloted for and elected the petitioner, Subsequently, when requested, he refused to surrender his dimlt or to sign the by·laws of
the Lodge.
The special committee to which the Grand Lecturer's Report was referred, lu their
report, say of this matter :His membership with the Lodge is so plainly a matter of fact, lo the opinion of
your committee, that they feel ioclioed to recommend that chargee. be preferred
against him for refusing to comply with the by·la.ws of the Lodge • but as they have
not nofrequently heard .the opinion expressed by old Masons that a b;other did uot
become a .member of a Lodge until he ha.d signed Its by-laws, they suggeet the reference of this matter of membership to the Committee oo Jurisprudence.
The matter was so referred, and your committee now offer the following iu rela·
tion thereto : Our Constitution, lo Section 1, Article I, Part V, declares that membership iu a
·
Lodge may be acquiredlet. By having regularly received the degree of Master Mason therein :
2d. By having been duly eleoted for affiliation therewith:
. Sd. By having been named in a dispensation for a new Lodge as one of the peti·
boners therefor : aod
4th. By the coi:isolidation into oue Lodge of two or more Lodges, of oue of which
he was a member, 10 the manner prescribed lo Section 11, Article II, Part III.
The ways lu which membership may be acquired a.re distinctly set forth io the fore·
going section, aod nothing is requisite to constitute one a member except that whioh
is therein stated. He must have been regularly me.de a Master Mason io the Lodge, or
dtd~ el.ected by it for affiliation ; or he must have been named iu the dispensation by
which 1t was formed, or have been a member of a Lodge which had consolidated with
another or others. "Signing the by·laws " is not named as a thing necessary to be
done. It is usual aod very proper to require that every ooe shall, after becoming a
member, signify his assent to the by-laws by subscribing his name thereto ; but the
thing which is required to constitute membership by affiliation is that the party be
duly elected, and that is all.
Sections 13 aod 8, of Article III, Part III, of the Coustitntioo, advise what is
meant by the words "d•uly elected." By Section 13 the- inhibition is poeltive-" No

rn

736

ProceW.ings of the

[Oct. 18,

Lodge shall r'eceive an application for affiliation unless it be accompanied by a
proper dimit from the Lodge of which the applicant was last a member, or a satisfactory explanation in writing of bis lnabili'ty to furnish such dlmlt." Equally pos·
itive is the direction of Section 3, that no ballot upon such an application shall be
had until the petition shall have been referred, and that the petitioner cannot be
declared elected unless the ballot is clear.
Suppose, how.ever, that a Lodge does receive a petition, as in this case, without a
dimit or written explanation, and does refer the petition to a committee, and does
subsequently decl~re by a clear ballot its purpose to elect, and that the Mast~.r does
declare that he is elected, 11.nd that he does thereupon sign the by·laws. Is he then duly
elected and a member? Your committee think not. The Constitution says that the
Lodge shall nut receive such a petition. Hence it follows that all that was done by
the Lodge in connection with that petition wllB void, and that no one thing that was
done was dul,y done. The applicant was not duly elected, and hiK subsequent re·
fusal to surrender his dimit and sign the by·laws was not an offense, because the
Lodge had no right to the dimit, and he was under no obligation to surrender it or
sign any by-laws. Tbe fault was with the Master and bis Lodge.
Relative to decisions of the Grand Master upon questions of MllBonlc law. During
the year the Grand Master deoidedlst. In the absence of the Master and Wardens, a Past Masler bas no authority to
open a Lodge for the transaction of its ordinary business, or for any purpose, in the
absence of the Master and Wardens. One of those officers, presiding! m~y call upon
a Past Master, or any well informed Mason, to confer degrees or assist in the trans·
action of business.
,
Under our Constitution, Article Il, Part IV, the Master is the presiding and execu·
tive officer of the Lodge, and in-his absence the Wardens, In the order of their rank,
succeed to his powers and duties. A Pasl Master, as such, has no more authority
than any other member of the Lodge, and, In the absence of the Master and Wardens,
no member of the Lodge., except by direct authorization from the Grand Master, can
have authority to open the Lodge for any purpose.
2d. No judgment of conviction or acquittal can be rendered ~y tria}-commls·
sioners except when a majority of the whole number elected concur 1n the Judgment.
In the case presented to the Grand Master, seven commissioners bad been elected,
and five heard the evidence, Of these, at the final determination, two voted guilty,
three not guilty. The Master, upon receiving the record of this action of the com·
missioners, declared the result to be an acquittal, and directed judgment of acquittal
to be entered. The Grand Master promptly ordered that the judgment entered be
vacated, as entered without authority, and that a new commission be elected for the
trial of the accused; and very properly also ruled that no one of those who had acted
on the former commission was competent to serve upon the new one.
The decision and ruling were clearly rip:ht. The language of the Constitution, see
Section 8, Article IV, Part VI, Is-" The judgment of a majority of all the commis·
sioners shall be taken BS the decision of the whole." It is plain that a majority of
all the commissioners elected for the trial must concur before any judgment can be
declared. If seven a.re elected, four may try the c11Be, and, if they agree, may render
a decision; but, If they do not agree, the result is a mis-trial, and the duty or the Mas·
ter is to so declare it and order the election of a new commission. So it was ruled
in the Grand Lodge in the ca8e of BLUH- see Proceedings of 1882, page 647.
3d. If a Mason, who has become a permanent resident ~f this State but h~s
' retained his membership and paid his dues in the State from which he _came, dies, it
is the duty of the Lodge within whose jurisdic~ion be res_i~ed, to ~nry him as a Mason
should be buried, if he bad so requested , without wa1tmg to mqulre whether the

probably recognize its ollligation to repay, but the duty must be performed and
can not be made dependent upon any contingency.

The ruling commends itself as right, and it is humilla.ting to snppose that there is
any Lodge of Masons In California that would, if it could, avoid the performance of
such a duty.
4th. The MllBter may, in the proper exercise of his discretion, exclude from a
meeting of his Lodge one of its members who presents himself for admission in a
state of intoxication.
No one can doubt the correctness of the decision that the M11Bter may exclude an
intoxicated member. A. drunken man is an offence anywhere, aud a Masonic meeting
Is a place where the presence of or.o should by no means be tolerated. IC a member
of a Lodge has so far lost respect for himself and his Lodge as to present himself in
that condition for admission to one. of its meetings, your committee think that the
Master not only might exclude him, but that his duty to do so would be ciear, and
that his discretion would lie in determining whether the o1fence was of such a char·
acter as to deserve further action.
5th. When the Grand Lodge has reversed a judgment o! one of its subordinates
and ordered a new trial, a new trial must be had, and the Lodge has no power to
dismiss the charges or to take any action in the matter except to elect a new com·
mission.
Under our Constitution, Article IV, Part VI, charges are presented to the Master,
and he mast determine whether the acts complained of constitute a Masonic oftense;
and if in his judgment they do, he must convene his Lodge for the single purpose of
electing trial-commissioners. The commissioners try the cllBe and render judgment,
and the Master ~clares the jud11:ment and causes it to be entered. In no stage of
the caRe has the Lodge any authority to determine whether the case should or should
not be dismissed, and when a new trial has been ordered by the Grand Lodge, even
the Grand Master could not countermand that order.
6th. The Grand Master has no authority to authorize a Lodge to confer the three
degrees upon the same candidate in one evening.
This is plainly as prescribed in Section 9, Article III, Part Ill, of the Constitution,
in which it Is declared that no Lodge "shall confer more than one degree upon any
one candidate at any one meeting."
7th. A Lodge in California has no authority to receive a petition for affiliation
·
from a Mason residing in another State.
The Grand M;aster found no express provision of our Constitution to govern the
case, still his conclusion was that the reception of such a petition would be an invasion of the rlg!its of another jurisdiction, and your committee approve his ruling.
8th. The Master of a Lodge has no anthority to open his Lodge at any other than
its llJlpointed plaoe, even for the purpotie of conducting a funeral. He should open
his Lodge in its Lodge-room, and proceed thence to the place where the funeral service is to be performed.
Your committee believe this ruling to be correct, as the charter of a Lodge gives
the name of the place where only it can exist as such.
9th. When a Lodge has heard objections made to the advancement of a candidate,
and bas determined by a proper vote that the cause assigned is not a valid and
Masonic one, the Master should not allow the same objection to be made a second
time.
Section 6, Article III, Part III, of the Constitution, prescribes exactly what shall
be done when an objection is made to the advancement of a candidate by any member of a Lodge. A committee must be appointed to inquire into the cause of the
objection. The duty of the party interposing the objection is to present before that
committee his cause of objection and the evidence to sustain it. That committee
must report to the Lodge, lind upon .t hat report, if a cause has been assigned, the
Lodge must netermine whether the cause be a valid and Masonic one. The deter·
mination of the Lodge is a final judgment upon the matter, and your committee think,

with the Grand Master, that the Master should not permit the same objection to lie
a second time brought before the Lodge; and further, that neither the Master nor
the Lodge has authority to entertain the objection a second time. If the objector,
for any reason, should need time to produce evidence,"the Lodge can and should
grant all the time necessary, but the judgment of the Lodge, once declared, should
be final.

11th. The Master has authority, at the request of the accuser, to dismiss charges

Our Constitution, Article IV, Part VI, makes the Master the judge, and imposes

In the Colony of Victoria, (Australia,) a Grand Lodge was formed on the second
day of July, 1883, with the M.·. w.·. GEORGE SELTH COPPIN as Grand Master, and the
R.·. W>. HENBY W. HOLLOWAY as Grand Secretary. There were at the time in that
Colony ninety-five Masonic Lodges, holding charters from the Grand Lodges of Eng·
land, Scotland, and Ireland. Only fl~en of those Lodges participated in the form&•
tion of the new Grand Lodge. Of these, one was English, six Scotch, and eight
Irish.
.
In the preceding month of April twelve Past M11stera had organized a Masonic
Union, "baving for its object the formation of a Grand Lodge of Victoria." That
Union s'nt circulars to tbe Lodges inviting their cooperation, but the proposition
does not seem to have been favorably received; and at the Convention which met on
the nineteenth day of June following, only fifteen out of the ninety.five Lodges in
the Colony were represented. A pamphlet was presented and circulated among all
the Lodges, in which the law iu regard to the formation of Grand Lodges is stated
in this wise:It is laid down in Masonic jurisprudence, and is an accepted landmark, that a
law of territory exists that the bonudar!ea of each terrlt~ry ar~ defined by generally
accepted national or natural eurroundmgs, that the said territory Is sacred to t.he
Grand Lodge existing therein, and that no other Grand Lodge has power to exesc1se
any authority within the boundaries. Indeed, so thorough is this principle that,
although in a country.where no Grand Lodge exists an}'. G~and Lodge of the world
baa a right to issue a warrant for a subordinate or Provmc1al Grand Lodge to meet
there, yet, upon the formation of a Grand Lodge within the ~rritory, all other Grand
Lodges Jose their right of jnrisdiction, and the Lodges acting under their warrants
must join the newly formed Grand Lodge and submit to its authority, or disband and
close their Lodges. This law of territory is undoubtedly founded upon good and
sufficient grounds, and has been thoroughly aocepted at all times, as witness Eng·
land, Scotland, Ireland, America, France, and every other country.
This law or territory also provides that any three duly warranted Lodges can meet
and form the Grand Lodge for the territory-thus fully complying with the require·
menta of the case. Therefore, three or more Lodges meeting in Victoria. can at any
time resolve to form a Grand Lodge of Victoria, according to established custom and
precedent.
Bro. FARNELL, the Grand Master of the Grand J,odge of New South Wales, and
Bro. MANNING, .his Deputy, attended the inauguration ceremonies, Bro. MANNING
officiating as Installing Officer; and at the .banquet Bro. FARNELL, upon this point,
said : "It is an inherent right of any number of Lodges, not being less than three,
within the geographical limits of any colony, such as New South Wales or Victoria,
to establish a Grand Lodge."
There is a certain coolness of assertion and ignoring of facts and history in the
paragraph above quoted that is ooneid~rably refreshing, and not a little surprising.
Your committee do not understand that it is an accepted landmark or general law
of Masonry, or that "it is an inher~nt right of any number of Lodges, not being Iese
than three," to establish a Grand Lodge in any State, Province, or Colony where no
Grand Lodge has been established; nor that necessarily," upon the formation of a
Grand Lodge " by three or more Lodges, all other Grand Lodges lose their right of
jurisdlctiou over 1.iodl\'es then qqlqing cha.rte!'!! or warrants from ihem; 11or that all

1884.J

Grand Lodge of OaJ,ifornia:

741

" Lodges acting under their warrants must join the newly formed Grand Lodge and
submit to its authority or disband."
It is certain that the Grand Lodge of England has never recognized any such law,
for it still maintains one Lodge in the Province of Ontario, within the territory of the
Grand Lodge of Canada, and recognized that Grand Lodge upon the express condition that Lodges holding its warrants and choosing to continue to work under
them, should be allowed so to do; and it still maintains more than one Lodge in the
Province of Quebec, o.nd has thus far refused to recognize the Grand Lodge of that
Province beoause of its insistence that all Lodges working under English warrants
must surrender them and submit to its authority. It is certainly new doctrine to
assert that three, or fifteen, or any number less than a majority of all, can, by form·
ing a Grand Lodge, compel the majority to submit to their authority or close their
doors.
It is recognized in the United States that when there are but three Lodges in a
State or Territory, the three may form a Grand Lodge, and that the Grand Lodge
thus formed will take and exercise exclusive jurisdiction over the terrlt<11;Y; but it
is not recognized or even asserted that, if there were twenty chartered Lodges in a
given territory, three of the twenty could even form a Grand Lodge, much less that,
having formed one, they conld compel the seventeen others to submit or close their
doors. We believe in the right of the majority to rule, but have never yet recognized
the doctrine that a small minority had the right to assume the mauag11ment of the
affairs of Masonry or of the Stl\te.
It is plain that a Colony with ninety five Lodges and it may be ten thousand
Masons ought to have an independent Masonic as well as political governm&nt, but,
in order to make such a government successful, it must have the cheerful support of
at least the majority.
Although your committee cannot approve the manner of Its formation, or its
present claims to exclusive jurisdiction, they will hope, for the good of the Craft
there and elsewhere, that the new Grand Lodge of Victoria may soon win to its sup·
port not only a majority but all the Lodges and Masons of that Colony; and that it
may entitle Itself to ask and receive the recognition of the mother Grand r,odges,
and then of all others. It is recommended that no action in the matter be taken at
this time by this Grand Lodge.
On the thirtieth day of July, 1888, a considerable number of Masons met at
Adelaide, South Australia, at the published call of Bro. H. M. ADDISON, a Past Master
of Harmony Lodge, No. 505, E. C., "to discuss e subject of the gravest importanoe
concerning the progress of Freemasonry in this Province.''
At the meeting a resolution proposed by Bro. ADDISON," that, in the opinion of
this meeting, It is desirable that a Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
South Australia be formed, a:id that Immediate steps be taken to that end," was
unanimously adopted, and ~ Masonic Union was formed, with Bro. ADDISON as its
Chairman, to take the necessary steps. Circulars were sent to all the Lodges, re·
questing them to take act.ion in the matter, and to all the members, so far as their
names and addresses could be ascertained, asking them to become members of the
Union and favor the project.
There were at the time in the Colony thirty-three Lodges, with a membership
exceeding .t wo thousand. Of these Lodges, twenty held charters under the Grand
Lodge of England, seven under the Grand Lodge oflreland, aod six under the Grand
Lodge of i!cotland. The question of the expediency and propriety of organizing a
Grand Lodge was most thoroughly canvassed in the Lodges and among the members,
and the result was that a very large majority of the memb~rs became memben of
the Union; and when the subject was brought before the Lodges for their official
~ction, twenty.eight Lodges voted unanimously, one with only one, and another with

and elected delegates to a Convention for that purpose. No official report was

On the sixteenth day of April, 1884, the Convention was held, twenty-eight Lodges
being represented by their delegates. and the Grand Lodge of South Au•tralia was
farmed and organized, with the M.·. W.·. SAMUEL JAMES WAY, the Chief Justice of the
Colony, as Grand Master, and the V.·. W.·. J. H. CUNNINGHAM as Grand Secretary.
It is evident that the time had come when it was expedient to form a Grand Lodge
for that Colony. The preliminary steps were taken in the right spirit. From the
very outset it was announced by the Union that they would not attempt to form a
Grand Lodge unless a large majority of the Lodges and Masons of the Colony 'vere
in favor of It, and that, if any Lodge should desire to continue its existing allegianoe,
there would be no attempt to interfere with it. At the meeting of delegates the
following resolution was unanimously adopted:Resolved, That all LodgeR holding warrants from the Grand Lodges of England,
Ireland. and Scotland shall be deemed legitimate. and if thev so elect, they may be
allowed to continue their allegiance to their parent Constitutions.
The Grand Lodges of England, Ireland, and Scotland have always insisted, and
very properly as we think, that in case of the formation of a Grand Lodge in terri·
tory occupied by their Lodges, the right of any on'e of their Lodges to continue its
allegiance must be respected. The new Grand Lodge of South Australia recognize&
that right. and your committee cannot doubt that those Grand Lodges will promptly
and cbeerfnlly recognize and enter into· friendly relations with that new Grand
Lodge. They will recognize the fact stated by Grand Master WAY in his Address,
that the Grand Lodge of South Australia has ·been established with the coneurrence
of the three Constitutions and of all the Lodges in that great Oolony, save two, and
with the practically unanimous sanction of all the Masons of the Colony: and that the
time had come when it was expedient and proper that the new Grand Lodge should
he established.
Your committee think that this new Grand Lodge should he recognized as a just
and duly formed Grand Lodge, hut that the right to extend such recognition belongs
first to the Grand Lodges by whose subordinates it was formed; and, having full
confidence that those Grand Lodges will promptly extend such recognition, it is,
with some reluctance, recommended that DO action be taken at this time by our
Grand Lodge.
